items.title: Detecting Primordial Black Holes By The Stars They Destroy
items.blurb: Astrophysicists wonder if primordial black holes could be part, or maybe all, of dark matter. They're theorized to have formed immediately after the Big Bang from pockets of dense matter. New research shows how they might be detected: in the bbright flash generated by the stars they consume from the inside out.

items.title: Ultra-Thin "Rainbow" Sails Could Power Spacecraft and Shade the Earth
items.blurb: For years, whimsically minded space enthusiasts have been dreaming of sailing across the vastness of the void on beams of sunlight. Photons, the massless particles that make up those beams of sunlight, still carry momentum, and can therefore impart a gentle push when they bounce off a surface. This force is the concept behind “solar sailing”, which has been having a bit of a moment in the last decade as several proof-of-concept flights have shown it is indeed actually feasible. Now a new paper, available in pre-print on arXiv from researchers at the Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT), has unveiled a clever technique that will allow these giant sails to steer sideways using a technology more commonly associated with flat-screen displays.

items.blurb: LISA, the ESA's Laser Interferometry Space Antenna, is being built to detect gravitational waves emitted when massive objects spiral together and merge. New research shows that exoplanets can exert a small but perceptible tug on those objects, leaving a signature on the gravitational waves. In some cases, LISA should be able to detect their signatures.

items.title: Bacteria and Nuclear Power Could Grow Ready-Made Homes on Mars Before Astronauts Arrive
items.blurb: As we gear up to eventually land a human on Mars, more and more ideas are coming out about how to prepare for that. A recent one from Pioneer Labs, a research institute founded by bioengineer Erika DeBenedictis to develop biological technologies for space exploration, is now available on arXiv, without any plans to release it in a paid journal as part of the “Open Science” policy of The Astera Institute, who funded the research. It details “Mars Seed” - a new architecture that is self-contained and can produce a full 870 sq meters of pressurized habitat using nothing but Martian inputs within roughly every four Earth years.

Scientists found evidence that a massive rotating structure near the galactic center is creating powerful shock waves that trigger star formation rather than suppress it. Even more unexpectedly, part of the Norma spiral arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a vast region where new stars are being born.

items.title: Two monster black holes from the dawn of time defy explanation

Weighing an astonishing 1.5 billion and 400 million times the mass of the Sun, these cosmic giants somehow grew to incredible sizes far earlier than current theories can explain.

items.title: Interstellar solar sails hit a bizarre problem at 75% of light speed
items.blurb: Scientists have discovered a surprising obstacle to interstellar travel: at extreme speeds, the light propelling futuristic solar sails could actually begin slowing them down. Once a spacecraft reaches 75% of the speed of light, some scattered light starts producing drag, potentially complicating humanity’s plans to reach distant stars.

items.title: A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded
items.blurb: Massive stars may be quietly collapsing into black holes without ever producing the spectacular supernova explosions scientists typically expect. A surprising pattern in 257 black hole mergers suggests these mysterious stellar disappearances could explain the origins of a large population of black holes throughout the universe.

items.blurb: An image from NASA's Hubble Space Telescope of galaxy cluster MACS J0417 is part of repeated observations to monitor for the reappearance of supernova Athena, which can help astronomers measure the expansion rate of the universe.

items.title: A nearly 100-million-year-old hairy snail pays tribute to the Prodigy's lead singer
items.blurb: Myanmar amber (more commonly known as "burmite") is one of the most important sources of information about biodiversity during the Mesozoic Era. This amber dates back to the age of the dinosaurs and is approximately 99 million years old. Burmite preserves numerous now-extinct organisms (animals, plants, fungi, etc.) as inclusions, often in astonishing detail. This is because amber can preserve even soft tissues, which would otherwise decompose rapidly, and do so in three dimensions.

items.title: A cactus that changes gears: How the prickly pear makes the most of desert rain
items.blurb: In the desert, water doesn't arrive steadily. It comes in short pulses: a winter storm, a few rainy days, then months of drought. A desert plant needs two skills to live there. It has to survive the long dry spells, and it has to make full use of the brief windows when water is plentiful. A new study from Ben-Gurion University of the Negev and the Volcani Institute shows that the prickly pear cactus has an unexpected way of doing both.

items.title: Overlooked symmetry group offers new geometric blueprint for the Standard Model and topologically protected vacuums
items.blurb: For more than half a century, physicists searching for a grand unified theory have followed one unspoken rule: go bigger. If you want to weave nature's fundamental forces into a single mathematical framework, the classic recipe says you need a giant "simple" symmetry group—structures like SU(5) or SO(10) that act like massive algebraic warehouses large enough to hold every force at once.

items.title: A hidden link between a flower's color and its scent revealed
items.blurb: Researchers discovered that the biological machinery behind flower color also helps shape fragrance. By disrupting a single gene in petunias, they changed the flowers' mix of scent compounds, increasing some associated with vanilla and cloves.

The larger Didymos asteroid—dominated by its dramatic equatorial ridge—is seen here from just 28.5 km (17.7 miles) away, variously in visible light, multispectral and thermal infrared vision.

items.title: Data center policy review reveals 'chaotic' patchwork of rules across all 50 states

Underlying these debates is the question of whether state and local governments should ban them outright, welcome them with open arms or choose something in between.

items.title: Satellite observations show how rain breaks up Earth's natural sunshades
items.blurb: Delivering on its promise, the European Space Agency's EarthCARE satellite is already yielding new insights into the role that clouds play in regulating Earth's climate. The latest findings shed light on one of the processes that leads to the breakup of vast, bright cloud formations that help keep our planet cool—with rain emerging as a key driver.

items.title: Some people claim to speak many languages. But what does it really mean to be a polyglot?

items.title: Stellar pulses reveal hidden binary in JWST calibration star sample
items.blurb: Stars used to calibrate the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) must have precisely characterized spectra so that their fluxes can be measured accurately. Yet some stars that appear single may in fact harbor unresolved companions that alter their predicted radiation. One such object, HD 158485—an A-type star in the JWST calibration program—has now been shown to be a binary system whose two stars both pulsate.

items.title: Which pollen is found in honey? Automated analysis closely matches conventional testing
items.blurb: Pure rapeseed honey—or not quite? Single-flower honeys must contain a certain proportion of pollen from the respective plant. This is assessed by pollen analysis, which is time-consuming and requires specialist expertise. As part of a collaborative project, a research team from the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research (UFZ) and the German Centre for Integrative Biodiversity Research (iDiv) in Leipzig worked with several partners to develop an automated, AI-based pollen analysis method for honey testing.

items.title: Discovery of curse ritual in trash dump surprises Egyptologist: 'It must have been widespread in ancient Egypt'
items.blurb: The discovery of 40 charred papyrus fragments at a temple in the ancient city of Thebes is changing researchers' understanding of one of ancient Egypt's most famous curse rituals. The fragments show that the ritual was probably far more widespread and commonplace than previously believed.

items.title: A fungus that can survive in Chernobyl could help create materials that trap and break down nerve agents and pesticides

It's set to intensify dangerous heat and cause severe drought across parts of Africa. This is likely to mean more heat-related illness and deaths, worsening water shortages and greater disruption to electricity, food supplies and essential services.

items.blurb: Turning genes on and off requires transcription factors—proteins that bind specific stretches of DNA and help control gene activity. But DNA is not laid out bare inside the nucleus. It is wrapped around proteins and folded into chromatin, which can make some regions easier to reach than others.

But a new study conducted by researchers from the School of Biological Sciences at The University of Hong Kong (HKU), together with international collaborators, reveals seasonal leaf changes hidden within this seemingly constant canopy. Largely undetected by conventional satellite observations, these changes have significant implications for estimating the rainforest's carbon uptake.

items.title: When the upwelling failed, Panama's fish oil trade collapsed within months
items.blurb: A year after scientists at the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute (STRI) in Panama reported the first recorded failure of the Gulf of Panama's seasonal upwelling, a follow-up study now documents how that failure moved through the system, from wind to plankton to fish to exports, using records that fishing companies rarely share.

The discovery challenges centuries of historical assumptions and suggests that a largely forgotten female leader may have changed the course of British history.

items.title: Robot submarine exploring world's deepest ocean trench finds unprecedented volcanic activity
items.blurb: Fifty-two million years ago, the Pacific tectonic plate began to slide under the Philippine Sea plate, forming the Mariana Trench, the deepest known valley on the Earth's ocean floor. The deepest part of this abyss, the Challenger Deep, is almost 11,000 meters (36,000 feet) below sea level. But why is it so deep? Scientists trying to answer this question sent a remotely operated vehicle to collect samples around the Deep, where they found evidence of the world's deepest underwater explosive volcanic eruptions.

items.title: This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s
items.blurb: A tiny California trapdoor spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome roughly 50% larger than a human's, despite being only about the size of a quarter. Scientists discovered that its enormous genome contains 4.6 billion DNA base pairs and 52 chromosomes, revealing surprising clues about spider evolution.

items.title: Mice slept 70% less after scientists switched off these brain cells
items.blurb: Scientists have discovered brain cells that actively generate the irresistible urge to sleep, and shutting them down allowed mice to sleep 70% less than normal. Remarkably, many of the animals avoided the severe behavioral consequences of sleep deprivation, raising intriguing possibilities for future sleep research.

items.blurb: The United States has lost its measles elimination status after more than 25 years, and a new survey reveals widespread misconceptions about the deadly disease and its vaccine. With measles cases surging, more than one-third of Americans still believe or are uncertain about the debunked vaccine-autism link, while most don't know the disease's risks or how many vaccine doses children need.

items.title: Scientists discover a surprising link between weak bones and faster brain aging
items.blurb: Weakening bones may reveal more about brain health than scientists previously realized, with new research linking lower spinal bone density to faster cognitive decline and accelerated changes in the brain's white matter. The surprising connection suggests that routine medical scans could help uncover hidden warning signs of brain aging and identify people at increased risk of dementia.

items.title: Cross-species dissemination of diverse plasmid lineages and mobile resistance modules shapes carbapenemase co-production in Chilean Enterobacterales
items.blurb: Carbapenemase co-production among Enterobacterales is an emerging clinical challenge, yet the relative contributions of clonal expansion, cross-species plasmid dissemination, and movement of resistance modules remain unclear. We integrated national surveillance data with plasmid-resolved hybrid genomes to investigate these processes in Chile. Among 414 isolates carrying at least two carbapenemase families referred during 2018-2024, annual numbers increased markedly alongside broader taxonomic and geographic representation. Thirty isolates were selected to span variation in year, species, region, and carbapenemase profile. These represented 11 species from six genera and contained 149 complete plasmids, 57 of which carried carbapenemase genes. Of 63 carbapenemase gene copies, 62 were plasmid-borne, and 55 of the 57 carbapenemase-carrying plasmids were predicted to be conjugative or mobilizable. Complementary plasmid typing, whole-sequence clustering, structural comparisons, and pan-plasmidome analysis identified three recurrent lineages: IncX3/blaNDM-7, IncN/blaKPC-2, and IncHI2A/blaVIM-1. Their occurrence across multiple species and sequence types supported cross-species dissemination, while numerous minor groups and singletons revealed a broader repertoire of plasmid architectures and accessory genes. Related backbones carried variable resistance regions, and equivalent class 1 integrons and transposon-associated platforms occurred in otherwise unrelated plasmids, indicating modular redistribution of carbapenemase genes. In selected isolates, co-resident plasmids created resistance redundancy, brought recurrent carbapenemase plasmid lineages together, or coupled resistance and virulence within the same cell. Thus, co-production did not arise through a single route: bacterial clones, plasmids shared across species, and mobile resistance modules each contributed to its emergence. Complete plasmid resolution is essential to distinguish these processes and track their dissemination.

items.title: Hyphosphere Hunting Grounds: Fungal Hyphae Guide a Protist Predator to its Bacterial Prey
items.blurb: Interactions between microeukaryotes mediated by prokaryotic intermediaries remain poorly understood. Here, we show that the hyphae of a plant pathogen guide bacterivorous protists into bacterial habitats, transforming a fungal dispersal route into a potential hunting ground. Although fungal hyphae are established dispersal corridors for bacteria, their capacity to guide individual protist cells remains largely unexplored. Time-lapse imaging of Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. vasinfectum Race 4 revealed bacteria and the flagellate Paracercomonas sp. moving bidirectionally along hyphae with significant axial alignment, despite contrasting motility regimes: rapid, superdiffusive bacterial movement and slower, subdiffusive protist movement. The ciliate Paracolpoda steinii also exhibited directional alignment along an inert glass rod, demonstrating that physical geometry can bias protist movement independently of fungal-specific cues. Across successive generational culturing of hyphal-baits, protist communities converged reproducibly toward Paracolpoda dominance, whereas bacterial assembly was largely stochastic, revealing contrasting assembly processes within the same habitat. In a dual-microcosm assay, fungal bridges enabled bacteria and protists to cross a 3 mm air gap, while the presence of P. steinii reduced bacterial arrival approximately 8-fold, consistent with predator-associated filtering. Together, these findings extend the fungal-highway concept beyond microbial transport, identifying pathogenic fungal hyphae as multi-kingdom ecological corridors where physical guidance, community assembly and predator-associated effects on dispersal intersect.

items.title: Robust parameter estimation and dose-fractionation for ptychographic single-particle analysis at near-atomic resolution
items.blurb: We present a complete workflow for the determination of biomolecular structures by single-particle cryogenic electron microscopy using ptychography. To account for the prominent dose damage in biological specimens dose-fractionated data acquisition and processing are introduced. Automated preprocessing techniques estimate the probe shape and scanning geometry before the ptychographic reconstruction by utilising the shadow image inside the Ronchigram. Standard ptychographic single-particle analysis is performed using tobacco mosaic virus, apoferritin and hepatitis B virus capsids. We finally give a demonstration of dose-fractionated ptychography utilising multiple scans of the same area at low dose reaching near-atomic resolution (3.3 [A]), allowing for the automated building of atomic models.

items.title: The mechanism of regulation of prokaryotic Na+ channels by their C-terminal domain
items.blurb: Prokaryotic voltage-gated Na+-channels (BacNaVs) closely resemble neuronal NaV channels in their structure and gating behavior and are found in multiple bacterial lineages, yet little is known about their biological function. In NaVSp1 from the marine bacterium Ruegeria pomeroyi, the cytoplasmic C-terminal domain (CTD) was proposed to function as a temperature sensor. Here, we use electrophysiology and computational methods to establish how the CTD can tune the temperature- and voltage-dependence of the NaVSp1 channel. We show that although the CTD of NaVSp1 is not a temperature sensor, its conformational dynamics are directly coupled to the gating of the pore. Additionally, we find that interactions between the CTD and the transmembrane domain can reduce or completely suppress the response of NaVSp1 to temperature by stabilizing the open state of the channel. Although BacNaV channels share low sequence identity in their CTDs, we provide evidence suggesting that most are structurally similar to NaVSp1 through the mining and modeling of more than 800 sequences from distinct bacteria. The mechanism we described could therefore be important for BacNaV channel regulation in response to environmental factors like temperature in a wide number of bacterial species.

items.title: Free-edge mechanics and hydrodynamic coupling shape membrane remodeling after pore opening
items.blurb: Membrane remodeling after pore opening occurs in electroporation, vesicle rupture, intracellular delivery, and pathogen escape from host cells. During this process, a pore may expand or close while the surrounding membrane curls at the rim, forms a neck, or everts. Using a sharp-interface framework for open membranes in Stokes flow, we study how free-edge elasticity and the dissipation mechanism determine post-opening remodeling. The model combines Helfrich bending, Gaussian-curvature and line energies, and local area inextensibility with viscous dissipation in the membrane and the surrounding fluid. We compare it with a local-drag model driven by the same energy over a range of line tensions, Gaussian rigidities, and spontaneous curvatures. Starting from a spherical cap, the membrane first adjusts near the rim as it relaxes toward the free-edge moment condition. The subsequent pore dynamics depend strongly on line tension, with trajectories that either continue to expand or reverse and shrink. Gaussian rigidity changes the rim orientation; for positive Gaussian rigidity, a pronounced internal neck develops behind an outward-moving free edge. Increasingly negative spontaneous curvature localizes deformation near the rim and, at sufficiently negative values, causes the first complete rim turn to precede cap inversion. Hydrodynamic and local-drag simulations can dissipate similar amounts of energy while following different shape trajectories, so in the strongly curved regime the pathway depends on the dissipation model as well as on the energy. Together, the edge tangent angle, neck radius, cap depth, and the relative timing of rim rolling and cap inversion provide measurable geometric signatures that distinguish post-opening remodeling pathways beyond the pore radius.

items.title: Dependence-Aware Conformal Prediction for 3D Uncertainty Quantification in Molecular Docking
items.blurb: Molecular docking plays a critical role in drug discovery by predicting three-dimensional (3D) binding poses of small molecules within proteins. However, docking predictions can contain substantial positional errors, making reliable uncertainty quantification essential. Conformal prediction (CP) provides a principled framework for uncertainty quantification, yet constructing compact 3D prediction regions with reliable joint coverage remains challenging due to heterogeneous atomic errors, dependence among spatial coordinates, and distribution shifts. We develop a dependence-aware CP framework for molecular docking that leverages a shared graph neural network (GNN) to estimate adaptive, asymmetric uncertainty intervals using local atomic and global molecular information. Copula-based joint calibration accounts for dependence among coordinate-wise nonconformity scores to construct compact 3D prediction boxes. We further introduce density ratio estimation (DRE) to adapt calibration under distribution shift. Experiments across three docking methods demonstrate that our approach reduces median prediction-box volumes by 37.40%, 95.00%, and 39.16% for AutoDock Vina, Protenix, and MedusaGraph, respectively, compared with a state-of-the-art CP baseline, while achieving empirical joint coverage close to the 90% target. Under the Molecular Group Split and controlled distribution shifts, DRE further reduces coverage deviations, highlighting the potential of dependence-aware and shift-adaptive calibration for reliable 3D molecular docking uncertainty quantification.

items.title: siGMA: Modeling Label Noise and Heterogeneity in siRNA Efficacy Prediction
items.blurb: Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) have emerged as a powerful class of therapeutics, yet identifying viable candidates remains costly and labour-intensive given the vast combination space that must be screened. This challenge is compounded by the need for chemical modifications, which are essential to mitigate off-target effects and enhance serum stability but frequently come at the expense of baseline knockdown efficacy. As a result, siRNA design requires careful, iterative optimization, further expanding the experimental burden and rendering exhaustive screening impractical. Computational prediction offers a compelling alternative, enabling rapid, low-cost identification of promising candidates prior to wet-lab validation. In this work we present siGMA, a heteroscedastic multimodal predictive model that integrates sequence, chemical, structural, and experimental information to predict the silencing efficacy of chemically modified siRNAs. Modelling in this domain is constrained by two principal obstacles: the scarcity of experimental data and the substantial noise arising from protocol heterogeneity across publicly available datasets. We therefore propose a model that quantifies predictive uncertainty rather than issuing confident mispredictions. We calibrated the model against such noise using a combined aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty prediction. The resulting model yielded well-calibrated estimates of predictive variability on held-out folds across datasets and outperformed current state-of-the-art approaches across noisy cross-dataset conditions, including previously unseen chemical modifications and target sequences. This demonstrates our model's ability to rank better than the baselines while rendering the noise ceiling measurable. This provides a scalable framework that could accelerate the therapeutic siRNA development pipeline while reducing the need for exhaustive empirical screening.

items.title: A2Holo: Dual-Stream Flow Matching of 3D Structure and a Protein Language Model for Conformational Transition Prediction
items.blurb: Modelling a ligand-bound holo conformation from a ligand-free apo conformation is essential in structure-based drug discovery. We present A2Holo, which casts apo-to-holo prediction as flow matching between two experimental structures rather than generation from noise. It transplants the dual-stream joint attention of in-context image generation to residue-aligned protein language model embeddings and structure. Without ligand conditioning or stochastic sampling, A2Holo's single deterministic trajectory reaches a median C RMSD of 0.809 [A] on the D3PM benchmark, the lowest among existing methods. Its TM-score exceeds even the best of 10 samples from every stochastic baseline on at least 144 of 150 pairs. Beyond performance, we directly measure the transplanted multimodal mechanism itself. Because sequence and structure are residue-aligned, its joint attention can be measured at residue resolution and tested for reproducibility across independently trained model variants. Within the structure stream, the attention a residue receives recovers moving residues better than the attention it emits, and this asymmetry is learned. A2Holo demonstrates a successful multimodal transplant from in-context image generation to protein conformational change, with strong deterministic apo-to-holo prediction. It also provides a quantitative account of how that mechanism organises residue-aligned sequence and structure around the residues that move.

items.title: Myosin II-FAK-paxillin Signaling Governs Mechanosensitive Responses of Neuronal Cells to Magnetic Stimulation
items.blurb: Recent work has highlighted transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) as a promising, non-invasive therapeutic approach for a variety of diseases such as Parkinsons disease (PD). Magnetic stimulation (MS) causes action potentials that result in dopamine release and increases in neuroplasticity. While secretion and the electrophysiology of MS have been well characterized, other downstream effects of MS are unknown. Here we characterize a mechanotransduction pathway that is activated in response to MS in a dopaminergic cell line (N27-A). Integrin tension was measured using DNA-based integrin tension sensors (ITSs), and cytoskeletal and focal adhesion structure was quantified in response to pharmacological inhibitors and activators of common mechanotransduction pathways. MS enhances ITS rupture in N27-A cells in a dose dependent manner. Additionally, both pulse frequency and number control ITS rupture. The ITS rupture that MS causes occurs through both cell migration-independent and -dependent mechanisms. Furthermore, MS enhances integrin forces in N27-A cells through a myosin II- and FAK-dependent pathway by creating more internal adhesions with increased phosphorylated paxillin. This work definitively demonstrates that MS can cause robust changes in mechanotransduction, which likely regulate neuroplasticity and provide an addition mechanism to explain the efficacy and potential of TMS therapy.

items.title: Rho family GTPase crosstalk through shared positive and negative feedback mechanisms underlies cytokinetic F-actin waves
items.blurb: Cortical excitability, characterized by the rapid polymerization and de-polymerization of cortical F-actin, has been reported in a variety of systems and cell types. In X. laevis, C. elegans, and echinoderm embryos, these oscillations are dependent on the small GTPase, Rho, which is regulated in turn by F-actin dependent negative feedback. We sought to investigate whether the Rho family GTPases, Cdc42 and Rac, contribute to specific regulation of F-actin waves and what feedback drives these dynamics. Using an artificial cortex system consisting of Xenopus egg extract and supported lipid bilayers, we showed that active Cdc42 and active Rac are dynamically patterned in a manner that is coordinated with active Rho and F-actin, suggesting that they contribute to the previously defined oscillatory circuit. We found that total Cdc42 and Rac cortical activity depends on Rho activity. Conversely, Rho activity and F-actin wave dynamics are modulated by Cdc42 and Rac activity. We determined that Cdc42 and Rac are differentially regulated by known regulators of the oscillatory circuit, including Ect2 and F-actin polymerization. We also observed that Rho and Cdc42 are segregated into defined activity zones by microtubule plus-end overlaps, presenting a possible mechanism for the division plane-specific F-actin wave dynamics. Our findings demonstrate that the major Rho family members participate in the cortical excitability circuit and reveal additional mechanisms that regulate Rho and F-actin waves. Additionally, this work supports a model wherein spatial segregation of Rho family GTPases differentially modulates cortical pattern dynamics.

items.title: Evidence for correlated evolution of sleep architecture in chronotype populations of Drosophila melanogaster created by artificial selection
items.blurb: Chronotypes are circadian variants in timing of a behaviour. In humans, some studies have associated differences in sleep timing and quality with underlying circadian clock driven chronotypes although confounding genetic, environmental and social factors complicate the interpretation of these relationships. Here, we present evidence from artificially selected early and late eclosion chronotype populations of Drosophila melanogaster which suggest that divergence in chronotype can lead to correlated evolution of changes in sleep architecture. We find that early chronotype flies exhibit greater sleep fragmentation and shorter sleep latency during night, whereas late flies showed weaker and less consistent changes in the same direction. These differences were broadly seen for both sexes. We also show that environmental cues like temperature cycles can modulate sleep timing and enhance chronotype differences, while increasing light intensity delayed nighttime sleep timing similarly across chronotypes. Additionally, when sleep was disrupted by mechanical perturbations, late flies could not recover lost sleep to the same degree as early and control in a time-of-day dependent manner. In contrast, following simulated jetlag-induced circadian misalignment, early flies showed a greater increase in daytime sleep after phase advances. Our findings suggest that sleep and circadian traits can coevolve, offering insights into the complex interactions between chronotypes and sleep architecture. These populations provide an evolutionary model to investigate how circadian timing, sleep architecture and homeostatic regulation may be linked.

items.title: Social information use promotes breeding synchrony but constrains adaptation to rapid environmental changes
items.blurb: Animals use social information to make decisions, yet how such processes influence predictions in reproductive timing and population adaptation under environmental change remains unclear. While social information can improve decision accuracy through information pooling, spatiotemporal heterogeneity in conditions and patterns of environmental changes creates noise that potentially limits the value of social information use among breeding individuals. Here, we established an evolutionary individual-based model to examine how social and private sensing interact to shape breeding phenology in species distributed across territories with peaked resources and facing annual fluctuations and rapid climate change. We show that when individuals incorporate social information from neighbours, behavioural responses become increasingly synchronised through positive feedback in decision-making. This emergent synchrony helps populations to adapt faster and can increase reproductive output under stable environmental conditions relative to relying only on private information. However, under directional climate change, the same mechanism reduces population responsiveness by constraining variation in individual responses, leading to systematic lag in tracking shifting environmental optima and reduced population reproductive output. Our results demonstrate that social information use can produce a general trade-off at the population level between synchronisation and adaptive flexibility across environmental contexts. Social interaction enhances population performance when environments are either consistent or changing drastically across both spatial and temporal scales. Rather than uniformly improving performance, social interaction may create conditions under which collective behaviour becomes maladaptive when environments change rapidly.

items.title: Population-level learning of non-additive effects enables accurate and efficient prediction of combinatorial perturbation responses
items.blurb: Combinatorial perturbations are widely used to study genetic interactions and to develop drug combinations, but the number of possible combinations grows quadratically with the number of perturbations, and only a small fraction can be measured in a screen experiment. Despite their growing sophistication, deep-learning and foundation models often fail to outperform a simple additive baseline based on measured single-perturbation responses. This suggests a simpler approach that builds on these measurements and directly learns deviations from additivity at the population level. We therefore developed GAIN, a lightweight model that implements these principles by predicting the pseudobulk response to a combination as the sum of its two single-perturbation responses and a learned interaction term. Across three single-cell datasets of genetic and drug combinations, GAIN corrected deviations from additivity and outperformed the additive model and cell-level methods across generalization settings and metrics, while training 3- to 64-fold faster. Applied to a combinatorial CRISPR screen of leukemia differentiation regulators, GAIN revealed synergy between key regulators of the differentiation block and genes that restrain differentiation but have little effect alone. It also revealed dampening by the histone chaperone FACT, which supports the induction of differentiation genes. These results establish population-level modeling of the deviation from additivity as a simple, accurate and scalable approach to predicting combination responses.

items.title: Evolutionary constraints on mitochondrial bioenergetics are reshaped in cancer
items.blurb: Mitochondrial DNA encodes thirteen subunits of the oxidative phosphorylation system, many of which are subject to strong purifying selection in humans. In cancer this selection is relaxed, which is usually read as a weakening of the inherited filter. Comparing somatic variants from 8,886 tumours with population variation using a unified analytical framework and a dataset-specific mutational null, we show that the tumour filter has a different shape. ATP synthase, the least constrained complex in the germline, becomes the most constrained in tumours, an inversion that holds within the tumour data alone and is not explained by the measurement ceiling. Holding residue position fixed, the germline avoids substitutions that change side-chain charge at the proton-loading sites of complex I, as does the human phylogeny, and around the haems of complex III, whereas tumours no longer distinguish them. Damage at the redox centres of complexes III and IV is tolerated mainly at low variant allele fraction, including within single cohorts, and tumours retain constraint on the electron-tunnelling medium of complex IV. At a complex I proton bridge, density-functional calculations separate substitutions that retune the transfer potential from those that abolish it, and a gated-tunnelling model predicts that removing the charge of one tumour-mutated residue changes the rate far more than the kinetic isotope effect.

items.title: Reproductive competition amplifies purifying selection and reduces genetic load
items.blurb: Deleterious mutations impose genetic load, and purging them through hard selection can carry substantial demographic costs. Competitive and sexual selection can instead remove deleterious variation through differential reproductive success. What remains unclear is when this process is more efficient than equivalent hard selection, and how competition generates this advantage. Here, we use forward-time simulations to express the impact of competition as an effective selection coefficient (se) calibrated against hard selection. Competition with multiple rivals strongly amplified purifying selection, whereas repeated contests improved discrimination by averaging stochastic and environmental variation. Strong competition also reduced genetic load relative to hard selection. These effects can shift weakly deleterious mutations from drift-dominated behaviour towards efficient purging. By front-loading purifying selection into reproduction, competitive selection can reduce genetic load at lower demographic cost. This provides a population-genetic mechanism by which genic capture can translate genome-wide genetic quality into more effective purifying selection. This may be particularly important in bottlenecked populations, where demographic recovery can relax purifying selection and allow genomic erosion to persist.

items.title: First Broad-spectrum Sami and Norse diets in northern Norway over the last 4000 years revealed by sedaDNA
items.blurb: The comprehensive specification of palaeo-diets has depended upon the preservation of plants and bones in archaeological deposits, which is limited by preservation conditions. Although middens at settlement sites in northern Norway can have comprehensive faunal archives they still may not reflect the full diet. Here, we apply sedaDNA metabarcoding and shotgun sequencing to two midden complexes in Finnmark, Norway. At both sites, this doubled the species identified. At the Bankgohppi "Gressbakken" house site (c.4.5-3.8 BP), items were added to all food categories (Figure below) including mammals such as reindeer, beaver, and bowhead whale, suggesting deep-sea fishing practice. At the Finnes coastal Sami Early Metal Age site (c.07-0.8 BP) and later Norse Medieval re-occupation, sedaDNA added terrestrial mammal (reindeer) and domesticated stock (goat, cattle) to the diet. The combination of traditional data with sedaDNA data provides us for the first time with a broad spectrum, suggesting seasonally balanced diets and fishing activity in northern Norway over the last 4000 years.

items.title: Barcoding the Past: A Cost-Effective ONT-Based Workflow for COI Recovery from Century-Old Spider Museum Specimens
items.blurb: Natural history collections contain vast amounts of undocumented biodiversity, yet degraded DNA has long limited their integration into modern barcode reference systems. Here, we present a cost-effective Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT)-based workflow for recovering COI barcodes from historical spider museum specimens, using the taxonomically challenging jumping spider genus Cytaea as a model system. We developed a mini-barcoding approach based on six short overlapping COI fragments (~130 bp), amplified in two multiplex PCR reactions and sequenced on ONT Flongle flow cells. The workflow was applied to 288 museum specimens ranging from 13 to 141 years old, preserved primarily in 75% ethanol under standard museum conditions. COI data were recovered from 284 of 288 specimens (98.6%). Reconstructed sequences ranged from 115 to 663 bp, and 260 of the 284 sequences (91.5%) contained at least 300 bp of resolved sequence. Amplification success differed strongly among primer pairs (31.6-98.3%), highlighting the importance of marker optimization for degraded DNA. Although older specimens generally yielded shorter sequences, informative barcode data were recovered even from century-old material. The combined ONT and Sanger dataset substantially expanded the documented barcode diversity of Cytaea, revealing 54 BINs, including 53 newly added to BOLD. Because fragmented mini-barcodes complicate standard clustering approaches, we placed short sequences onto a reference backbone constructed from full-length COI barcodes. This enabled their assignment to major lineages, although placement confidence varied among specimens. Our results demonstrate that historical museum specimens can be efficiently transformed into usable barcode resources using a simple, scalable, and affordable ONT-based workflow. This approach provides a practical bridge between legacy museum collections and modern DNA-based taxonomy, enabling degraded historical material to be incorporated into global biodiversity reference systems.

items.title: Kinetic windows for abiogenesis
items.blurb: The origin of life on Earth occurred within a narrow window delimited by cessation of intense late accretion bombardment at about 4.4 Ga on the one hand, and younger evidence gleaned via molecular phylogenetic studies, isotopic biosignatures and morphological traces on the other. Molecular clock analyses tentatively place the median age for the Last Universal Common Ancestor LUCA population of all contemporary DNA life at about 4.2 Ga. Cryptic isotopic biosignatures go back as far as 4.1 Ga in Hadean zircons and more robustly in Eoarchean rocks at about 3.83 Ga. Morphological remains including microfossils and microbially mediated sedimentary structures are almost as ancient, around 3.5 Ga. To make better sense of this early and rapid timeline and its implications for a biosphere on Hadean Earth, we parameterize the kinetic windows for that transition from non-living to living chemistry, abiogenesis. Here, we reinforce the finding that before the LUCA, a RiboNucleic Acid RNA and RiboNucleoProtein RNP World could have persisted for less than 130 Myr. Furthermore, we show that conditions which define the kinetic windows for early Earth stand out compared to other worlds in our Solar System considered as candidates for abiogenesis. Specifically, these are sustained stable liquid water from 4.4 Ga, wet-dry cycling on dry land under an atmosphere, effective crustal recycling to rejuvenate disequilibrium chemistry, available key elements for synthesis and growth, mechanisms to concentrate prebiotic reaction products without also destroying them, and sufficient spatial scales for subsequent evolution and diversification. We argue that the steps from abiogenesis to DNA required chemistry coordinated with environmental conditions overlapping in time with each transition from prebiotic synthesis to cellular life governed by distinct rate limiting processes operating over geologically short timescales. Our analysis suggests that if DNA life had not emerged, an informationally deficient and thermally unstable RNA biosphere would eventually have gone extinct.

items.title: RustBEARS: Survival-Conditioned Likelihoods, Uniformization Stochastic Mapping, and Uncertainty Quantification for Historical Biogeography
items.blurb: Probabilistic discrete-range models, including dispersal-extinction-cladogenesis (DEC), DIVALIKE, BAYAREALIKE, founder-event speciation (+J), spatial modifiers, and time stratification, underpin historical biogeography. As empirical datasets grow, however, BioGeoBEARS workflows face slow multi-area optimization and branch-wise rejection stochastic mapping that fails on rare stepping-stone pathways and scales poorly across posterior trees. Standard fixed-tree pruning likelihoods also retain an absorbing null range without conditioning on extant tip survival, which often drives extinction estimates toward zero and inflates founder-event support, whereas DEC* avoids null absorption only by forbidding single-area extirpation. Boundary Hessian failures and single-tree point estimates also leave parameter, model, phylogenetic, and mapping uncertainties unquantified. Here we present RustBEARS, a Rust engine with BioGeoBEARS-compatible R and Python packages. Across 1,339 configurations from 77 studies, RustBEARS matches BioGeoBEARS log-likelihoods (median |delta lnL| = 9.95 x 10^-14) and ancestral probabilities (<= 1.50 x 10^-14), accelerates 64- to 256-state optimization 2.8- to 17.3-fold on one core and 4.1- to 36.1-fold on eight cores over the fastest BioGeoBEARS setting, and replaces trial-limited rejection with Uniformization stochastic mapping (170.9-fold median speedup for 200-map Python runs across 30 studies). RustBEARS also introduces whole-tree tip-survival conditioning for unstratified and chronologically emerging island models alongside five frequentist uncertainty tools. Across 58 extant clades from this 77-study archive, survival conditioning cuts near-zero DEC extinction estimates from 62.1% to 0.0% (87.9% finite interior, 12.1% ceiling-censored) and lowers AICc preference for DEC+J from 75.9% to 36.2%.

items.title: Complementary roles among traits in community assembly processes of benthic foraminifera
items.blurb: Organismal traits play a distinct role in shaping community assembly, yet they have received comparatively little attention in marine communities. Here, we focus on living benthic foraminifera, a diverse group of marine protists that inhabit the seafloor. Benthic foraminifera are protists that have evolved different test-construction strategies: either by selecting and agglutinating grains from their surrounding environment or by biomineralization. In addition, taxa exhibit distinct morphologies have been hypothesized to reflect microhabitat partitioning within sediments. Here, we investigate their metacommunity patterns by analysing a co-occurrence network covering the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. We found that test-construction strategies significantly explained the structure of the network, whereas the general test shape did not. We hypothesize that test-construction strategy act as a broader-scale filter on the regional species pool, whereas morphological differences may be more closely related to local-scale coexistence and habitat partitioning. This study supports the idea that different organismal traits have different roles in the community assembly process.

items.title: TXNDC17 and glutathione cooperate to prevent cystine-induced cell death
items.blurb: Glutathione (GSH) supports diverse metabolic and antioxidant functions, yet the cellular processes most vulnerable to its depletion remain incompletely defined. Using genome-wide genetic screening in GSH depleted cells, we identified the cystine reductase TXNDC17 as essential for survival under GSH limitation. GSH depletion in TXNDC17-knockout cells caused intracellular cystine accumulation, increased protein cysteinylation, and cell death. Inhibiting the cystine/glutamate antiporter system xC- prevented cell death, linking this vulnerability to cystine uptake and impaired intracellular reduction. GSH depletion also markedly suppressed the growth of xenografts derived from TXNDC17-knockout, KEAP1-mutant lung cancer cells with high system xC- activity, accompanied by reduction-sensitive changes in cytoskeletal proteins. We further identified an electrophilic fragment that induced dose-dependent cytotoxicity in GSH-depleted cancer cells in a cystine-uptake dependent manner. Together, our findings establish TXNDC17 and GSH as central regulators of cystine-driven cytotoxicity, uncovering a therapeutic vulnerability in cancers with high cystine uptake.

items.title: Structural analysis of DNA binding and flexibility of the homohexameric AAA+ helicase SaPIbov1 Rep
items.blurb: The replication initiation proteins (Reps) encoded by Staphylococcus aureus pathogenicity islands (SaPIs) are helicases that recognize their own origins of replication (oris). Despite their ability to melt the cognate ori without accessory proteins, the nature of the transition from origin-loaded to actively unwinding states remains poorly understood. Here, we report crystal and cryo-EM structures of the SaPIbov1 Rep, a homohexameric superfamily 6 (SF6) helicase, in apo and nucleotide plus duplex DNA-bound states. Comparison to superfamily 3 (SF3) SaPI Reps and archaeal/eukaryotic MCMs reveals differing structural adaptations for DNA engagement. Notably, SaPIbov1 Rep retains pore-loop 1 (PL1) and the pre-sensor 1 {beta}-hairpin (PS1) for DNA-binding, but lacks the Helix-2 insertion (H2i) conserved in MCM helicases and instead possesses an elongated PS1 providing extended DNA contact. 3D variability analysis (3DVA) resolved multiple ring-open conformational intermediate states, with ring asymmetry correlating to DNA binding. The duplex-bound single hexamer captured here likely represents a pre-replicative intermediate preceding double hexamer assembly. We also show that the disordered N-terminus of SaPIbov1 Rep binds its cognate primase and predict that the primase recruits the host DNA polymerase III.

items.title: Viral genetic variation programs divergent neuroimmune states during rabies infection
items.blurb: Viral burden does not necessarily predict the extent or composition of the host immune response, reflecting the complexity of virus - host interactions. Rabies virus (RABV) provides a powerful model to investigate this question because genetically distinct RABVs differ in replication, immune evasion, and neuroimmune activation. Here, we performed integrated temporal proteomic and spatial imaging analyses of recombinant RABV, including pathogenic, attenuated, and a newly generated interferon-sensitive variant with disrupted phosphoprotein antagonistic activity. Following intracerebral infection of mice, viruses established distinct neuroimmune states that diverged over time in antiviral signaling, complement activation, and immune response. Notably, the pathogenic field viruses rDogA and rFox both exhibited substantial viral accumulation, but elicited markedly different central nervous system (CNS) responses, with rDogA inducing limited host immune engagement, whereas rFox triggered early and broad antiviral, complement, and immune recruitment programs. Disruption of phosphoprotein-mediated interferon antagonism in rDogA enhanced interferon-stimulated gene expression and antiviral effectors, restricting viral accumulation without inducing broad neuroimmune remodeling. Conversely, the attenuated glycoprotein-modified rSAD GASGAS elicited strong complement activation and T cell recruitment with little detectable viral levels, revealing a highly immunogenic neuroimmune state. Spatial profiling further identified virus-dependent patterns of myeloid, astrocyte-associated, complement, and lymphocyte responses across brain regions. Together, these findings demonstrate how viral genetic background and its modulation of host antiviral responses shape divergent neuroimmune states in which viral accumulation, antiviral immunity, and CNS immune activation are differentially coordinated.

items.title: Identification of two novel lipoteichoic acid synthases essential for viability in Clostridioides difficile.
items.blurb: Lipoteichoic acids (LTAs) are major components of the Gram-positive bacterial cell envelope that contribute to cell morphology, division, and resistance to antimicrobial stress. Clostridioides difficile produces a type V LTA composed of repeating GlcNAc-GlcNAc-glyceric acid subunits anchored to the membrane by a glycolipid. Here, we identify two previously uncharacterized enzymes involved in C. difficile LTA synthesis: LtaB, which is required for LTA production and cell envelope integrity, and LtaA, which influences apparent LTA polymer length and partially compensates for reduced LtaB activity. Loss of LtaB causes growth and morphological defects, including aberrant septation and cell lysis, while LtaB depletion in the absence of LtaA is lethal. LtaA and LtaB contain two distinct domains: an LTA synthase-like domain and a glycosyltransferase (GT) C-like domain. Site-directed mutagenesis of conserved residues shows that the GT-C-like domain of LtaB is critical for both LTA synthesis and viability, whereas mutations in the LTA synthase-like domain have little effect on viability and only modest effects on LTA chain length. Production of several LtaB homologs from related species restored viability and, in some cases, LTA synthesis when a C. difficile {Delta}ltaA mutant was depleted of LtaB. These findings establish LtaA and LtaB as distinct but functionally overlapping enzymes required for type V LTA synthesis in C. difficile.

items.title: maoP impacts biofilm formation via csgD in Salmonella Typhimurium
items.blurb: Biofilm formation is a key process in the life cycle of most bacteria and involves the formation of multicellular aggregates, frequently attached to a surface. Despite extensive research into the complex regulatory pathways controlling this process, many aspects are not fully understood. Originally named for its role in chromosomal organisation, MaoP has previously been shown to have an important impact on biofilm formation in Escherichia coli and Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium. Here we continued to explore how MaoP impacts biofilm formation in S. Typhimurium 14028S. We show that deletion of maoP significantly reduces biofilm formation through reduced production of the biofilm matrix components curli and cellulose, and that this is associated with a reduction in transcript abundance of the central biofilm regulator csgD. Comparison of the transcriptomes of WT and maoP deletion strain biofilms confirmed the substantial impact of MaoP on csgD and its regulon. To further explore how MaoP impacts biofilm formation we conducted a biofilm evolution experiment to select for suppressor mutants that had restored curli production in a {Delta}maoP background. Sequencing of these mutants identified single nucleotide polymorphisms upstream of csgD that increased csgD transcript abundance and recovered biofilm formation to wild-type levels. In conclusion, our findings suggest a pathway where MaoP is involved in the regulation of biofilm formation through the control of the central biofilm regulator CsgD.

items.title: Fungal abundance and community composition associations with environmental and operational factors within and between manufacturing facilities.
items.blurb: Fungal communities in manufacturing environments remain understudied despite their potential implications for product quality and occupational health. Surface swabs collected from 19 footwear factories in Vietnam between 2023 and 2025 were used to assess culturable fungal counts, genus-level diversity and community composition. Associations with operational factors and environmental conditions, including temperature, relative humidity (RH), CO2 and PM10, were examined by separating environmental variation into within-factory and between-factory components. Fungal counts were associated with both operational and environmental factors, with object type showing the strongest operational association. Higher PM10 tended to be associated with lower surface fungal counts within factories, while factories with higher average CO2 also showed lower counts. Alternaria and Neurospora were positively associated with within-factory RH, and Aspergillus showed a negative between-factory association with CO2. Community composition varied most strongly among factories, while environmental associations were limited to the combined effects of between-factory conditions at the community level. Overall, environmental indicators showed clearer associations with culturable fungal burden and individual genera than with overall community composition, indicating that fungal counts and community structure capture distinct aspects of contamination in manufacturing environments.

items.title: The ACDC domains of AP2-O3 and FD3 contribute to protein interactions and ookinete development
items.blurb: The Apicomplexan AP2 (ApiAP2) family of transcription factors are key regulators of Plasmodium spp. parasite development. In addition to containing AP2 DNA-binding domains, nine ApiAP2 proteins also encode an apicomplexan-specific ACDC domain whose function remains largely unknown. Here, we dissect the biological role of the ACDC domain from two female-specific regulators, AP2-O3 and FD3, using the rodent malaria model Plasmodium yoelii and the human malaria parasite P. falciparum. In Plasmodium yoelii, deletion of the ACDC domain preserved AP2-O3 and FD3 protein presence and nuclear localization without significantly affecting asexual growth or gametocyte production. However, deletion of these domains impaired the gametocyte-to-ookinete transition, reducing ookinete conversion efficiency. Proteomic and biochemical studies indicate that the AP2-O3 ACDC domain interacts with FD3, while the FD3 ACDC domain preferentially associates with full-length FD3. Transcriptomic data showed that over 80% of transcripts that increased after FD3 ACDC deletion were also higher following AP2-O3 loss, with female gametocyte marker expression largely unchanged. In Plasmodium falciparum, removing the FD3 ACDC domain did not affect female lineage-specific expression of FD3, nuclear localization of FD3, or the asexual growth and gametocyte maturation of parasites. Leveraging the high sequence conservation of ACDC domains across the Plasmodium genus, we conducted structure-based virtual screening of 283 compounds targeting the predicted PfAP2-O3 and PfFD3 ACDC interaction interface. Seven compounds ranked among the top candidate inhibitors for both domains, and the highest-priority ligand for each domain was further evaluated by molecular dynamics simulations. Collectively, our findings support a role for ACDC domains in ApiAP2 protein interactions and identify candidate compounds for future experimental evaluation as potential transmission-blocking leads.

items.title: Modular innate recognition in conventional T cells through FcRγ reconstitution
items.blurb: Engineered T cells can elicit durable tumor responses but largely rely on TCRs or CARs for target recognition. Here we show that FcR{gamma}, an innate signaling adaptor not expressed by conventional T cells, enables full-length innate receptor function in adult human {beta} T cells. FcR{gamma} reconstitution enabled endogenous NKp30 surface expression and cytotoxicity without inducing an innate-like state. Stable co-expression of NKp30 and FcR{gamma} maintained receptor expression after activation withdrawal, supported sustained tumor killing, delayed leukemia progression in mice, and enabled cytotoxicity against primary myeloid leukemia. FcR{gamma} also supported functional import of receptors spanning natural cytotoxicity, Fc receptor, and C-type lectin families, extending conventional T cell responses to tumor ligands, antibody-coated targets, IgE receptor engagement, and microbial patterns. These findings establish a shared-adaptor strategy for expanding innate recognition in engineered T cells while preserving the identity and functional properties of the widely adopted conventional T cell platform.

items.title: Distinct effects of aging and hearing loss on mouse auditory cortex
items.blurb: Age-related hearing loss is accompanied by changes in auditory cortical activity, but it remains unclear which changes reflect aging itself and which depend on the loss of peripheral input. Here we compared spontaneous and sound-evoked activity in the auditory cortex of awake C57BL/6J (C57) mice, which develop early-onset hearing loss, with that of C57BL/6J x CBA/Ca F1 hybrid mice, which retain their hearing. In both strains, aging increased the irregularity of spontaneous firing and reduced the spike-timing precision of narrow-spiking neurons during natural sound presentation. In C57 mice, aging was additionally associated with a greater loss of sound-responsive neurons, increased spontaneous firing of broad-spiking neurons and more variable sound-evoked spike trains. At the level of individual neurons, the effect of sound on contrast entropy, a firing-rate-normalized measure of spike-pattern diversity, also diverged between strains with age and became negative in middle-aged and old C57's neurons. Nevertheless, population activity discriminated spontaneous, natural sound-evoked and noise-evoked conditions with high accuracy at every age in both strains. Thus, aging and hearing loss have distinct effects on the spiking of individual auditory cortical neurons, whereas population activity continues to discriminate sound conditions.

items.title: Shared Neural Dynamics of Sentence-Level Language Processing in Verbally Proficient Autistic and Non-Autistic Adults
items.blurb: Autistic individuals often show atypical language development during childhood, yet many attain typical language proficiency by adulthood. This raises the question of whether the neural processes supporting language differ in autism once language has been acquired. Using electroencephalography (EEG), we compared verbally proficient autistic and non-autistic adults during rapid serial visual presentation of structured sentences and pseudoword lists. Sentence processing elicited oscillatory responses across theta, alpha, beta, and gamma frequency bands, with distinct spatiotemporal profiles and hemispheric lateralization most pronounced in the theta, alpha, and beta bands. Notably, beta-band activity increased over sentence position and was positively associated with verbal ability, consistent with a role in the maintenance and integration of linguistic information. These effects were highly comparable across groups, with similar patterns observed at both the individual and group levels and across sensor- and source-level analyses. Together, these findings indicate largely shared neural dynamics of sentence-level language processing in verbally proficient autistic and non-autistic adults, suggesting that atypical language-related neural organization is not an inevitable feature of autism in adulthood.
