items.title: Sucrose Non-fermenting Related Kinase (SNRK) Deficiency-Mediated Osteogenic Differentiation in Vascular Smooth Muscle Cells Exacerbates Vascular Calcification
items.blurb: Background: The differentiation of vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) into an osteogenic phenotype is a critical step in vascular calcification progression. Sucrose non-fermenting related kinase (SNRK), a member of the AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) family, has been implicated in diverse cellular functions and pathological conditions. However, whether SNRK is involved in VSMC osteogenic differentiation and calcification remains undefined. Methods: Three mouse models were used to evaluate the contributions of SNRK in vascular calcification: Myh11-CreERT2-driven VSMC-specific SNRK knockout in C57BL/6J mice subjected to vitamin D3 overload or adenine diet, and Apoe-/- mice with VSMC (Myh11-CreERT2)-, endothelial cell (Cdh5-Cre)-, or macrophage (LysM-Cre)-specific SNRK knockout on a chronic western diet. The in vitro calcification was modeled by treating primary mouse aortic VSMCs and human aortic VSMCs (HASMCs) with phosphate (Pi). Results: Cross-species transcriptomic analyses reveal reduced SNRK expression in murine vascular calcification and human calcified plaques. Human femoral artery samples from the elderly individuals with calcification exhibited reduced SNRK protein levels compared to non-calcified samples. In patients with chronic kidney disease, leukocyte levels of SNRK antisense RNA 1 (SNRK-AS1) were positively correlated with thoracic artery calcification Agatston scores. In parallel, decreased SNRK expression was observed in aortic arteries from three mouse models of calcification and in VSMCs treated with phosphate. Notably, VSMC-specific deletion of SNRK exacerbated calcific lesions, accompanied by upregulation of both runt-related transcription factor 2 (RUNX2) and msh homeobox 2 (MSX2). Conversely, SNRK deletion in either endothelial cells or macrophages had no impact on vascular calcification. Further, overexpression of SNRK in VSMCs, achieved via intravenous injection of an adeno-associated virus (AAV) ligated with VSMC Tagln promoter encoding Snrk, significantly attenuated vascular calcification along with reduced expression of osteogenic markers. Further interactome analysis demonstrated that SNRK directly binds to {beta}-Catenin, a critical regulator of vascular calcification, through the amino acid sequence 270-765. Mechanistically, SNRK facilitated the interaction between {beta}-Catenin and cullin 1/{beta}-TrCP E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, promoting ubiquitin-proteasome-mediated degradation of {beta}-Catenin and subsequently reducing the expression of osteogenic markers in VSMCs. Conclusions: We conclude that SNRK safeguards against vascular calcification by preventing {beta}-Catenin/RUNX2/MSX2-mediated VSMC osteogenic differentiation.

items.title: APOBEC3 Activation Drives Epitranscriptomic Remodeling and Clonal Hematopoiesis
items.blurb: Stress and inflammatory cytokine-inducible APOBEC3 (A3) enzymes promote clonal evolution in many malignancies. We identified A3C overexpression in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) following spaceflight-associated accelerated aging and in precancer myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs). However, the role of A3 in age-associated clonal hematopoiesis (CH) and precancer initiation remains unclear. To investigate the functional hierarchy among A3 enzymes, we performed lentiviral A3B, A3C, A3D, A3F, and A3G overexpression, whole genome, whole transcriptome and single-cell RNA sequencing analyses, and functional HSPC assays. While A3C and A3F induced more C-to-T DNA mutations; A3B, A3C, and A3G deregulated RNA splicing; and all A3 enzymes induced C-to-U RNA edits in HSPCs. In aged HSPCs, A3C overexpression enhanced replating and myeloid lineage skewing in humanized inflammatory niche mouse models typical of CH. Moreover, A3C-induced editing of CH-associated transcripts distinguished MPN from normal HSPCs. Thus, future strategies focused on APOBEC3C inhibition may prevent CH and precancer initiation.

items.title: Compensatory Creatine Secretion Protects Against Drug-Induced Liver Injury via Desuccinylation
items.blurb: ackground and aims: Effective therapeutic interventions for Drug induced liver injury (DILI) remain limited. N-myc downstream regulated gene-1 (NDRG1), a stress-responsive proteins, has an incompletely defined role in acetaminophen-induced liver injury. Method: Wild-type (WT), NDRG1Hep-flox, Hepatocyte-specific NDRG1 conditional knockout mice (NDRG1Hep-KO) were subjected to APAP-induced injury modeling. Liver and blood sample from patient were analyzed. Liver sample of mice subsequently underwent RNA sequencing (RNA-Seq), untargeted metabolomic profiling, single-cell sequencing, succinylation sequencing. For in vitro studies, AML-12 hepatocytes, RAW264.7 macrophages, and bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs), human Monocyte-Derived Macrophages, human hepatocyte organoids were utilized in experiments. Result: NDRG1 was upregulated in mouse and human DILI livers. NDRG1 conditional knockout significantly exacerbates DILI. Mechanistically, NDRG1 inhibited GAMT ubiquitination to enhance creatine production, and hepatocyte?derived creatine attenuated M1 polarization of liver macrophages by suppressing PHB1 succinylation at lysine 128. CXCL2? macrophages were identified as a major subpopulation regulated by NDRG1. Conclusion: Hepatocyte NDRG1 protects against APAP-DILI by driving GAMT-dependent creatine production and PHB1 K128 succinylation-dependent macrophage reprogramming.

items.title: Effects of sequence splitting and negative-set selection on antimicrobial peptide prediction
items.blurb: Sequence partitioning and negative-set selection determine the prediction problem posed by an antimicrobial peptide (AMP) benchmark. We quantified their effects using a DRAMP 5.0 audit, controlled comparisons with frozen ESM-2 classifiers and additional benchmark configurations. On DRAMP, random splitting increased Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) from 0.718 under cluster-disjoint splitting to 0.932. This difference of 0.214 exceeded the gains from the architectural additions tested, and 75.6% of randomly assigned test sequences shared a homology cluster with training sequences. Across three additional dataset configurations, random-minus-cluster MCC differences ranged from -0.04634 to +0.05682, showing that the magnitude and direction of the split effect depended on benchmark composition. With the fitted classifiers and APD6 positives held fixed, replacing DRAMP test negatives with external hard negatives reduced the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve from 0.9833 to 0.9018 (paired difference 0.08149, bootstrap 95% CI 0.07196 to 0.09181). These comparisons quantify substantial sensitivity to evaluation design and show why split effects require assessment within each benchmark. AMPBenchAudit provides the audited records, split assignments and evaluation code needed to examine this sensitivity and interpret model comparisons under explicit test conditions.

items.title: A Strategy to Identify Endogenous Ligands for a Protein
items.blurb: Protein-metabolite interactions are essential to numerous metabolic processes and underly many disease mechanisms. However, detecting these interactions is a challenge due to the transient nature of protein-metabolite associations. Here, we employ an untargeted functional metabolomics screening strategy to uncover low-affinity interactions between an entire metabolome and a kinase. We first utilize high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC)-guided fractionation to separate a whole-metabolome extract into multiple fixed-time fractions. A metabolite fraction library (mFL) of one-dimensional (1D) proton (1H) NMR spectra is then generated from these fractions. After adding the protein to the same fractions, saturation transfer difference (STD) NMR is then performed on each to detect weak protein-metabolite interactions and develop an STD library. Using the binding resonances from the STD library as a guide, the identity of the binding ligand can be determined. We demonstrate this strategy using frutosamine-3-kinase (FN3K) to identify and validate both known and novel binders. This workflow serves as a practical and simple way to screen an organism's metabolome for endogenous effector molecules, further strengthening our knowledge of protein-metabolite interactions and the functional metabolome.

items.title: How Much Coordination Does an AAA+ Motor Require? A Case Study of the Archaeal Cdc48/p97 Homologue
items.blurb: AAA+ (ATPases Associated with diverse cellular Activities) motors harness ATP hydrolysis to remodel substrates, often through a spiral staircase architecture which is commonly associated with a sequential "hand-over-hand" translocation mechanism. However, the extent to which motor activity requires strict sequential order and interprotomer coordination remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigate the functional resilience of an archaeal AAA+ unfoldase, VAT, using reconstituted heterohexamers containing wild-type protomers and variants defective in nucleotide binding, hydrolysis, substrate engagement, or regulatory control. Quantitative modeling of steady-state ATPase activity and substrate unfolding reveals motif-dependent partial cooperativity. ATP hydrolysis is best described by local interprotomer coupling, whereas substrate unfolding exhibits a threshold-dependent response to defects in conserved mechanochemical motifs. Walker A and Arginine-finger lesions inhibit neighboring ATPase activity but are partially tolerated during unfolding. Pore-loop mutations stimulate ATP turnover while more strongly impairing unfolding. In contrast, N-terminal domain-mediated autoinhibition follows an independent model in both assays, consistent with controlling catalytic output predominantly at the individual protomer level while preserving interprotomer coordination for function. Together, these findings reveal that ATP turnover and substrate unfolding respond differently to local perturbations, with tolerance to protomer defects determined by the mechanochemical element affected. This motif-dependent resilience highlights the operational plasticity of an AAA+ ring and challenges strictly sequential models in which a single defective protomer arrests the motor.

items.title: BASIN: Background-Anchored Signal Normalization with Integrated Quality Control for CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
items.blurb: Quantitative comparison of CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag datasets is complicated when a perturbation changes the global abundance of the profiled chromatin feature or when there is substantial variability between replicates. Read-depth normalization removes global differences by design, whereas exogenous spike-in normalization can introduce substantial technical variability. We developed Background-Anchored SIgnal Normalization (BASIN), an endogenous-reference framework that exploits recurrent, peak-like background in IgG controls as a quantitative internal reference. BASIN Anchor Regions (BARs) act as reproducible read sinks whose representation rises as specific signal falls, allowing global differences to be inferred from the balance between specific and nonspecific reads. BASIN comprises three pipelines: OVERTURE identifies and evaluates BAR panels, HARMONY derives and applies robust sample-specific scale factors from trimmed BAR signal, and CODA determines whether the assumptions supporting normalization are satisfied. BASIN provides a validated, ready-to-use universal BAR panel for Drosophila melanogaster, and the OVERTURE pipeline enables BAR panel development in other organisms. We tested BASIN against independent expectations and compared its performance with spike-in normalization. BASIN remained quantitatively stable across a >100-fold cell-input titration and detected global depletion of H3K36me3 in Set2 mutants that read-depth normalization concealed. BASIN also preserved expected H3K9me3 differences even when target signal overlapped anchor regions. Applied to a variety of profiling experiments, CODA distinguished normalization failures arising from both biological and technical causes. BASIN thus converts reproducible background from a nuisance signal into an internal reference standard, enabling spike-in-free quantification of global chromatin changes while providing an explicit framework to test when and why that normalization can or cannot be trusted.

items.title: A specialized extracellular matrix patterns the conserved cortical protein EFA-6 at neuron-epidermal interfaces
items.blurb: Sensory neurons establish intimate connections with the surrounding epidermis, where specialized extracellular matrix (ECM) help maintain neuron-epidermal interactions. However, whether and how this specialized ECM regulates the spatial organization of cortical proteins at these interfaces remains poorly understood. Here, we show a specialized ECM patterns the cortical microtubule regulator EFA-6 at neuron-epidermal interfaces in Caenorhabditis elegans. We show that EFA-6 in the epidermal cortex is enriched adjacent to the neurites of touch receptor neurons, characterized by discrete foci at the distal neurite and a diffuse distribution in the proximal neurite. We identify the specialized ECM components MEC-1 and HIM-4/hemicentin as regulators of EFA-6 spatial patterning at the interface between epidermis and neuronal processes. EFA-6 proteins contain an intrinsically disordered region (IDR) that is necessary and sufficient for EFA-6 targeting to and patterning at the neuron-epidermal interface. Within the IDR, we further identify an 8 residue motif that regulates enrichment and patterning of EFA-6 IDR at this interface. Finally, we find that EFA-6 contributes to age-dependent neurite defects in him-4 mutants. Together, our findings reveal how a specialized extracellular matrix and an intrinsically disordered region coordinate the spatial organization of a cortical MT regulator at neuron-epidermal interface.

items.title: Transmural compression drives lymphatic endothelial dysfunction through Piezo1-CaMKII signaling
items.blurb: Background: Secondary lymphedema is characterized by progressive lymphatic dysfunction, chronic inflammation, and tissue fibrosis, but how mechanical changes during disease progression contribute to lymphatic failure remains poorly understood. Lymphatic vessels initially undergo intraluminal pressure-induced dilation, whereas advanced disease is associated with extraluminal compression resulting from tissue remodeling. We investigated how these different mechanical stimuli affect lymphatic endothelial function. Methods and Results: We developed a human lymphatic vessel-on-chip model enabling independent control of intra- and extraluminal pressure. In contrast to vessel dilation, extraluminal compression profoundly disrupted lymphatic endothelial barrier integrity, increasing permeability and causing junctional disorganization, while also inducing a strong pro-inflammatory transcriptional response. Mechanistically, compression induced sustained intracellular Ca2 influx and activated the mechanosensitive ion channel Piezo1. Piezo1 inhibition attenuated compression-induced Ca2 responses and protected endothelial barrier integrity, identifying Piezo1 as an upstream mediator of compression-induced dysfunction. Downstream, compression-induced Ca2 signaling activated Ca2 /calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII), whose inhibition preserved endothelial junctional integrity and reduced both barrier dysfunction and inflammatory activation. In a murine model of secondary lymphedema, CaMKII inhibition improved lymphatic function and reduced lymphedema-associated tissue remodeling. Conclusions: These findings identify a Piezo1-CaMKII signaling axis that links pathological extraluminal compression to lymphatic endothelial dysfunction and inflammation. Targeting this pathway may help preserve lymphatic function during lymphedema progression.

items.title: Oral microbiome and DNA virome profiling in pigs reveals age-associated dynamics and extracellular recovery of Streptococcus suis-associated phage lineages
items.blurb: The pig oral cavity is a critical interface for microbial transmission and herd health monitoring, yet its microbiome and virome remains poorly characterised. We performed shotgun metagenomic sequencing of oral fluids from pigs across 15 commercial farms in Ireland, using paired bulk and virus-like particles (VLP) enrichment to capture comprehensive microbial and DNA virome diversity. Microbial communities shifted progressively with age, with early post-weaning animals enriched in environmental genera such as Pseudomonas and Staphylococcus and later stages dominated by lactic acid bacteria and anaerobes. Only 20.6% of vOTUs could be assigned to a known genus, with the most abundant being Astrithrvirus, which increased with age. Both microbiome and DNA virome exhibited predictable, coordinated age-associated succession with strong cross-domain coupling supported by virus-host networks. Functional profiling of the microbiome revealed that predicted carbohydrate substrates tracked the dietary transitions, while accessory viral functions partitioned by lifestyle and host. The early post-weaning stage was characterised by high abundance of viral integration and excision functions, as well as elevated resistome diversity that was almost exclusively of prokaryotic origin rather than viral. Importantly, 26 of the 25,223 vOTUs identified were predicted to target Streptococcus suis, providing the first metagenomic catalogue of such phages from pig oral environments. These findings expand our understanding of oral microbiome-virome dynamics and establish a framework for integrated microbiome and viromics approaches that could enable therapeutic phage discovery and inform microbiome-targeted interventions in pig production systems.

items.title: Transcranial temporal interference stimulation increases slow waves during human NREM sleep
items.blurb: Slow waves are a hallmark of sleep homeostasis and a target for enhancing restorative sleep. Transcranial temporal interference stimulation (tTIS) can non-invasively deliver a low-frequency envelope to deep targets and has been shown to increase spectral slow-wave activity during sleep. It remains untested whether tTIS also alters discrete slow waves, how their cortical expression changes, and whether the field each brain receives relates to the response. During non-rapid eye movement sleep, 32 participants received 1 Hz tTIS and 11 a carrier-only control in 3-min episodes targeting the left insula/ventromedial prefrontal cortex. Combining high-density electroencephalography (EEG), source reconstruction and individualized field modeling, we found that tTIS increased slow-wave density by about 20% during and 30% after stimulation, across shallow and deep waves, with limited morphology change. The carrier-only control showed no detected density change. In source space, each wave involved more cortex in both arms, while wave origins did not change. A dose-response analysis showed that tTIS participants who received a stronger modeled field shifted further toward N3 sleep during stimulation, a relation not seen in the control. These results support tTIS as a candidate EEG-compatible tool for modulating slow waves and motivate individualized field modeling to interpret its effects.

items.title: Cognitive Load modulates the exploration-exploitation trade-off Through Reconfiguration of an IPS-Centered Decision Network
items.blurb: In dynamic environments where rewards continuously change, adaptive decision-making requires ongoing updates of option-value and uncertainty estimates to balance exploration and exploitation. This process depends on cognitive resources and involves coordinated interactions among multiple brain regions; however, how cognitive load affects directed exploration in such dynamic environments, and whether these effects are accompanied by changes in interactions among exploration-related brain regions, remains unclear. We embedded a working-memory load manipulation within a dynamic four-armed bandit task. Experiment 1 compared computational models and quantified load-related changes in exploration; Experiment 2 examined these behavioral effects in an independent sample and investigated their neural correlates using fMRI. Across both experiments, high load reduced the uncertainty bonus parameter ({varphi}), indicating weaker directed exploration. Experiment 2 additionally showed lower inverse temperature ({beta}) under high load, indicating more stochastic choices. Directed exploration relative to exploitation more activated the frontopolar cortex (FP), intraparietal sulcus (IPS), anterior insula (aIns), and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC). Psychophysiological interaction (PPI) analyses indicated stronger functional coupling between the right aIns and IPS under low load. Guided by the candidate connections identified by PPI, dynamic causal modeling (DCM) focused on a three-region subnetwork. Bayesian model selection favored the model with directed-exploration-related input to the IPS, while condition-specific comparisons suggested stronger aIns-to-IPS effective connectivity under low load. Together, these findings link cognitive resource demands to reduced uncertainty-guided directed exploration in a dynamic environment and suggest that this behavioral change is accompanied by selective reconfiguration of interactions within an IPS-centered decision subnetwork.

items.title: Confidence-Guided Machine Learning Staging of the Mouse Estrous Cycle from External Anatomical Images Reduces Cytology Burden
items.blurb: Although the 2015 National Institutes of Health mandate to consider sex as a biological variable in preclinical studies has increased sex-inclusive study designs, many research groups continue to cite the complexity of monitoring female-specific physiology as a barrier to adoption. Central to this challenge is the murine estrous cycle, a hormonally driven process comprising four stages (proestrus, estrus, metestrus, and diestrus), each associated with distinct hormonal and cytological profiles. Current staging methods rely primarily on vaginal cytology, which requires skilled animal handling, specialized expertise in cytology observation, and considerable time, limiting their routine application outside of reproductive endocrinology. To address these barriers, we developed and evaluated a machine learning framework for estrous cycle staging based on photographs of the mouse external vaginal opening. Using 2,297 photographs from C57BL/6J and BALB/c female mice paired with concurrent cytological assessments and partitioned strictly at the animal level, we trained and evaluated three models of varying granularity: a four-stage model, a three-stage model combining metestrus and diestrus, and a two-stage binary model separating the follicular from the luteal and transitional phases. In a held-out evaluation cohort of 466 photographs from 29 unseen mice, overall classification accuracy was 47.4% (95% CI: 40.7-51.9%) for the four-stage model, 54.5% (47.6-62.9%) for the three-group model, and 69.5% (61.8-75.3%) for the binary two-group model. Misclassifications occurred predominantly between biologically adjacent stages, particularly between proestrus and estrus. Crucially, applying a calibrated confidence threshold to the two-group classifier increased accuracy to 82.8% (95% CI: 71.1-92.1%) among the 43.8% of photographs with confidence [≥] 0.80, and to 92.5% (95% CI: 87.1-96.6%) among the 20.0% of photographs with confidence [≥] 0.90. While external photography does not support standalone four-stage classification, confidence-guided photographic assessment offers an accessible decision-support framework to selectively triage uncertain cases for cytology and reduce the wet-lab burden of estrous monitoring in preclinical research, including cohort assembly for hormone-dependent models of genital tract infection.

items.title: Adjuvant myeloperoxidase inhibition promotes B and T cell mediated control of murine melanoma metastasis
items.blurb: Metastasis is the spread of cancer cells from primary tumors to distant organs and accounts for the majority of melanoma deaths, with a 5-year survival rate of only 30%. Despite strong evidence that myeloid cells promote metastasis, there are limited clinically effective myeloid-directed therapies. Here, we demonstrate that targeting myeloperoxidase (MPO), a myeloid-lineage restricted enzyme, significantly reduced multi-organ metastatic burden using an immunocompetent mouse model of spontaneous melanoma. Adjuvant MPO inhibition remodeled the metastatic microenvironment by a reduction in Ly6G+Ly6C+ myeloid cells and enrichment of B and T cell populations. Importantly, adjuvant MPO inhibitor-mediated metastatic control was dependent upon B, CD8+ T cells and CD4+ T cells, and rapidly reduced circulating and disseminated tumor cells. MPO inhibition markedly decreased NET release, while NET deficiency and inhibition recapitulated the anti-metastatic effects of targeting MPO, implicating NETs as a potential downstream mediator of MPO-driven metastasis. We further validated these findings in a distinct spontaneous breast cancer model where adjuvant MPO inhibition similarly reduced multi-organ metastatic burden with comparable changes within the metastatic immune microenvironment. Collectively, our studies introduce MPO as a druggable regulator of metastasis where MPO inhibition limits metastatic disease by targeting immunosuppressive myeloid cells.

items.title: Synovial Fluid Spatial Microrheology is Shaped by Extracellular Matrix Identity and Mucin Integrity
items.blurb: The interfacial organization of synovial fluid (SF) contributes to cartilage protection and lubrication, yet how articular cartilage extracellular matrix (AC-ECM) identity influences the rheological response of supramolecularly assembled SF films remains to be elucidated. Here, depth-resolved multiple-particle tracking microrheology was used to examine diluted SF (dSF) near immobilized collagen type II (Col-II), collagen type I (Col-I), and fibronectin (FN). Untreated dSF exhibited increased relative apparent viscosity near Col-II and FN, whereas the response near Col-I was comparatively negligible. Treatment with StcE, a mucin-selective protease previously shown to cleave lubricin's mucin domain in SF, resulted in more pronounced effects of the interface on the depth dependent viscosity profiles across all three substrates. Analysis of the complex modulus and viscosity revealed significant effects with depth changes and StcE treatment. Quartz crystal microbalance measurements further revealed that the adsorbed amount of the fluids onto AC-ECM substrates did not directly correspond to the magnitude of microrheological modulation, with Col-I showing limited retention despite a pronounced near-interface response following StcE treatment. Together, these findings indicate that AC-ECM identity and StcE-sensitive SF constituents are associated with spatial variations in viscoelasticity that are not directly reflected by far-field tracer dynamics or interfacial adsorption alone.

items.title: Zero-shot virtual knock-out rankings do not recover causal genes from observational single-cell data
items.blurb: Background: Virtual knock-out methods rank genes by the change predicted after deleting one gene in silico and nominate targets without perturbation data. That use assumes the ranking reflects the causal consequence of removal; we tested it for three zero-shot methods in four configurations under one criterion. Results: We compared scTenifoldKnk (R and Python), CellOracle and Geneformer on 438 real, 3,585 synthetic and 330 DepMap knock-outs. Top-20 lists of different knock-outs overlapped by a median of 12 to 14 of 20, against 0.08 by chance. Displacement followed out-degree (R^2 = 0.825; 0.852 with six further features). Decoupling causal effect from topology left criterion value and grade unchanged (36 of 36 RED). For scTenifoldKnk, the ranking showed no evidence of recovery above chance where causal genes were planted (AUROC 0.538 and 0.528 in the two constructions). CellOracle's displacement showed no detectable relation to the data-built network (rho = -0.212, P = 0.556). Geneformer's shift tracked token coverage inconsistently (+0.41, +0.40, -0.27). Against DepMap essentiality, scTenifoldKnk's Python implementation (scTenifoldpy 0.5.1) reached AUROC 0.459 (95% CI 0.357-0.566), not distinguishable from chance; detection rate reached 0.588 (95% CI 0.497-0.677). Conclusions: For scTenifoldKnk and CellOracle, the ranking reports network properties, not the causal consequence of removal. No measured structural feature accounted for more than a small fraction of Geneformer's shift. Detection rate, needing no network, gained +0.129 (95% CI 0.0017-0.2543; 97.6% of resamples positive) over the tool.

items.title: Integrating CRISPRi perturbation responses and transcription-factor binding priors for regulatory network inference in triple-negative breast cancer
items.blurb: Triple-Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC) represents an aggressive breast cancer subtype that lacks actionable cell-surface receptors, restricting frontline systemic management to cytotoxic chemotherapy. While recent functional epigenomics shows that TNBC progression is governed by non-coding regulatory remodeling at distal super-enhancers, conventional Gene Regulatory Network (GRN) inference methods rely on observational transcriptomic co-expression, which suffers from technical dropouts and confounding correlations that inflate false discoveries (>30%). Here, we present an interventional network inference framework that integrates large-scale single-cell CRISPR-interference perturbation sequencing (Perturb-seq; GSE224986, 95,678 cells across 11,975 sgRNAs) with ENCODE Factorbook ChIP-seq physical transcription factor binding priors across 819 somatic mutation-associated enhancer loci in human TNBC (MDA-MB-231). Our pipeline reconstructed a tripartite network yielding 5,935 physical TF-enhancer edges, 383,757 functional enhancer-gene edges, and 542,760 unique TF-target gene functional pairs across 372 active enhancers. Topological centrality prioritized master transcriptional drivers governing TNBC oncogenic signaling, including CTCF, POLR2A, EP300, JUND, MYC, and FOS, which regulate Hallmark programs for Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition (p = 1.2 x 10-9) and cell cycle progression. Explainable machine learning (SHAP TreeExplainer) revealed non-linear, thresholded transactivation dynamics for AP-1 and MYC. Quantitative benchmarking against held-out CRISPRi ground truth demonstrated strong discriminatory accuracy (AUROC = 0.8999, AUPRC = 0.8745, Precision = 90.13%, FDR = 9.87%), substantially outperforming GENIE3 (AUPRC = 0.6323, FDR = 35.73%) and co-expression correlation (AUPRC = 0.6814). In silico-simulated driver feature silencing correlated with experimental responses (R2 = 0.473, p < 10-122), and master driver signatures significantly stratified overall survival in the METABRIC (n = 320) and TCGA-BRCA (n = 160; p [≤] 0.019) cohorts. Finally, in silico perturbation modeling indicated that multi-target epigenetic combinations achieved 93% topological disruption of oncogenic regulatory connectivity, nominating prioritized candidate circuits for experimental validation.

items.title: TrailMix: Mixture Proportion and Placement Estimation of Ancient Hominin mtDNA Samples using a Pangenomic Reference
items.blurb: Hominin mitochondrial DNA extracted from sediments or ancient environments is sometimes a mixture of multiple contributing sources. Researchers must subsequently computationally identify from which mitochondrial lineages the DNA sequences comes (e.g. Denisovan vs. modern human superhaplogroup) and ideally, quantify their abundance. Bioinformatics approaches described in the literature to achieve this involve in-house scripts or heuristics applied to tools designed for other datasets. However, such approaches have neither been fully tested nor do they provide credible intervals on model parameters. To address this, we introduce TrailMix, a C++ program for estimating contributing mixture proportions as well as individual source placements on the hominin mitochondrial tree for ancient environmental DNA. Using a pangenome reference graph to mitigate reference-related bias, TrailMix works well to accurately deconvolve mixtures of multiple mitochondrial lineages and place each contributor within its respective phylogenetic context. Crucially, it allows users to place minor contributing sources on the tree even on ancestral nodes without needing to reach consensus in the presence of multiple sources. TrailMix is part of the vgan suite of tools and is available at https://github.com/grenaud/vgan.

items.title: deeprok: highly accurate prokaryotic gene prediction through deep learning and overlap-aware decoding
items.blurb: Prokaryotic gene prediction is often considered solved, yet widely used tools still disagree on many genes, chiefly short genes and translation starts. We present deeprok, an ab initio prokaryotic gene prediction method that combines a base-level neural network with an overlap-aware decoder, and refines start-site predictions with a self-trained neural ranker. On four curated genomes distant from its training data, deeprok made 10-18% fewer exact-match errors than Prodigal and GeneMarkS-2, and on 2,925 experimentally verified starts it made 21-41% fewer start errors. Furthermore, deeprok's base-level architecture reveals lineage-specific translation initiation signals. These results show that per-base deep learning combined with overlap-aware decoding can improve prokaryotic gene prediction, especially for resolving translation starts.

items.title: Multiscale superinformation reveals structured organization of genomic sequence features
items.blurb: Genomic sequence organization varies across spatial scales, but sequence complexity measures are often evaluated at a single resolution. Superinformation (SI), introduced by Bose and Chouhan, measures heterogeneity in local sequence entropy by taking the entropy of the distribution of block-level Shannon entropy values. We characterize SI across 14 Sequence Ontology-defined genomic feature classes in seven species and seven block sizes from 20 to 200 bp. SI profiles were non-increasing for 72 of 86 evaluable species-feature combinations, although this pattern was not universal. Observed SI generally exceeded both a block-count-controlled random null and a species-level GC-controlled null. Associations with mononucleotide entropy, dinucleotide entropy, and GC content were modest, with no individual descriptor explaining more than 10.4% of the observed variation. For the 13 complete feature-level profiles used in geometric analysis, the first two principal components explained 97.859% of the variance, and hierarchical clustering grouped features with similar SI trajectories. We also summarize the profiles using the Characteristic Information Scale and Information Persistence Score. These analyses extend the original superinformation framework to a comparative, multiscale analysis of genomic feature heterogeneity while keeping the interpretation of SI limited to the sequence properties measured here.

items.title: Multifunctional CNT-based Platform for Enhanced Dopaminergic Differentiation and Electrochemical Dopamine Sensing from Human iPSC-derived Neurons.
items.blurb: Pairing neuro-electrochemical sensors with physiologically relevant neuronal models represents a new frontier in the study of neurodegenerative diseases. In this work, we reported an electroactive platform for in situ detection of dopamine, combining human iPSC-derived neurons with carbon nanotubes. In this system, carbon nanotubes served a triple role: enhancing the electroactive area, catalyzing dopamine oxidation, and promoting subtype-specific dopaminergic differentiation. We developed a robust protocol achieving functional dopaminergic neurons, confirmed via qPCR, immunocytochemistry, MEA electrophysiology, and calcium imaging. CNT substrates were associated with a significant increase in the TH/neurofilament overlap (37.90 {+/-} 3.80% vs. 26.01 {+/-} 3.75% in controls). Applying differential pulse voltammetry and chronoamperometry, we quantified extracellular dopamine at 1.25 M and confirmed the stimulus-dependent release induced by benztropine and KCl depolarization. Post-electrochemical immunostaining confirmed that neurons retained their morphology and TH expression. Overall, this work establishes a novel framework for neurodegenerative disease modeling that recapitulates key electrophysiological and neurochemical features of dopaminergic neurons, representing a powerful tool for disease modeling, drug screening, and the development of next-generation neuro-biosensors.

items.title: Reproducible and open-source statistical shape models of the pose-normalized adult lower body: development and comparative evaluation
items.blurb: Accurate skeletal geometry is important for subject-specific musculoskeletal modeling, but the choice of statistical representation may affect anatomical reconstruction. This study developed a reproducible workflow and compared four statistical shape model families of the pose-normalized adult lower body: pooled global, articulated shape-pose, sex-conditioned shared-basis, and independently fitted sex-specific models. Models were developed from computed-tomography-derived geometries of 20 adults and evaluated using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. Model coefficients were estimated from each held-out subjects complete registered surfaces, assessing dense-surface representational generalization. Outcomes included model compactness, whole-body and bone-wise surface root-mean-square errors, and reconstruction errors for hip, knee, and ankle joint centers. A pelvis-referenced bounding-box anisotropic-scaling baseline was included as a geometric comparator. The pooled global and sex-conditioned models shared a principal-component basis and therefore identical compactness spectra, with the first component explaining 90.16% of the variance. These models provided the most consistent reconstruction performance. The articulated model had ankle and knee joint-center errors 9.1 and 5.4 mm higher, respectively, than the pooled global model. Independently fitted sex-specific models did not improve whole-body reconstruction over the pooled global or sex-conditioned models in this small cohort. Under the present evaluation, the pooled global and sex-conditioned models reduced whole-body surface errors by approximately 4.1 and 4.0 mm, respectively, relative to scaling. The pooled global model also reduced ankle and knee joint-center errors by 12.5 and 11.0 mm. These results characterize the implemented representations within the available dataset. The scaling comparison was not input matched, and sparse-input and external validation remain necessary. The accompanying LowerBodySSM workflow and interactive Companion provide a reproducible resource for further anatomical modeling and evaluation.

items.title: RUBRIC: rapid quality assessment tool for RNA 3D structures
items.blurb: Cryo-electron microscopy has transformed RNA structural biology, revealing increasingly large and complex structures at an unprecedented pace. However, validation methods have lagged behind, and deposited models can contain distorted base pairs, incorrect ribose puckers and backbone conformational outliers. Here, we introduce Rapid Unified Base-pair, Ribose and backbone Integrity Check (RUBRIC), an open-source program that combines RNA structural annotation with local validation of base pairs, sugars, and backbones. RUBRIC assigns Leontis-Westhof classes and identifies geometrically ambiguous pairs that cannot be confidently assigned to a single class. It scores unambiguous pairs against reference geometries for each type and class, identifying the parameters responsible for low scores. It also assigns backbone suites to known conformers, suggests target torsions for unassigned suites and flags incorrect ribose puckers. RUBRIC analyzes a complete human ribosome in under a second, with base-pair detection and classification consistent with leading annotation programs. These programs disagreed significantly more often on pairs RUBRIC flagged as ambiguous than on unambiguous pairs. The geometric problems flagged by RUBRIC were reduced in higher-resolution models of the same RNA or after refinement targeting the affected geometry, indicating that these problems are correctable. A PyMOL plug-in and machine-readable output support model building, correction before deposition and assessment of deposited structures before reuse. RUBRIC can therefore help improve RNA structures in the PDB and the datasets used to train and evaluate RNA structure prediction methods.

items.title: AlphaFold-assisted design of a modular Laminin E8 Fragment Panel
items.blurb: Laminins are large, heterotrimeric glycoproteins that are a major structural component of basement membranes and the extracellular matrix. Although they are difficult to produce recombinantly because of their large size, a smaller fragment of the laminin heterotrimer that supports cell adhesion and cell migration, termed E8, can be recombinantly expressed. Here, we use AlphaFold to optimize laminin E8 fragments and design a panel of interchangeable laminin , {beta}, and {gamma} chains that can be combined to produce all isoforms recombinantly. These recombinant E8 fragments support adhesion of cells bearing their cognate integrins, and will be useful tools for stem-cell, organoid, and laminin-binding integrin biology research.

items.title: Joint Estimation of Mother and Daughter Protein Regulatory Networks Quantifies Inheritance in Yeast Lineages
items.blurb: Live-cell imaging tracks multiple protein levels within individual cells across divisions in real time, enabling direct measurement of how regulatory dynamics are inherited by a daughter cell from her mother. This technology presents a unique opportunity to directly observe longitudinal dynamics, in contrast to single-cell RNA sequencing, which can only measure cells cross-sectionally. However, there is a lack of computational methods for analyzing live-cell imaging data. Existing frameworks based on ordinary differential equations (ODEs) estimate networks from individual time series, but adapting them to mother-daughter pairs poses a dilemma: pooling both cells forces complete inheritance, while fitting each cell separately starves the short daughter trajectory of timepoints needed for reliable estimation. To address this gap, we develop PRNODE (Protein Regulatory Networks via ODEs), which models each cell's network as a deviation from a shared regulatory scaffold and estimates the scaffold and both deviations jointly under a fused group-lasso penalty. The mother's longer time series thereby supports the daughter's estimate, while allowing the two networks to differ wherever the data demand it. We then propose a novel measure of inheritance based on comparing the rate of change of protein levels between the mother's and daughter's networks. Across simulation studies, we find that PRNODE outperforms existing ODE estimation methods in recovering the networks of daughter cells and in estimating inheritance. Finally, we apply PRNODE to many mother-daughter pairs of Saccharomyces cerevisiae observed over a 9-hour period at 12-minute intervals. Many estimated networks show a negative feedback loop between the cell-cycle inhibitor Whi5 and the cyclin Clb2, which together sustain cell-cycle oscillations. We also find that the measured inheritance tracks the number of regulatory edges a daughter shares with her mother with the same sign, more than the presence of any single edge. PRNODE is available as an R package at https://github.com/shirmath/LIC_methods.

items.title: Agreement between structure prediction tools does not indicate biological plausibility in cancer fusion proteins
items.blurb: While protein-folding software has made great strides in recent years, reliability is known to be poorer on novel structures and failure modes are not fully characterised. Cancer fusion proteins present a unique case of proteins absent from model training data but constructed from parents with known structures. This study tests four popular protein-folding tools on three categories of protein: control, cancer-associated, and uncharacterised fusion proteins. We assessed computational performance, accuracy, and distinct failure modes. For well-characterised proteins, all tools tested returned the correct structures in all but one case, with some tools returning an average of two distinct structural forms in the exception. For characterised cancer-associated proteins, most predictions were highly accurate; poorer predictions often still returned some consistent high-confidence domains but produced divergent results in other areas that were both variable between tools and at odds with experimental structures. For cancer fusion proteins having available parent-protein reference structures, results fell into two clear categories. Roughly half contained structures matching to the functional domains of their parent proteins at high confidence, in keeping with biological expectation for these proteins; the others contained little evidence of matching structures, independent of the tool used. Predictions for fusion proteins differed far more between tools than those for characterised proteins with a median inter-tool TM-score 0.272 versus 0.853 respectively. However, agreement between tools did not indicate a more biologically plausible prediction. For example, all tools predicted drastically different structures for fusion protein TMPRSS2-ERG, but all predictions still contained the core ERG functional domains; conversely, all tools produced highly consistent structures for DNAJB1-PRKACA, but none of the predictions contained the expected functional regions. We recommend that users of these tools use care and caution in the assessments of outputs and consider biological knowledge before blindly trusting results.

items.title: ViruDB: An Assay-Aware Molecular Database and Endpoint-Adaptive Multimodal Learning Framework for Antibiofilm, Quorum-Sensing Inhibition, and Antivirulence Research
items.blurb: Antibiofilm and quorum-sensing inhibitory molecules have become increasingly attractive candidates to complement traditional antibacterial approaches, but the experimental evidence ranges from heterogeneous assays, organisms, methods of activity measurement, and chemical representation. We created ViruDB, a molecular evidence resource that is assay-aware, and tested an endpoint-adaptive multimodal learning framework for quantitative activity prediction. Curated collection of 8765 experimental evidence records for 3563 unique molecules: 2,959 quantitative observations, of which 2,345 were antibiofilm, 569 were quorum-sensing inhibition [QSI], and 45 were antivirulence. Molecular representations included 217 2D descriptors from RDKit, 2,048-bit ECFP4 fingerprints, molecular graphs, and some information about the biological context. A molecule- and scaffold-disjoint primary partition was used, which resulted in 2,339 observations in the training set, 265 observations in the validation set and 355 observations in the independent test set. ViruFusion-TaskExpert-MTL and an endpoint specific combination with classical regressors were selected by validation. The final predictor yielded an RMSE value of 0.5460 and an R2 of 0.4816 on the antibiofilm activity dataset (n=286) and an RMSE value of 0.5744 and an R2 of 0.4082 on the QSI dataset (n=67) in the reported frozen independent evaluation. Exploratory anti-virulence regression (n=2 test observations). The results validate quantitative, endpoint based prioritization under chemical novelty and highlight the significance of assay provenance, assay leakage control and external biological assay validation.

items.title: Age- and sex-related variation in TREC and KREC and the association of rs2204985 with TREC in adults
items.blurb: Background: T-cell receptor excision circles (TREC) and kappa-deleting recombination excision circles (KREC) are indirect markers of new T- and B-cell production. Recorded zero values complicate the analysis of age-related and genetic associations in adult cohorts. Methods: We analyzed 574 adult outpatients aged 39-95 years, including 250 men and 324 women. TREC and KREC were quantified by multiplex real-time PCR and normalized per 100,000 cells. The rs2204985 variant was evaluated using age- and sex-adjusted genetic models. A two-part model separated TREC positivity from quantitative TREC levels among participants with positive values. Alternative regressions and receiver operating characteristic analyses were used for sensitivity and age-classification analyses. Results: Age was more strongly associated with log10(TREC + 0.1) than with log10(KREC + 0.1) (beta = -0.0365 and -0.00728 per year, respectively). Women had higher levels in the main-effects models, although the KREC age association differed by sex. There was no clear evidence of an additive rs2204985 association with TREC positivity (odds ratio = 0.836, p = 0.290). Among the 481 TREC-positive participants, the G allele was associated with higher log10(TREC) (beta = +0.0688 per allele, 95% CI +0.0177 to +0.1199, p = 0.0084; q = 0.0126 across three conditional genetic-model tests). Smearing-corrected marginal predictions for a 58-year-old woman were 40.4 copies/100,000 cells for AA and 53.5 for GG. In the common-positive subset (n = 465), TREC showed higher age-classification AUCs than KREC or their ratio. Conclusions: The rs2204985 association was apparent in conditional TREC levels but not in recorded positivity or full-cohort regression. Analyzing these outcomes separately makes the association easier to interpret, without establishing that zero TREC denotes absent thymopoiesis or that the variant directly alters thymic function.

items.title: Local macrophage and cDC1 cooperation in the liver drives T-cell immune surveillance against pioneering metastatic cancer cells.
items.blurb: The liver is one of the most frequent sites for hematogenous metastasis across different types of cancer, but how the liver mounts effective immune responses against arriving tumor cells is not fully understood. Using intravital imaging, we have visualized the initial steps of liver metastasis and delineated three phases in the immune response at the earliest stages of liver metastasis: first, there is continuous surveillance of the liver parenchyma by discrete immune cell subsets in the premetastatic tissue. Second, upon metastatic cell arrival, there is massive neutrophil recruitment and tumor-cell material uptake mediated by resident macrophages. Third, antitumor-specific T-cell activation takes place in situ within intrahepatic leukocyte clusters. We find that tumor-derived material uptake triggers transcriptional programs in liver myeloid cells that upregulate chemoattraction programs in Kupffer cells and cDCs, leading to T-cell activation. Antigen cross-presentation and a functional partnership between cDC1s and local macrophages to recruit and form T-cell activation clusters are required for the elicitation of these intrahepatic T-cell responses. Consequently, prior expansion of cDCs by Flt3L-Ig treatment significantly enhances immunosurveillance, curtailing successful metastasis development. Collectively, our findings identify coordinated immune responses that are essential for anti-metastatic immunity within the liver, uncovering a program to mount defenses against tumor cells arriving in the liver.

items.title: VisioWell, an all-in-one high-throughput platform to study haematopoietic cells division
items.blurb: Live-cell imaging has the potential to unravel crucial parameters for haematopoietic normal and leukaemic stem and progenitor cells. Yet, this technology requires a combination of technical and analytical skill sets that can be difficult to find in a traditional haematology lab. We present VisioWell, an all-in-one experimental platform specifically designed to measure the early division dynamics of blood stem and progenitor cells, from a simple brightfield long-term acquisition. We combined a simple custom-made microwell array to trap thousands of individual cells with a powerful semi-automatic analytical pipeline, able to segment, correct, and retrieve the division times for the first three sets of divisions. We validated VisioWell with primary cells from human cord blood and with a cellular model of myeloid leukaemia, revealing that CDK4/6 inhibition induces an increase in asynchronous division. By lowering the technical and analytical barriers to live-cell imaging, VisioWell makes label-free, non-destructive analysis of division dynamics accessible to any haematology lab, while preserving cells for downstream fate and functional readouts.

items.title: Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years
items.blurb: Medications taken years or even long ago may leave lasting changes in your gut microbiome, according to a study of more than 2,500 people. Researchers discovered that common drugs, including antidepressants, blood pressure medications, and anxiety treatments, can leave microbial “fingerprints” long after patients stop taking them. Surprisingly, some anxiety medications had effects comparable to broad-spectrum antibiotics.

items.title: Type 2 diabetes linked to 53% higher Alzheimer’s risk, major review finds
items.blurb: People with type 2 diabetes face a 53% higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease, according to a major new review of 40 studies. Researchers estimate that nearly five out of every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes develop Alzheimer’s each year. By focusing specifically on these two conditions, the study offers a clearer understanding of a potentially serious connection between metabolic health and brain health.

items.title: Silver briefly forms a rare crystal structure seen in radioactive polonium
items.blurb: How atoms are arranged in a material shapes many of its properties. The same carbon atoms, for example, can form diamond and graphite depending on how they are arranged, giving rise to materials with vastly different chemical and physical properties. Now, researchers at Hokkaido University have discovered a new crystal structure of silver with unusually high chemical reactivity. The findings, published in Nano Letters, could open new avenues for exploring materials with desirable properties.

items.title: New Species of Flying Frog Discovered in Indonesia
items.blurb: And it’s got a very unusual way of laying eggs

items.title: DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth
items.blurb: Scientists have uncovered a surprising reason why early life may have survived Earth's intense ultraviolet radiation: a key component of DNA appears to turn potentially destructive damage into something easier to repair. The discovery could help solve a decades-old evolutionary mystery and reveal how life endured the harsh conditions of our planet's earliest days.

items.title: A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA
items.blurb: At an astonishing 194 years old, Jonathan the giant tortoise is the world's oldest living land animal, and scientists may have finally uncovered the secrets behind his extraordinary lifespan. Researchers identified 287 unique genetic variants linked to processes that help repair damaged DNA, control inflammation, regulate insulin, and suppress cancer.

items.title: Scientists discover a hidden eye disease that slowly steals night vision
items.blurb: Scientists have discovered a new genetic eye disease that can silently damage peripheral and night vision while leaving central sight largely unaffected for years. The condition may be detectable through an unusual difficulty adjusting to darkness, offering a potential early warning sign before irreversible retinal damage occurs.

items.title: AI uncovers hidden bladder cancer warning signs years before diagnosis
items.blurb: Scientists have developed an AI tool that can uncover hidden warning signs of bladder cancer up to five years before diagnosis, identifying 85% of cases in a major study involving nearly 70,000 patients. By revealing subtle patterns that conventional screening misses, the technology could help doctors detect cancer earlier and spare patients unnecessary invasive procedures.

items.title: Alzheimer’s breakthrough exposes a hidden flaw in the brain’s cleanup system
items.blurb: Scientists have identified a gene that helps the brain’s immune cells contain harmful plaques linked to Alzheimer’s, potentially revealing a new way to fight the disease. When the gene malfunctioned in mice, toxic buildup accelerated and cognitive abilities declined, raising hopes that restoring its function could help protect the brain.

items.title: A common blood pressure drug has a surprising effect on calorie-burning brown fat
items.blurb: Scientists have discovered that a common blood pressure drug can activate calorie-burning brown fat in mice, potentially opening a new path toward improving metabolic health. An analysis of more than 100,000 patients also revealed surprising links between brown fat and lower rates of heart disease, diabetes, anxiety, and depression.

items.title: Read&Tag enables antibody-independent combinatorial and multifactorial chromatin profiling
items.blurb: Genome-wide chromatin profiling methods based on in situ tagmentation have expanded access to epigenomic information but generally rely on antibodies, thereby limiting their multifactorial capacity and the direct measurement of combinatorial chromatin states. Here, we introduce Read&Tag, in which engineered chromatin reader domains or intrabodies are fused directly to the Tn5 transposase to target specific chromatin features in situ. Read&Tag profiles active and repressive histone modifications, DNA methylation, and elongating RNA polymerase II, with signal amplitude increasing with target abundance and remaining robust in frozen tissue and low-input samples. Because the targeting module is a protein of defined structure and affinity, two specificities can be combined within a single complex. Tagmentation by such a dual-specificity reader requires H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 to be present together in the same chromatin fragment. The co-occurrence of both marks thus becomes a precondition of the measurement rather than an inference drawn from independently measured profiles. Combining barcoded reader-Tn5 complexes with primer-timed signal augmentation enables the measurement of four chromatin features in a single reaction. Read&Tag therefore provides a modular, antibody-independent platform for combinatorial and multifactorial profiling.

items.title: Single-molecule in situ detection and quantification of mitochondrial DNA heteroplasmy
items.blurb: The mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is a multi-copy genome present in most eukaryotic cells and essential for life. The presence of different mtDNA variants within a cell, or heteroplasmy, may cause pathology when the level of deleterious variants exceeds a critical threshold. However, the mechanisms that control heteroplasmy levels remain poorly understood, in part due to a lack of technologies to visualise mtDNA heteroplasmy in situ and correlate it with intracellular processes. mtDNA single-molecule fluorescence in situ hybridisation (mtDNA-smFISH) allows in situ visualisation of mtDNA molecules and sequence-specific detection of heteroplasmic variants. Here, we provide protocols for sequence-specific detection of mtDNA, large-scale single mtDNA deletions and species-specific haplotypes, in fixed human and Drosophila cells and in whole-mount Drosophila tissues. Combining mtDNA-smFISH with immunohistochemistry using biotin-labelled primary antibodies that resist heat-based denaturation, allows concomitant detection of intracellular proteins. We further describe two image-analysis pipelines, one for 3D quantification and one open-source for 2D quantification of mtDNA deletions in Drosophila tissues and cell culture. This enables estimation of single-cell heteroplasmy levels, observation of cell-to-cell variability, and detection of mtDNA variants at a subcellular level, making mtDNA-smFISH a powerful tool to study the intracellular processes regulating heteroplasmy and mtDNA quality control.

items.title: Smyd1 regulates H3K4me3 to support adaptive fatty acid oxidation in the adult heart during lipid overload
items.blurb: Obesity and metabolic syndrome are major risk factors for heart failure, and impaired fatty acid oxidation (FAO) is a key contributor to metabolic dysfunction in obesity-related cardiomyopathy. However, how the heart maintains FAO and adapts to chronic lipid overload remains poorly understood. Here, we identify SET and MYND domain-containing protein 1 (Smyd1), a muscle-specific histone methyltransferase, as an early compensatory regulator of cardiac metabolism in response to lipid overload. In wild-type mouse hearts, high-fat diet (HFD) feeding induced transient increases in Smyd1 expression and H3K4me3 levels during the early-to-mid phase of metabolic stress, both of which returned to baseline levels during prolonged HFD exposure. Single-cell RNA sequencing further revealed that this adaptive increase in Smyd1 expression occurred predominantly in cardiomyocytes. In contrast, cardiac-specific Smyd1 heterozygous knockout mice exhibited accelerated cardiac dysfunction, left ventricular dilation, increased myocardial fibrosis, and reduced survival following HFD feeding. Mechanistically, Smyd1 deficiency impaired the adaptive upregulation of key FAO-related genes and reduced cardiac FAO activity. Furthermore, co-immunoprecipitation analysis revealed an interaction between Smyd1 and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPAR), suggesting a potential mechanism by which Smyd1 supports FAO gene expression. Taken together, these findings identify Smyd1 as an early compensatory regulator that supports FAO-dependent metabolic adaptation and protects the heart against lipid overload-induced cardiac dysfunction. This adaptive mechanism, involving H3K4me3 regulation and the Smyd1-PPAR interaction, may provide potential therapeutic targets for therapeutic strategies aimed at preserving cardiac metabolic flexibility in obesity-related cardiomyopathy.

items.title: A latent tau amplifier in the neuronal proteome lowers the seeding threshold for Alzheimers disease pathology
items.blurb: The stereotyped spread of tau pathology through connected brain regions is accompanied by striking differences in the vulnerability of individual neuronal populations, pointing to cell-intrinsic determinants of susceptibility. Using a combination of computational APR analysis, in vitro and cellular aggregation assays, and quantitative proteomics of human postmortem brain, we identify the splicing factor TRA2B as an endogenous modifier of this susceptibility. TRA2B enhances the activity of patient-derived tau seeds, promotes tau pathology in vivo, and progressively redistributes from the nucleus into insoluble tau-associated material in Alzheimers disease brain. Mechanistically, TRA2B contains two aggregation-prone regions (APRs) homologous to tau nucleation sites that are required for tau interaction and seeding enhancement. Yet this activity is not constitutive: isolated TRA2B APRs promote aggregation, whereas the full-length protein can inhibit, amplify or have little effect on tau aggregation depending on protein state and seeding context. Perturbation of the regulatory RS2 region switches TRA2B away from its amplifying state, revealing that its sequence-encoded aggregation potential is regulatable. Thus, TRA2B acts as a latent tau amplifier, providing a mechanism by which the neuronal proteome can tune cellular susceptibility to the propagation of pathological tau.

items.title: Metabolic priming recruits tumour cells across a mitochondrial vulnerability threshold and sensitizes them to chemotherapy
items.blurb: Intratumour heterogeneity allows a fraction of cancer cells to escape otherwise effective treatment. Here we ask whether metabolic priming can recruit heterogeneous tumour cells into a transient mitochondrial state that is selectively vulnerable to photodynamic damage. Tetramethylrhodamine methyl ester (TMRM) has previously been shown to act as a mitochondria targeted photosensitizer; we exploit its voltage-dependent accumulation and dynamic fluorescence during pulsed illumination to quantify vulnerability in single cells. The response is a reproducible fluorescence excursion, a rise to a maximum followed by a decay, accompanied by reactive oxygen species production. Comparing seventeen descriptors of this excursion against subsequent fate in 195 cells across four arms shows that quantities referenced to each cell's own resting value outperform static intensity. The simple difference Fmax F0 predicts death with held-out areas under the curve of approximately 0.75 to 0.79, whereas resting intensity alone carries little transferable information and time to peak does not discriminate fate in the datasets tested. Metabolic priming with the PKM2 activator TEPP46 or with ethyl pyruvate increases the fraction of responding cells; under TEPP46 almost the whole population enters the responding state. PKM2 abundance is associated with faster entry into that state, and PKM2 is heterogeneous in human skin tumour sections. Four hours of camptothecin shifts the response distribution, increasing the fraction of cells above the untreated median from 50% to 76%, identifying a candidate intervention window. In combination experiments, TMRM photodynamic treatment produced survival below the Bliss-independence expectation with camptothecin or TRAIL, in both treatment orders and across three cell lines; these combination measurements are descriptive and require independent replication. The study therefore identifies a perturbation-revealed mitochondrial vulnerability that can be pharmacologically recruited and followed dynamically at single-cell resolution. It is a proof of concept in cultured cells and human tumour sections and has not been tested in vivo.

items.title: YAP activity sustains mitochondrial adaptation to NAMPT inhibition in triple-negative breast cancer
items.blurb: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) is an essential metabolic cofactor, and maintenance of NAD+ homeostasis is critical for cancer cell survival. Pharmacological inhibition of nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT), the rate-limiting enzyme of the NAD+ salvage pathway, induces NAD+ depletion and energetic stress, although the development of resistance limits its therapeutic potential. We have previously shown that acquired resistance to NAMPT inhibition in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) cells is associated with extensive metabolic rewiring. Here, we investigated the role of the Hippo pathway effector YAP in the cellular adaptation to NAMPT inhibition. Stable YAP downregulation markedly decreased the sensitivity of MDA-MB-231 cells to the NAMPT inhibitors FK866 and CHS-828, whereas re-expression of constitutively active YAP5SA partially restored sensitivity to FK866. YAP-silenced cells maintained NAD(H) and ATP levels during FK866 exposure and showed reduced oxidative stress and caspase 3/7 activation. Comparative proteomic analysis of YAP-silenced cells and cells with acquired FK866 resistance revealed common alterations in mitochondrial, cell-cycle, and RNA-processing programs. Consistently, YAP downregulation altered the cell-cycle response to FK866 and increased mitochondrial respiration, spare respiratory capacity, and mitochondrial mass. These findings identify YAP as a modulator of the cellular response to NAMPT inhibition and suggest that sustained YAP downregulation contributes to the establishment of an adaptive state characterized by reduced proliferative and biosynthetic programs together with increased mitochondrial capacity.

items.title: Media matters: A resource for understanding the determinants of migratory potential of malignant and non-malignant cells
items.blurb: Cell mobility is critical for homeostatic processes such as wound repair and diseases like cancer metastasis. While the advent of migrastatic and antimetastatic therapies has promise, the identification and translation of pathways important for migratory plasticity into druggable targets approved in clinical trials are considerably lacking. To better understand why, we developed an unbiased high-throughput wound-healing/invasion assay to screen for the migratory potential of >60 non-malignant and malignant cell lines derived from the pancreas, colon, skin, breast, prostate, and lung. The goal of this phenotypic screen was to provide a resource of migration/invasion potential and insight into the differential properties not only between malignant and non-malignant cells but also the various carcinomas. Surprisingly, we found non-malignant epithelial cells of the lung, skin, and pancreas migrated/invaded faster than their malignant counterparts. We observed perturbation of glucose metabolism, via inhibition of glycolysis, restricted the migration of non-malignant but not cancer cells, whereas inhibition of oxidative phosphorylation limited the mobility of malignant more than normal cells of the lung, skin, and pancreas. Short-term acclimation of cancer cells in low-nutrient media, containing low/no serum, low calcium, and physiological concentrations of glucose, increased in vitro migration/invasion and in vivo metastatic potential of lung but not pancreatic carcinomas. Phenotypic and metabolic screens presented here could identify prospective therapeutics not only for cancer metastasis, but also diseases driven by the dysregulation of wound-healing/regeneration.

items.title: Syngeneic human iPSC Macrophages and Microglia possess distinct neuroinflammatory profiles, responses to HIV infection, and ART treatment
items.blurb: Macrophages are innate immune cells that primarily function as professional phagocytes, playing essential roles throughout the body in host defense and maintaining homeostasis. The CNS is populated by two anatomically distinct macrophage populations; parenchymal microglia and border-resident CNS-associated macrophages (CAMs). These populations coordinate the neuroinflammatory response to pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) through Toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling and are exposed to distinct microenvironmental cues that could shape their functions. CNS macrophages are also involved in infection with neurotropic viruses such as HIV, where the persistent infection contributes to chronic neuroinflammation and the constellation of other neurological symptoms collectively termed neuroHIV. Although antiretroviral therapy (cART) has transformed HIV care and lessened the severity of many neuroHIV symptoms, the persistence of CNS viral reservoirs and neurological deficits remains a major comorbidity and barrier to cure. Understanding specific contributions of microglia and CAMs to inflammation and neuroHIV has been challenging due to the lack of genetically matched human model systems enabling direct mechanistic comparison between of microglia and CAMs. To address this, we optimized the generation of syngeneic, human-induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) derived microglia-like (iMg) and CAM-like (iMacs) cells. These are generated simultaneously from a single donor line and have the same genetic background, enabling side-by-side characterization and functional analyses of inflammation and HIV infection. Transcriptomic profiling by RNA sequencing revealed substantial baseline differences in inflammatory and immune signaling pathways between iMg and iMacs. These intrinsic differences were also observed in TLR-specific NF-{kappa}B responses. Stimulation of TLR4 drove heightened response in iMg relative to iMac, correlating closely with morphological changes, while stimulating TLR2 had a contrasting effect, eliciting a stronger and more robust early NF-{kappa}B response in iMacs. In HIV infection studies, iMacs were more permissive to viral replication at baseline, whereas iMg showed a reduced susceptibility to infection. However, iMacs responded more robustly to cART, while iMg exhibited relative resistance to cART-mediated suppression. These findings delineate fundamental inflammatory and virologic differences between human microglia and CAMs and provide a robust foundation on which to further examine HIV infection, cART efficacy, and immune function in these distinct CNS myeloid populations.

items.title: High GPX4 Expression Marks an Oxidative-Metabolic, PD-L1/CD47-Low and Stroma-Poor Tumor State in Hepatocellular Carcinoma
items.blurb: Background: Glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) protects cancer cells from ferroptosis and is a candidate therapeutic target in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). How GPX4 expression relates to the immune and metabolic features of patient tumors is not well characterized. Methods: We analyzed RNA-sequencing data from 366 primary tumors of the TCGA-LIHC PanCancer Atlas cohort (365 with survival data). Associations between GPX4 and ten immune and stress-response markers were tested by Spearman correlation with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, then re-estimated after adjustment for consensus tumor purity, CTNNB1 and TP53 mutation, age and sex. A T-cell-inflamed profile, a CD8 T-cell score and an NRF2 target-gene score, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of GPX4-high versus GPX4-low tumors, and Cox models were added as further tests. Results: Higher GPX4 expression was associated with lower expression of PD-L1 (CD274; rho = -0.34, 95% CI -0.43 to -0.24, p = 2.4 x 10^-11), CD47 (rho = -0.21), the macrophage marker CD163 (rho = -0.17) and a fibroblast/extracellular-matrix score (rho = -0.22). These associations persisted after adjustment (CD274 rho = -0.37 in the fully adjusted model). GSEA showed enrichment of oxidative phosphorylation, mitochondrial, fatty-acid, xenobiotic and glutathione metabolism programs and depletion of extracellular-matrix, TGF-beta and cell-adhesion programs in GPX4-high tumors. GPX4 was not associated with a T-cell-inflamed profile (rho = -0.07), a CD8 T-cell score (rho = -0.03), cytolytic activity (rho = 0.04) or an NRF2 target-gene score (rho = 0.03), although NFE2L2 mRNA was inversely correlated with GPX4 (rho = -0.32). GPX4 expression was not associated with overall survival (stage-adjusted hazard ratio per SD 1.09, 95% CI 0.91-1.29). Conclusions: In TCGA-LIHC, high GPX4 expression marks a metabolically active, PD-L1/CD47-low and matrix-poor tumor state, with no evidence of T-cell exclusion, NRF2 pathway activation or prognostic value. These correlative findings come from a single cohort and require external validation and functional testing. Keywords: hepatocellular carcinoma; ferroptosis; GPX4; PD-L1; CD47; tumor microenvironment; NRF2; gene set enrichment analysis; TCGA

items.blurb:

Credit where credit is due: it takes some nerve for Amazon to open its latest holiday romcom, Clashing Through the Snow, with characters bemoaning the enervated state of the book industry. Publishing isn’t the cultural epicenter it once was, reports boutique press head Jeremy (PJ Byrne) before announcing some impending new year’s layoffs. Alas, things have changed – “if Faulkner were alive today, he’d be making ASMR videos with Mr Beast” (or, perhaps, competing on Prime Video’s Beast Games?)

Self-awareness can be key to the ludicrous joys of a Christmas romcom confection, though Clashing Through the Snow, starring 1923’s Michelle Randolph and homegrown Amazon star Christopher Briney (The Summer I Turned Pretty), tests one’s patience for beating you to the branded punchline. Briney’s Ryan, a numbers-driven, macro-counting kind of book editor, pitches a “financial trends with benefits” romance that could be “Rebecca Yarros big”. Soulmates, says Randolph’s rival workhorse editor Hannah, are as mythical as “ethical billionaires and pain-free bikini waxes”. Due to said budget cuts, both have a week to land “a book so big it makes Harry Potter look like a Buzzfeed listicle” for only one to keep their job. What are two LA workaholics going to do on Christmas but take meetings in New York?

items.title: Chemicals, Covid and cabbage: why 2026 has been an amazing year for documentaries
items.blurb:
With Musk, NAZA and You Can See Everything finding large audiences, non-fiction cinema is poised to break through. But there are plenty more gripping stories waiting for their turn in the spotlight

There comes a time in the life of every film enthusiast when they must set aside foolish fictions and face up to some hard truths. Specifically, that time arrives each November in the form of the International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam (IDFA for short), with its tales of crisis and strife, angry resistance and everyday human kindness. The world’s largest documentary festival plays out in the city’s twinkling downtown district, quite near the torture museum, and provides a sharp corrective to the confected dramas and A-list pageantry of Cannes, Toronto and Venice. The forecast is bracing, stormy, and occasionally chilling. Hours of darkness; no stars.

We might not wish to live in the world IDFA shows us, but unfortunately we do, and so it pays to stay informed, be engaged. This year’s lineup of 250-plus documentaries steers us around the geopolitical hot spots, from tales of forced displacement in the West Bank to the rolling hell of Gaza; from a jungle-based guerrilla army in Myanmar (in White Tiger Column, the event’s opening night film) through to the traumatised children of the Vietnamese boat people (Carol Nguyen’s superb Still Night, Burning House). Some of these films could have been torn from the headlines. Others, like Raluca Lupascu’s gripping kitchen-sink tragedy A Modern Roma Fairytale, contain stories previously tucked away out of sight, just waiting to be told.
