items.title: Blade Runner 2099: fans will have no idea what is happening in this sci-fi sequel. Why is it even on TV?
items.blurb:
If you’re a cyberpunk who loves ennui and watching actors you can’t see speak words you can’t hear, get stuck in! The rest of us will just be baffled and bored

Why is James Bond not a TV series by now? Harry Potter, Lord of the Rings, Alien, Star Wars – all given the TV treatment. Franchise-mining is fantastic business, maximising attention share in order to sell adverts. So why not Bond, which is co-owned by Amazon? Maybe watching a punchy sex addict every week, saying his name with weirdly administrative syntax, might just be … too much?

I entertained these thoughts while struggling to get through another series expansion: Blade Runner 2099 (Prime Video, from Wednesday). I’m a fan of the films. Before the original, cinema had imagined the future as serene and orderly. Blade Runner introduced many of us to novelist Philip K Dick’s vision, in which tech has colonised every aspect of life, but inequality has got worse. Surveillance, artificial beings and unchecked corporate power hollow out whatever remains of society. (The fact the new series is on Amazon is the closest it gets to making a joke.)

items.title: ‘Reminds me of home’: why Coming to America is my feelgood movie
items.blurb:
The latest in our series of writers picking their most rewatched comfort films is an ode to Eddie Murphy’s beloved culture-clash comedy

“Good morning, my neighbors!” A young Eddie Murphy shouts from the balcony of a shady apartment building. In the bustling Queens neighborhood, he sticks out like a sore thumb with his foreign accent, tailored blazing jacket and red tie. “Hey, fuck you!” A voice yells from below and Murphy repeats the phrase, believing that it’s a greeting rather than an insult. It’s one of the standout scenes from the film Coming to America, because it’s so absurd but effective in that there is a cultural clash going on here.

In Coming to America, Prince Akeem, played by Eddie Murphy, is the sole heir to the throne of Zamunda, a fictitious African country. Instead of having an arranged marriage, Prince Akeem exercises his autonomy and intends to find his own bride somewhere far away from the continent, much to his parents’ chagrin. With the coin-flip and a roll of the personal globe, Akeem and his sidekick Semmi go to America but more specifically Queens because where else would be more fitting to find his bride? While trying to assimilate to the fast pace of New York living, he pursues Lisa, the heiress to a different kind of throne – that of a fast-food business called McDowell’s. The problem is, she’s already engaged to another. Akeem hides his identity as a royal prince and works at her father’s fast-food restaurant to get closer to her. Will Akeem and Lisa fall in love as he cosplays being working class. Will Lisa leave her rich but arrogant fiance? Will their families accept their Lisa and Akeem if they do decide to marry? Spoiler alert: there’s a happy ending. The plot progression is simple but the character development is full of heart and candor.

items.title: Bill Wyman’s Rock & Roll Lists review – greatest hits and biggest misses
items.blurb:
The rock critic’s obsessive yet incisive sorting of musical genius is a contrarian delight

As veteran US music journalist Bill Wyman (no relation to the Stones bassist) would be the first to point out, the listicle is not a revered form of internet journalism. It labours under a ghastly portmanteau name that simply jams together “list” and “article” but somehow carries a hint of the diminutive about it, which the listicle’s detractors would say is absolutely right: a chart – a Top 20 or 50 or 100 – with each entry warranting a brief paragraph of explication, they are reviled as a cheap, largely effortless way to fill space online. They are also astoundingly popular, particularly when the subject is music, perhaps because people were compiling rock and pop’s history into listicles decades before the internet came along.

The NME got there first, in 1974, with what it called a “Writers’ All-Time Top 100 Albums” list – a bold early attempt to define a canon of classic rock, with Sgt Pepper at No 1 and black and female artists sorely under­represented. But it wasn’t until the 90s that the idea really grew legs. Suddenly the music press was awash with retrospective charts, evidence that an increasingly rosy view of rock history was abroad: the 90s also saw the rise of the heritage rock magazine, the expensively packaged retrospective box set and, indeed, of Britpop, an entire genre more or less predicated on evoking vague memories of the past, as if something of its magic might rub off through imitation.

items.title: Adder Stone by Clare Clark review – the story of a drowned Welsh village
items.blurb:
A real-life flooding becomes a flashpoint in this novel exploring family relationships, female liberation and the drive for Welsh independence

In the author’s note accompanying her eighth novel, Adder Stone, Clare Clark recalls first learning how a lake in the Welsh valleys shrank during the drought of 1976 only to reveal an abandoned village underneath. As a child, Clark became obsessed with the idea, envisaging a sort of Welsh Pompeii – houses and lives frozen in time, buried beneath the water and the mud.

Fifty years since that uncanny occurrence, Clark’s richly researched novel seeks to tell the story of that forgotten Welsh village: not abandoned by choice, but forcibly evicted in order to make way for a new reservoir needed to service Liverpool’s growing population. Clark charts how this event had a profound impact on individual lives, but also how it served as a flashpoint in the broader conversation around Welsh independence.

items.title: ‘My name was poison’: Donny Osmond on fame, failure – and his friend Michael Jackson

He was the child star of the Osmonds who become a global celebrity by 14. Then, at 21, his career came crashing down. Here, he reveals how he survived his years in exile – and what happened when Jackson was accused of child abuse

For a brief period in the early 1970s, Donny Osmond ruled the world. He was the global teenage heart-throb. Even Michael Jackson trailed behind him. He was 14 when his most famous song, Puppy Love, spent five weeks at No 1 in the UK. My sister had a huge poster of him on her bedroom wall. Then again, everybody’s sister had a poster of him on their bedroom wall. Between 1972 and 1973 he had six Top 5 hits in the UK, three of them No 1s (including The Twelfth of Never and Young Love). He was equally successful back home in the US.

Osmond was clean-cut, religious and respectful, with a mighty ability to punch out cover versions of saccharine standards. From his purple velvet cap to his doleful eyes and dazzling all-American smile, he was a marketing dream. We’d only just finished with Beatlemania. And now there was Donnymania.

items.title: ‘What if joining the resistance got your friends executed?’ The chilling new films casting Nazi collaborators in a fresh light
items.blurb:
For decades, films about Nazi-occupied Europe were all about the fearless resistance while despicable collaborators deserved all they got. So what’s behind the spate of movies portraying turncoats in a more sympathetic light?

A young maid busies herself in a vast, high-ceilinged apartment, serving her master steaming coffee in fine china and polishing the hefty family silver, as she picks her way across the checkerboard parquet lit by stylish Poul Henningsen lamps. Woman Unknown, which won the Golden Lion at the Venice film festival this year, is set in the immediate aftermath of Denmark’s liberation from Nazi rule, but you wouldn’t know that from the opening scenes: five years of occupation, martial law and rationing have left the splendour of the Danish bourgeoisie miraculously untouched.

The trauma of wartime violence only comes rushing back in occasional bursts: blurry flashbacks show shadowy figures pointing guns at temples and bodies thudding to the floor. But the red fabric billowing through the fog of her memory is not the Nazi flag but liberated Denmark’s white-crossed Dannebrog. The black-clad executioners are not SS officers but resistance fighters reckoning with collaborators.

items.title: ‘He’s open and affable – I avoid being recognised like the plague’: Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon on celebrity, friendship and their trip to the Arctic circle
items.blurb:
The northern lights, fine food, Melvyn Bragg impersonations – The Trip has landed in Scandinavia. We take in the sights with its stars, as they ruminate on ageing, activism and the best car to take a nap in

Morning in Valldal, and in the pale September light, the Juvet Landskapshotell stands quite still amid mountains, pines and yellowing birch. In the hotel dining room, Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon are taking breakfast; coffee and muesli and compote spread out before them as they settle into a discussion of the playwrights August Strindberg and Henrik Ibsen, and their enduring infatuations with much younger women. “When Ibsen was 60, he fell in love with a teenager called Emilie,” Brydon says. “Can you imagine doing that?” Coogan swallows his muesli: “I can imagine it, doesn’t mean I’d do it.”

The conversation shifts, taking in the persecuted genius of Galileo, a short exhortation on the subject of Palestine, and how the aurora borealis has just been spotted in the skies above Great Yarmouth. After a time, Brydon falls into an extended impersonation of Melvyn Bragg presenting In Our Time. “Can you expand on that?” he barks at Coogan. “Expand … Expand … Expand.” The edges of Coogan’s mouth begin to flicker.

items.title: The Guardian view on Cop31: a just transition needs more than fine words | Editorial
items.blurb:
Petrostates blocked ambition while wealthy nations withheld cash support. The climate crisis demands the next UN summit turns promises into action

In a negotiation the maxim is usually that no deal is better than a bad deal. But the failure of Cop31 in Turkey to get a climate pact – the first time this has happened in 17 years – should not be an excuse for leaving the planet with the damaging status quo. A hard bargain needs a credible route to agreement: by making commitments, seeking concessions and getting others to reciprocate. This did not happen at the weekend.

Responsibility for the breakdown lay principally with petrostates resisting a transition away from fossil fuels and wealthy nations that are unwilling to finance it properly. With the US absent, the EU was foremost among the latter. European governments’ objection to fossil-fuel backsliding by a Saudi-Russian coalition was right, but they were wrong to rule out fresh EU funding for developing countries’ climate action. Despite their reservations, others – notably China and the African group – were prepared to accept a flawed package to keep multilateralism alive.

items.title: Madness erupts as Sevilla deny Betis in wild end to Spain’s ‘derby of derbies’
items.blurb:
Rivals have been heading in opposite directions in recent years but latest clash showed some things never change

“If we didn’t celebrate a goal, especially in this game, that would be madness,” Kike Salas said. Instead, this was madness, the kind of moment a derby is meant to have, even if it has nothing else. It was late, it was lucky, and there wasn’t even a winner but right there, right then, at 24 minutes past 8pm on Saturday evening in the Ramón Sánchez-Pizjuán Stadium, it felt like there was. Frankly it was a bit rubbish, as bad a goal as you’ll see, but it was also the best, practically Pelé against the Nazis. Suddenly there were arms and legs everywhere, tears too. Cameras confirmed it. Zoom in and there they are: actual, real life tears.

In the 91st minute of the 146th meeting between Sevilla Fútbol Club and Real Betis Balompié – “derby of derbies” according to Luis García, the Sevilla coach for whom it was the first – Salas’s shot from 18 yards went through Marc Bartra’s legs and Álvaro Valles’s hands. The ball dribbled into the Betis net so apologetically it barely touched the net at all and hadn’t got there before Sevilla’s vice-captain was gone. Raised in Morón de la Frontera, to the south of a city divided, Salas joined Sevilla at 11; now, having levelled the game at 1-1, he went tearing towards the terraces, absolutely losing it like they were.

  • Read our World Chess Championship watch guide

Javokhir Sindarov has a problem. The fast-rising 20-year-old Uzbek grandmaster, who is challenging for the world chess championship over the next three weeks in Switzerland, can’t stop playing for keeps. Even when he is off the clock and meant to be relaxing with friends, a compulsion to win takes hold. His preferred escape is Counter-Strike, the tactical first-person shooter that has become one of the world’s most popular esports. But he also plays EA Sports FC (née Fifa), the all-conquering soccer kickabout, and approaches both with the same seriousness of purpose that has propelled him toward the pinnacle of his day job.

“I’m the guy who can’t play games just for fun,” Sindarov tells the Guardian less than 48 hours before Tuesday’s world championship opener in Geneva, smiling at the absurdity of it. “If I play something, I always try to learn, trying to become better.”

The manager’s first game in charge was a disaster and he needs to lift the mood within a sunken squad if a relegation battle is to be avoided

  • Sign up for our free newsletter here

In as much as any derby can ever be a free hit, there was always a sense that Mauricio Pochettino’s first game as Manchester United manager wouldn’t matter too much; nobody expected them to win away to Liverpool. This was not a game on which anybody was going to judge him, and that feeling only magnified when Leny Yoro was sent off after eight minutes. United’s victory at Anfield last season was their first for a decade; what’s difficult to do with 11 men is only going to get harder playing a man down for 82 minutes. But that does not mean that it did not matter.

Although Roy Keane was determined to reject the suggestion, there was perhaps even some credit to be gleaned from having lost only 4-0. Certainly when they were 2-0 down after 13 minutes, there was reason for United to fear an embarrassment akin to their 7-0 defeat against Liverpool in 2023. Perhaps Pochettino deserves credit for his switch to a back three, which brought a degree of stabilisation, but United could easily have lost far more comfortably than they did. Liverpool had 18 shots in the game three-and-a-half years ago, eight of them on target; on Sunday they had 28, 11 of them on target. When you’ve conceded an xG of 4.38, there’s not much point quibbling over the details; you’ve been hammered.

items.title: Afghanistan: Enough Room to Return? Where 7.2 million Afghan returnees settled, and whether public health services, rentals, and wages can accommodate them
items.blurb:
Countries: Afghanistan, Iran (Islamic Republic of), Pakistan
Source: Data for Afghanistan

Please refer to the attached file.

Author: Ahmad Zia Wahdat, PhD

Between 2021 and October 2026, about 7.2 million Afghans returned from Iran, Pakistan and elsewhere, and one in seven people now living in Afghanistan is a returnee. This independent report by Data for Afghanistan places every returnee in one of Afghanistan's 401 districts. It then measures that number against the people, inhabited land, public health workers, wages, rent and prices already there. It draws only on open and publicly accessible data from IOM, UNHCR, the Ministry of Public Health, WFP and the National Statistics and Information Authority. It introduces a district typology that separates two kinds of pressure: the returnee share of residents and spatial crowding (returnees per km² of inhabited land). The report also includes a stress test for a further one million returnees, recommendations for organizations, and profiles of all 34 provinces with district-level tables.

Return is highly concentrated. Ten districts hold 21% of all returnees, and in Kunduz, Daykundi and Herat close to one resident in four is a returnee. In "saturated" districts, both the returnee share and crowding are above the national average, and 45% of returnees live in these districts. Nationally, there are 252 returnees for every public health worker, and more than 550 in Takhar and Kunduz. Yet new public health facilities over the past five years mostly opened elsewhere. In no province can one unskilled wage keep a returnee household of 6.1 members above the poverty line: it covers only 37% to 76%. Rent for a modest four-bedroom house takes up to 33 days of unskilled wage a month. About 2.7 million returnees are of school age, and half of returnee children aged 5 to 14 are not in education, mainly because of cost and the need for children to work. If one million more people return following the 2026 pattern, Nangarhar, Herat and Kabul would receive 46% of them. Holding today's ratios would then need at least 537 more health workers and 65 more public health facilities.

The report is available in English, Dari and Pashto, with interactive web pages:

English: https://dataforafghanistan.org/returnees/

دری: https://dataforafghanistan.org/returnees/fa/

پښتو: https://dataforafghanistan.org/returnees/ps/

items.title: Nepal: Rasuwa Flood Response 2026, Situation Report 16
items.blurb:
Country: Nepal
Source: Nepal Red Cross Society

Please refer to the attached file.

Situation Update

Following the devastating flash flood, thousands of people remain displaced, and uncertainty remains about the future. The flood response has entered a longer-term relief and early recovery phase, while search and rescue efforts continue in parallel with initiatives to restore access, basic services, and support for displaced and affected families. According to the latest update from the NDRRMA, 1,457 people have lost their lives, 5,285 remain missing, 13,795 have been rescued. To date, authorities have identified and handed over 112 bodies to their families. Currently, 417 people are taking shelter in 11 holding centers across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading districts, including 229 people in 6 centers in Rasuwa, 67 people in 1 center in Nuwakot, and 121 people in 4 centers in Dhading. Recognizing the need for greater flexibility and dignity among displaced families, the Government of Nepal will provide monthly cash assistance to those who choose not to stay in holding centers. The support will help cover accommodation and livelihood expenses for up to six months, or until alternative housing is arranged. Each family who do not wish to stay in holding centers and until alternative housing arrangement willreceive NPR 15,000 per month for families up to four members, with an additional NPR 2,000 per month for every family member beyond four, enabling families to make decisions that best suit their circumstances during recovery.

items.title: World: Qatar Charity Urges Support for 70 Winter Relief Convoys Across Seven Countries [EN/AR]
items.blurb:
Countries: World, Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Djibouti, Kenya, Lebanon, Somalia, Sudan
Source: Qatar Charity

Please refer to the attached files.

Doha, November 21, 2026

As part of its ongoing “Winter Heroes” campaign, Qatar Charity (QC) has announced plans to dispatch 70 humanitarian convoys carrying food and winter essentials to seven countries. The organization called on individuals and businesses to support the convoys, helping reach as many displaced people, refugees, and families facing winter hardships as possible.

Food and Winter Essentials

The convoys will carry food, winter kits with blankets and warm clothing, and fuel vouchers to help families cope with the cold. Each convoy is expected to benefit 1,500 people.

Countries to Receive Aid

With support from donors, the convoys will deliver assistance to Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Lebanon, Somalia, Sudan, Kenya, and Djibouti. These countries host refugees, internally displaced people, and other vulnerable communities facing protracted crises, disasters, and seasonal hardships.

Qatar Charity thanked donors who have contributed to the “Winter Heroes” campaign and urged individuals and businesses to continue supporting its relief convoys. Their contributions will help families facing difficult living conditions meet their winter needs and prepare for cold weather, heavy rain, and, in some locations, snow.

The Impact of Previous Convoys

Over the years, Qatar Charity has regularly dispatched humanitarian convoys as part of its seasonal winter campaigns, providing food, shelter supplies, winter essentials, and other urgent assistance to displaced people, refugees, and families most in need.

In 2021, Qatar Charity organized relief convoys under its winter campaign to support internally displaced people in Syria, with aid delivered across the Turkish-Syrian border, as well as Syrian refugees in Jordan and Lebanon. The convoy involved 200 trucks and reached 120,000 people with assistance to meet their basic and urgent needs.

In 2023, the “Qatar Relief Convoys” continued under the “Warm Hearts” campaign, reaching Beqaa, Akkar, and Arsal in Lebanon. During a delegation’s visit, assistance was distributed to Syrian refugees and vulnerable Lebanese families. The aid included 1,200 food baskets, 1,900 winter kits, 300 packages of heating supplies, and 225 tent tarpaulins.

Qatar Charity has also delivered relief to crisis-affected areas through humanitarian land and air bridges. In October 2026, it launched a humanitarian bridge from Qatar to Sudan comprising 50 trucks carrying essential medicines and medical supplies. The initiative was organized in partnership with Qatar Fund for Development (QFFD), Hamad Medical Corporation (HMC), and Aspetar, a specialized orthopedic and sports medicine hospital.

The organization has also contributed to the State of Qatar’s wider humanitarian response, including relief delivered to the Gaza Strip through Egypt and Jordan between 2023 and 2026.

**Ends**

items.title: 100 days after the earthquake, fear and uncertainty still grip communities in Colombia
items.blurb:
Countries: Colombia, Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of)
Source: Canadian Lutheran World Relief

By Muhammad Tahir

For Yuranni Venegas, the fear has not gone away.

One hundred days after a powerful earthquake struck her community in Colombia’s Chocó department, she still remembers the terrifying moments when the ground shook, damaging homes and leaving families afraid of what might happen next.

“We’d never been through anything like that,” she recalls. “It was one of the longest and strongest earthquakes we’d ever felt in the community.”

On August 10, 2026, a magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck western Colombia, severely affecting Chocó, Valle del Cauca, Risaralda and Caldas. In Chocó alone, more than 776,000 people were affected, with over 104,000 homes left uninhabitable and nearly 19,150 destroyed.

The disaster came less than seven weeks after two powerful earthquakes struck neighbouring Venezuela on June 24, leaving an estimated 1.3 million people in need of humanitarian assistance, particularly in the northern coastal state of La Guaira.

In both countries, the earthquakes struck communities already struggling with poverty, insecurity and limited access to essential services.

Canadian Lutheran World Relief (CLWR), working through the Lutheran World Federation (LWF), mobilized emergency assistance with support from Canadians, helping families access food, safe drinking water, shelter materials and other essentials.

But 100 days after Colombia’s earthquake, the challenge is no longer simply surviving the disaster. For thousands of families, it is finding a way to rebuild their lives.

100 days later, the damage remains

In Chocó, many families are still living in damaged homes, unable to afford repairs or find somewhere else to stay.

“Some homes are not habitable, but people are still living in them because they have nowhere else to go,” says Sandy Paola Salgado Castillo, LWF Operations Officer in Colombia.

In Chocó, where heavy rainfall is a fact of life, repairing earthquake-damaged homes has become even more urgent. For families living under leaking roofs or inside damaged wooden houses, each downpour brings another reminder of how far they remain from recovery.

Families have also lost belongings and sources of income, while access to safe water and basic services remains difficult.

Children’s education has suffered too. Some damaged schools cannot accommodate all their students safely, forcing children to attend classes in shifts, sometimes for only two or three hours a day.

For Venegas, an auxiliary nurse from San Agustín de Terrón in Chocó, the emotional impact has been just as difficult.

“Some people here have high blood pressure, and they’re still feeling the effects of what happened. So are the children, the older adults and the community as a whole,” she says. “We’ve been left with this fear, wondering when it’s going to happen again.”

The field team has also identified growing protection concerns, including reports of increased gender-based violence, alongside a greater need for psychological support.

Helping families regain a sense of normality

So far, CLWR’s response through LWF Columbia has reached 4,670 people across 1,663 families in Chocó, including communities in Quibdó, Istmina, Alto Baudó and Medio Baudó.

Assistance has included food, hygiene kits, household items, emergency shelter supplies and cash to help families cover medicines, transportation and other basic expenses.

The response also provided 9,000 litres of safe drinking water and hundreds of hygiene kits.

CLWR’s earthquake response in Colombia, along with part of its response in Venezuela, has been funded through the Canadian Humanitarian Assistance Fund (CHAF), administered by the Humanitarian Coalition with support from the Government of Canada. In Chocó, this funding has also helped provide tools and materials for debris removal and basic household repairs.

Where many homes are made of wood, even simple repairs can make a difference. Replacing boards, fixing leaking roofs or repairing partitions can help make damaged homes habitable again.

Venegas has seen how that support extends beyond individual households.

“If a neighbour was given a board, for example, we’d go over and help nail it in place,” she says.

Community leaders have also helped identify families most in need and connect them with assistance.

Army Lemus Córdoba, president of the Association of Rural Community Councils in Quibdó municipality, says the support has been important, but communities need more than emergency supplies.

“This assistance has helped a lot of people. What I’d ask is that you don’t leave us on our own, that you keep supporting us. We still need a lot of help.”

He hopes families can eventually grow food or raise animals, reducing their dependence on outside assistance.

A second disaster across the border

Less than seven weeks before Colombia’s earthquake, neighboring Venezuela had been struck by two powerful earthquakes measuring 7.2 and 7.5, just 39 seconds apart, on June 24. The disaster caused widespread destruction, particularly in La Guaira state, leaving communities in both countries struggling to recover from overlapping humanitarian crises.

The disaster deepened an already prolonged economic and humanitarian crisis in Venezuela, leaving families without homes, income or reliable access to essential services.

In Venezuela, the emergency response has included activities partly funded by Humanitarian Coalition, with support from the Government of Canada.

The response has so far reached approximately 7,500 people, providing food, hygiene and shelter supplies, primary health care, protection services and psychosocial support.

In Mamo, La Guaira, Father José Manuel Colmenares, known locally as Father Cheo, opened the doors of San José Obrero Church, where he serves as a priest, to 140 families displaced by the earthquakes.

What began as a place of refuge soon grew into something more. With equipment and technical support, Father Cheo and local volunteers turned the church into a centre for coordinating humanitarian assistance, bringing together organizations and community members to help families in need.

Equipment and technical support by CLWR, through LWF have helped strengthen the community’s own response, identifying vulnerable families, organizing assistance and connecting residents with food, safe water, health consultations and psychological support.

For Father Cheo, the assistance also carries a personal message for families who have endured years of hardship: they “have not been forgotten”.

The hardest part of recovery is still ahead

Back in Colombia, emergency supplies helped families through the first weeks. Now, many need help repairing homes, restoring livelihoods and getting children back into safe classrooms.

Plans for the next phase include expanding access to safe water, cash assistance, psychological support and safe spaces for women and children.

Reaching isolated communities is another challenge. Some Indigenous communities require hours of travel by boat, while armed groups and movement restrictions complicate humanitarian access.

For Carmen García, LWF’s Regional Program Coordinator for Latin America and the Caribbean, responding to two earthquakes in less than two months has reinforced the importance of sustained support.

“These are communities enduring crisis after crisis,” she says. “They need us to stay.”

That need for continued support remains central to CLWR’s response.

“The generosity of Canadians has helped families put food on the table, access safe drinking water and make their damaged homes safer,” says Linnet Damien, CLWR’s Program Manager for Colombia and Venezuela.

“But recovery takes more than a few weeks or months. Families need more than help getting through another day. They need the support to rebuild their homes, restore their livelihoods and get their lives back on track. That’s why continued support is so important.”

In Chocó, the earthquake lasted only moments, but its consequences continue to shape daily life.

For families like Venegas’s neighbours, recovery means having a safe roof overhead, children back in school and a way to earn a living again.

One hundred days on, those hopes remain out of reach for many. Yet, amid the damaged homes and continuing hardship, neighbours are helping neighbours rebuild, one wooden board, one repaired roof and one family at a time.

The challenge now is making sure they have the support to finish what they have started.

items.title: Humanitarian Feedback Bulletin: Accountability to Affected Populations - Aweil, South Sudan I October 2026 Issue #7
items.blurb:
Country: South Sudan
Sources: Concern Worldwide, World Food Programme

Please refer to the attached file.

The Concern Worldwide (CWW) Accountability to Affected Populations project, supported by WFP, aims to create a bottom-up feedback and communication mechanism between responders and people we serve, that is community-based, easily accessible, and built on mutual understanding and genuine information-sharing.

Through local responders and community correspondents, Concern, Community Engagement Network (CEN), and the Radio Community (TRC) work together to deliver a complete community feedback mechanism that is accessible to all participants regardless of their literacy levels and access to assets and internet. Drawing on TRC’s and CEN’s extensive experience in radio broadcasting and community engagement, the project ensures a wide outreach beyond people with access to written updates.

Together, and alongside WFP, the project partners respond to information and feedback gaps. By consolidating and sharing the feedback received, the project increases accountability to affected populations in the targeted areas.

Countries: World, Australia, French Polynesia (France), Marshall Islands, New Zealand, Samoa, United States of America, Vanuatu, Wallis and Futuna (France)
Source: Pacific Community

Please refer to the attached Map.

Éléments nouveaux/faits marquants intervenus depuis la diffusion de la carte précédente sur PacNet, le 10 novembre 2026 :

Dengue

• Îles Marshall : Le vingtième rapport de situation sur l’épidémie de dengue, couvrant la période allant du 15 août au 12 novembre 2026, fait état de 173 cas positifs (confirmés et probables) sur 615 prélèvements testés : 128 à Majuro et 45 à Ebeye, contre 171 au cours de la période allant du 15 août au 2 novembre (dix-huitième rapport). Depuis le 29 octobre, tous les nouveaux cas positifs ont été détectés à Ebeye, la date de début des symptômes du cas le plus récent étant le 9 novembre. À Majuro, le dernier cas confirmé remonte au 18 octobre (date des premiers symptômes). Depuis le début de l’épidémie, 18 personnes (des enfants uniquement) ont été hospitalisées (13 à Majuro et 5 à Ebeye) ; aucun décès n’a été signalé. Le taux de positivité s’élève à 26 % à Majuro et à 35 % à Ebeye, et les taux d’attaque s’établissent respectivement à 5,5 et 4,6 pour 1 000. Les moins de 20 ans représentent 71 % des cas positifs. Seul le sérotype DENV‑1 a été identifié. L’alerte pour la dengue (sérotype DENV‑1) passe du rouge au bleu. – Source : Ministère de la Santé et des Services sociaux des Îles Marshall, Rapport hebdomadaire sur les maladies transmissibles (semaine épidémiologique 45) incluant le vingtième rapport de situation sur l’épidémie de dengue à Majuro et Ebeye, communiqué au point de contact du Groupe de coordination du ROSSP le 16 novembre 2026.

• Samoa : Le rapport de situation sur l’épidémie de dengue no 81, portant sur la semaine épidémiologique 44 (du 26 octobre au 1er novembre 2026), fait état de 37 nouveaux cas, soit une augmentation de 3 % par rapport à la semaine précédente. On compte 1 cas confirmé biologiquement (contre 2 au cours de la semaine 43) et 2 nouvelles hospitalisations, mais aucun décès. Depuis le 1er janvier 2025, 20 553 cas diagnostiqués cliniquement et 5 550 cas confirmés biologiquement ont été enregistrés, de même que 9 décès liés à la dengue. Le sérotype DENV‑1 représente 52 % des cas ayant fait l’objet d’un sérotypage, contre 48 % pour le sérotype DENV‑2. Les enfants de moins de 15 ans représentent 73 % des cas. L’alerte bleue pour la dengue (sérotypes DENV‑1 et DENV‑2) est maintenue. – Source : Ministère de la Santé du Samoa, Rapport de situation sur l’épidémie de dengue no 81, communiqué au point de contact du Groupe de coordination du ROSSP le 16 novembre 2026.

• Vanuatu : Le rapport de situation no 16 sur l’épidémie de dengue fait état de 259 nouveaux cas confirmés biologiquement entre les semaines épidémiologiques 41 et 45 (du 5 octobre au 8 novembre 2026). La majorité des cas ont été recensés à Tanna (152) et à Santo (76), les autres étant signalés à Efate (20) et Malekula (17). Au total, on dénombre 476 cas confirmés sur les quatre îles : 178 à Efate, 167 à Tanna, 100 à Santo et 18 à Malekula. Le nombre hebdomadaire de cas a atteint un pic au cours de la semaine 42 (109 cas, dont 73 à Tanna), avant de reculer à 41 au cours de la semaine 43, puis à 22 au cours de la semaine 44 et 22 au cours de la semaine 45. La maladie, qui circulait au départ essentiellement dans la province de Shefa, a vu sa transmission fortement augmenter à Tafea entre les semaines 40 et 42. Dix-sept hospitalisations liées à la dengue ont été signalées. Tous les patients sont sortis de l’hôpital. Aucun cas grave ni aucun décès n’ont été rapportés. Le sérotype DENV‑1 a été confirmé dans 16 échantillons prélevés à Efate et Santo ; le sérotypage est en cours pour Tanna. Tant qu’aucune décrue durable n’est constatée sur l’ensemble des îles touchées, le ministère de la Santé continue de suivre de près l’évolution de la situation. L’alerte rouge pour la dengue (DENV‑1) est maintenue. – Source : Ministère de la Santé de Vanuatu, Rapport de situation no 16 sur l’épidémie de dengue à Efate, Santo, Tanna et Malekula, communiqué au point de contact du Groupe de coordination du ROSSP le 17 novembre 2026.

Maladies diarrhéiques

• États fédérés de Micronésie (État de Yap) : Le bulletin hebdomadaire de l’État de Yap pour la semaine épidémiologique 45 (du 2 au 8 novembre 2026) indique qu’après dix semaines consécutives d’alerte, le nombre de cas de maladies diarrhéiques est resté inférieur au seuil pour la deuxième semaine consécutive, avec 3 cas contre 5 au cours de la semaine 44 (le seuil d’alerte se situant à 7). L’un des quatre échantillons de selles testés s’est révélé positif à l’adénovirus. L’alerte bleue pour les maladies diarrhéiques est maintenue pour les États fédérés de Micronésie (État de Yap). – Source : Département de la santé de Yap, Rapport hebdomadaire sur les maladies transmissibles, communiqué au point de contact du Groupe de coordination du ROSSP le 13 novembre 2026.

Rougeole

• Australie : Le 12 novembre 2026, le ministère de la Santé de Nouvelle-Galles du Sud (NSW Health) a fait état d’un cas confirmé de rougeole chez une personne récemment rentrée d’Asie du Sud, où des épidémies sont en cours. Cette personne s’est rendue dans plusieurs lieux publics (dont l’aéroport international Kingsford Smith de Sydney et un centre de santé) alors qu’elle était contagieuse. Depuis le 1er janvier, 58 cas confirmés ont été recensés en Nouvelle-Galles du Sud. Dans le Queensland, un cas a été signalé au cours de la semaine qui a débuté le 2 novembre ; aucun cas n’avait été recensé depuis trois semaines. Dans l’État, 18 cas de rougeole ont été enregistrés en 2026 (13 contaminations à l’étranger et cinq cas autochtones). Au niveau national, le système de surveillance des maladies à déclaration obligatoire faisait état de 125 cas au 17 novembre, contre 181 en 2025. L’alerte rouge pour la rougeole est maintenue. – Source : NSW Health, Measles alert for Sydney, Queensland Health, Notifiable conditions weekly totals and summary information et Système national de surveillance des maladies à déclaration obligatoire (NNDSS), pages consultées le 17 novembre 2026.

Coqueluche

• Vanuatu : Le point de situation no 7 sur l’épidémie de coqueluche dans la province de Penama indique qu’aucun nouveau cas n’a été signalé sur l’île d’Ambae entre les semaines épidémiologiques 43 et 46 (du 26 octobre au 15 novembre 2026). Le nombre total de cas est toujours de 634, dont 7 confirmés biologiquement. Les derniers cas (7 au total) datent de la semaine 41, après un pic au cours des semaines 36 et 37 (266 et 307 cas). La semaine 46 marque la cinquième semaine consécutive sans nouveau cas ; il est donc possible que la maladie ait cessé de circuler. Les autorités n’ont pas encore déclaré la fin de l’épidémie. Le ministère de la Santé pourra envisager cette mesure 42 jours après la date d’apparition des symptômes du dernier cas (soit deux périodes maximales d’incubation). Deux personnes ont été hospitalisées depuis le début de l’épidémie et ont pu quitter l’hôpital ; aucun décès n’a été enregistré. L’alerte pour la coqueluche passe du rouge au bleu. – Source : Ministère de la Santé de Vanuatu, Rapport de situation no 7 sur l’épidémie de coqueluche dans la province de Penama, communiqué au point de contact du Groupe de coordination du ROSSP le 17 novembre 2026.

Maladies respiratoires

• Polynésie française : La Polynésie française est restée en phase épidémique pour la grippe au cours de la semaine épidémiologique 45 (du 2 au 8 novembre 2026), le nombre de cas confirmés biologiquement passant à 111, dont 79 cas de grippe A. Trente-huit personnes ont été hospitalisées, dont 4 en réanimation. Aucun nouveau décès n’a été signalé. Depuis le 5 octobre (semaine 41), 283 cas confirmés (dont 233 cas de grippe A), 93 hospitalisations, 7 admissions en réanimation et 3 décès ont été recensés. Ces chiffres doivent encore être consolidés. Le nombre de consultations pour infection respiratoire aiguë au sein du réseau sentinelle a lui aussi augmenté, mais leur proportion reste stable. Le nombre de médecins déclarants est également plus élevé que lors des deux semaines précédentes. Les autres pathogènes respiratoires détectés sont les suivants : adénovirus, métapneumovirus, rhino/entérovirus et parainfluenza 4. La campagne de vaccination contre la grippe est en cours. L’alerte rouge pour la grippe A est maintenue. – Source : Agence de régulation de l’action sanitaire et sociale (ARASS), Bulletin de surveillance sanitaire de Polynésie française no 40, communiqué au point de contact du Groupe de coordination du ROSSP le 17 novembre 2026.

• Nouvelle-Calédonie : Le 9 novembre 2026, la direction des Affaires Sanitaires et Sociales (DASS) de Nouvelle-Calédonie a déclaré la fin de l’épidémie de grippe, la totalité des indicateurs cliniques et virologiques ayant retrouvé leur niveau habituel. La maladie continue de circuler à bas bruit. L’épidémie de grippe A(H1N1) avait été déclarée le 25 septembre 2026 (semaine épidémiologique 39). Après un pic au cours de la semaine 40 (151 cas confirmés), le nombre de cas est tombé à 2 au cours de la semaine 45, tandis que le taux de positivité passait de 20 % au cours de la semaine 44 à 5 %. Entre les semaines 37 et 45, 599 cas confirmés biologiquement ont été recensés, le sous-type A(H1N1) représentant 99,3 % des 420 échantillons ayant fait l’objet d’un sérotypage. Les personnes âgées de 65 ans et plus représentent 36 % des cas. Les infections respiratoires aiguës ont représenté 1,8 % des consultations aux urgences au cours de la semaine 45, contre un pic à 13 % au cours de la semaine 41 ; 29 % des consultations pour une infection respiratoire aiguë en période épidémique ont donné lieu à une hospitalisation. L’alerte rouge pour la grippe A est levée. – Source : Direction des Affaires Sanitaires et Sociales (DASS) de Nouvelle-Calédonie, Vigilance DASS, bulletin 2026 no 12, communiqué au point de contact du Groupe de coordination du ROSSP le 10 novembre 2026.

• Nouvelle-Zélande : Le rapport hebdomadaire de virologie relatif à la semaine 45 (qui s’est achevée le 8 novembre 2026) fait état de 5 960 prélèvements positifs à la grippe depuis le 1er janvier 2026 : 5 514 cas de grippe A (963 de sous-type A(H1N1)pdm09, 877 de sous-type A(H3N2) et 3 674 non sous-typés) et 446 cas de grippe B. Ce sont 138 cas de plus qu’au cours de la semaine 43, signe d’un ralentissement du nombre de détections. La dernière mise à jour hebdomadaire du tableau de bord des infections respiratoires aiguës pour cette saison portait sur la semaine qui s’est achevée le 25 octobre ; le prochain point devrait être publié le 26 novembre. L’alerte bleue pour la grippe A est maintenue. – Source : PHF Science, Rapport virologique hebdomadaire pour la Nouvelle-Zélande et tableau de bord des infections respiratoires, pages consultées le 17 novembre 2026.

• Tonga : Le rapport hebdomadaire de surveillance syndromique pour la semaine épidémiologique 45 (du 2 au 8 novembre 2026) fait état d’un recul du nombre de cas de syndrome grippal pour la quatrième semaine (il passe de 54 à 49), tandis que le nombre d’infections respiratoires aiguës sévères augmente, passant de 3 à 9. Entre le 3 août et le 8 novembre 2026, 623 cas de syndrome grippal sur 835 ont été testés (74,6 %) : 270 étaient positifs à la grippe A (43,3 %), 6 à la grippe B et 31 au VRS. Au total, 101 personnes souffrant d’une infection respiratoire aiguë sévère (IRAS) ont été hospitalisées et un cinquième décès a été enregistré parmi les cas d’IRAS (on en dénombrait 4 au cours de la semaine 43). L’alerte rouge pour la grippe A est maintenue. – Source : Ministère de la Santé des Tonga, Rapport hebdomadaire de surveillance syndromique sur les maladies transmissibles, communiqué au point de contact du Groupe de coordination du ROSSP le 12 novembre 2026.

• Vanuatu : Le premier rapport de situation sur l’épidémie de grippe A dans les provinces de Shefa et Tafea, portant sur les semaines épidémiologiques 30 à 45 (du 20 juillet au 8 novembre 2026), fait état de 114 cas de grippe A confirmés biologiquement sur les 232 échantillons testés. Le nombre de cas confirmés est passé de 2 au cours de la semaine 41 à 40 au cours de la semaine 43, avant de reculer à 32 au cours de la semaine 44 et 12 au cours de la semaine 45. Quatre-vingt-dix-huit cas ont été recensés à Efate (86 %) et 16 à Tanna (14 %), où les premiers cas avaient été détectés au cours de la semaine 44. Le sous-typage a révélé que la souche en circulation est A(H1N1)pdm09. Sur les cas confirmés, 33 personnes ont été hospitalisées. Aucun décès n’a été signalé. Sur la période, 7 315 cas de syndrome grippal ont été signalés (5 943 à Shefa et 1 372 à Tafea), avec un pic à 981 cas au cours de la semaine 43 puis un repli au cours des deux semaines suivantes (754 cas puis 533), des chiffres qui restent supérieurs au seuil d’alerte. L’épidémie, déclarée à Shefa au cours de la semaine 42 et à Tafea au cours de la semaine 44, est toujours en cours. L’alerte rouge pour la grippe A est maintenue. – Source : Ministère de la Santé de Vanuatu, Rapport de situation no 1 sur l’épidémie de grippe A dans les provinces de Shefa et Tafea, communiqué au point de contact du Groupe de coordination du ROSSP le 17 novembre 2026.

Rotavirus

• Vanuatu : Le premier rapport de situation conjoint pour l’épidémie de rotavirus dans les provinces de Tafea et Sanma, portant sur les semaines épidémiologiques 30 à 45 (du 20 juillet au 8 novembre 2026), fait état de 1 202 cas, dont 12 confirmés biologiquement (3 à Tafea, 9 à Sanma). Au total, 929 cas diagnostiqués cliniquement (78 %) ont été recensés à Tanna, contre 259 à Santo (22 %) et 2 à Malo. Le pic a été atteint au cours de la semaine 37 (251 cas) et le nombre de cas recule progressivement depuis, avec 8 cas au cours de la semaine 45, même si la maladie continue de circuler de façon sporadique. Les enfants de moins de 5 ans représentent 82 % des cas. On compte à Tafea 46 hospitalisations et 1 décès depuis le début de l’épidémie. Aucun patient ne se trouve actuellement à l’hôpital. L’alerte bleue pour le rotavirus est maintenue. – Source : Ministère de la Santé de Vanuatu, Rapport de situation no 1 sur l’épidémie de rotavirus dans les provinces de Tafea et Sanma, communiqué au point de contact du Groupe de coordination du ROSSP le 17 novembre 2026.

Autres informations :

Dengue

• Samoa américaines : Le 12 novembre 2026, les Centres de lutte contre la maladie (CDC) des États-Unis ont publié, dans leur rapport hebdomadaire sur la morbidité et la mortalité, une étude sur l’épidémie de dengue aux Samoa américaines. Entre juin 2025 et août 2026, 1 048 cas confirmés de dengue ont été signalés (soit 211 pour 10 000 habitants) ; la contamination était autochtone dans 95 % des cas et associée à un voyage chez 49 personnes. Au total, 371 malades ont été hospitalisés (35 %) et aucun décès n’a été enregistré. Sur les cas confirmés, 78 % étaient des personnes de moins de 20 ans, l’incidence la plus forte étant constatée chez les 10–14 ans (652 pour 10 000). Sur les 146 cas sérotypés, 93 % étaient positifs au sous-type DENV‑1 et 7 %, au sous-type DENV‑2. Aucun cas lié à un voyage n’a été signalé depuis le 15 février 2026 et le nombre de cas a reculé entre février et août 2026. – Source : CDC des États-Unis, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, Notes from the Field: Dengue Outbreak, American Samoa, 2025–2026, page consultée le 17 novembre 2026.

Hantavirus

• Monde : Le 12 novembre 2026, l’Institut Pasteur a publié les résultats du séquençage génomique coordonné du foyer de syndrome pulmonaire à hantavirus qui s’est déclaré à bord du navire de croisière MV Hondius (avril à mai 2026, 13 cas et 3 décès) réalisé par les laboratoires de sept pays. Les séquences génomiques du virus présentent une faible diversité génétique, ce qui soutient l’hypothèse d’un événement unique d’introduction du virus suivi d’une transmission humaine liée à un contact étroit et prolongé. Huit des dix mutations apparentes se sont avérées être des artefacts techniques et les données épidémiologiques ne soutiennent pas un mode de transmission aéroportée massif. – Source : Institut Pasteur, Hantavirus Andes : caractérisation d’un foyer de contagion rare grâce à un séquençage génomique coordonné, page consultée le 17 novembre 2026.

Maladies respiratoires

• Îles Mariannes du Nord : Le rapport hebdomadaire de surveillance syndromique pour la semaine 44 (du 1er au 7 novembre 2026) fait état de 24 cas de grippe confirmés biologiquement (22 cas de grippe A et 2 cas de grippe A(H1N1)pdm09), contre 11 au cours de la semaine 43 et 427 depuis le début de l’année. Le nombre de cas de syndrome grippal a également augmenté, atteignant 41 cas, soit 64 % de plus que la moyenne des trois semaines précédentes. Le sous-typage réalisé par le laboratoire de santé publique de Guam, dont les résultats ont été publiés le 22 octobre 2026, a mis en évidence trois virus A(H1N1)pdm09. – Source : Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, Weekly Syndromic Surveillance Report, communiqué au point de contact du Groupe de coordination du ROSSP le 16 novembre 2026.

items.title: DR Congo: MSF DRC: Child dies while awaiting medical evacuation as intensified clashes disrupt access to care in Nyabiondo, Masisi territory
items.blurb:
Country: Democratic Republic of the Congo
Source: Médecins Sans Frontières

23 November, 2026 – Intensifying armed clashes in Nyabiondo, Masisi territory, North Kivu, have put civilians at serious risk since 18 November. Those clashes have led to the tragic death of a 15-year-old child who suffered from bullet wounds while awaiting urgent referral, blocked due to the ongoing hostilities. Médecins Sans Frontières / Doctors without Borders (MSF), which supports several health facilities in the area, is deeply concerned about the disruption of essential healthcare and the safety of affected communities. The organisation calls on all parties to the conflict to take immediate measures to protect civilians, healthcare facilities, patients and humanitarian personnel.

On 18 November, clashes between the Front pour la Refondation de la Nation (FRN) and Wazalendo armed groups intensified in Nyabiondo, Masisi territory, North Kivu. Many people sought refuge at the MSF-supported Nyabiondo Referral Health Centre, despite stray bullets occasionally reaching the facility's perimeter. The deteriorating security situation also forced MSF teams working in surrounding areas to take shelter and temporarily suspend their activities. ​

As of 21 November, the Nyabiondo Referral Health Centre has treated 19 people with conflict-related injuries, including several children, while the violent clashes continue. Three patients requiring urgent medical evacuation to the MSF-supported Masisi General Referral Hospital for specialised care remained stranded for nearly 24 hours because of the ongoing hostilities, placing their lives at serious risk. Tragically, a 15-year-old child who had sustained multiple gunshot wounds died while waiting urgent referral for surgery.

“This death illustrates the devastating impact of insecurity and obstacles to care on people trapped in conflict," says Olivier Pennec, MSF project coordinator in Masisi. "No child should die from gunshot wounds because they were unable to access the care they need."

The latest escalation takes place against a backdrop of prolonged insecurity, food scarcity and repeated displacement. Several front lines are surrounding Nyabiondo. Recurring clashes along roads in the area have forced successive waves of people to flee their homes and seek refuge in increasingly precarious conditions, with limited access to healthcare.

"We demand that all parties involved in the conflict act right now to keep civilians safe, along with healthcare structures, patients and aid workers," says Pennec. "Protecting people and keeping healthcare accessible has to come first, even while the fighting goes on."

END

In Masisi, MSF provides comprehensive support to Masisi General Referral Hospital and five health facilities, ensuring access to primary and secondary healthcare, including emergency medical and surgical care, medical and psychological support to survivors of sexual violence, responses to disease outbreaks such as measles and cholera, and the support of water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) activities.

Zoe Bennell

Press Officer (Features), MSF UK

items.title: Nine months on, the humanitarian emergency in Lebanon is far from over
items.blurb:
Country: Lebanon
Source: Medair

Please refer to the attached file.

Beirut, [November 18, 2026] – Nine months after the renewed escalation of conflict in Lebanon, hundreds of thousands of people remain displaced, while communities struggle to rebuild amid continued insecurity and widespread destruction.

Although a ceasefire was agreed on 20 June, hostilities have not ended: more than 6,000 attacks have since been recorded. Approximately 11,000 displaced people remain in collective shelters, while more than 300,000 remain displaced outside their areas of origin. Many face prolonged displacement with little clarity about when—or whether—they will be able to return home.

Across affected areas, families have lost homes, livelihoods and any sense of security. In southern Lebanon, access restrictions around and beyond the so-called Yellow Line, continuing insecurity and extensive damage are preventing people from returning to their communities. At the same time, an estimated 700,000 people have returned to conflict-affected areas, often finding homes, livelihoods and essential services damaged or completely destroyed. Made more vulnerable by the war, they are trying to rebuild amid profound uncertainty over whether the cessation of hostilities will hold, as neardaily airstrikes continue in the South.

“Since we were forced to flee our village in the South, my thoughts have never left our home. We lost the house we spent years building, our olive groves and the livelihood we depended on. My wife is 70 and I am 72, and living with our health conditions in displacement makes everything harder. We are now staying in a classroom turned into a shelter, unsure of how long we can remain here or whether we will ever return home. All we want is a safe place to live, some stability and the chance to rebuild our lives with dignity,” says Hassan, 72, internally displaced from southern Lebanon currently staying with his family in a public school turned collective shelter.

Since the escalation began on 2 March, Medair has scaled up its emergency response across the Bekaa Valley, Beirut and Mount Lebanon, and southern Lebanon. Working in hard-to-reach and conflict-affected areas, teams provide basic assistance, shelter support, water, sanitation and hygiene services, primary healthcare, and mental health and psychosocial support. To date, Medair has served 118,080 internally displaced people, distributed 181,416 core relief items and kits, and reached 459 collective shelters.

Medair also supports families facing prolonged displacement—prevented from returning home and uncertain when a safe and sustainable return will be possible. In Al-Abbassiyeh, Medair converted an unused vegetable market into safer, more dignified accommodation for 57 families, approximately 300 people. The move enabled families to leave overcrowded school shelters and allowed classrooms to return to their intended educational purpose. Teams are rehabilitating other collective shelters across southern Lebanon for people likely to remain displaced for longer.

Despite access constraints and security risks, Medair continues to adapt its response and prioritise those most vulnerable, helping families meet urgent needs, access essential services and cope with the psychological toll of prolonged conflict and displacement.

“Nine months into this conflict, Lebanon may no longer be making international headlines, but the emergency is far from over. The destruction we are witnessing is unlike anything Lebanon has seen in generations—dwarfing even the devastation of the civil war in many affected communities. Every day, our teams navigate complex logistical and security challenges to reach people in hardto-access areas while keeping our staff safe. Our work will not be finished until families can return safely to their communities of origin, exercise their right to go home, and receive the support they need to rebuild their lives with dignity,” says Kirollos Fares, Medair Country Director in Lebanon.

Lebanon continues to face overlapping economic, social and humanitarian pressures, and the conflict is deepening existing vulnerabilities. Sustained humanitarian assistance is essential both to meet immediate needs and to help communities recover from repeated displacement and destruction.

Nine months on, the war’s impact continues to echo across Lebanon. For families still displaced, those prevented from returning home, and returnees living amid damaged infrastructure and disrupted services, the emergency is not over. Medair remains committed to providing impartial, needs-based assistance and helping conflict-affected communities recover with dignity.

END

items.title: Colombia: Informe de Tendencias e Impacto Humanitario en 2026 | Datos acumulados entre enero - agosto de 2026 | Fecha de publicación: 23 de noviembre de 2026
items.blurb:
Country: Colombia
Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached file.

  • Entre enero y agosto de 2026, Colombia continuó enfrentando una crisis humanitaria marcada por la acumulación de impactos del conflicto armado y de eventos de origen natural recurrentes. La situación se agravó tras el terremoto de agosto, que incrementó las necesidades humanitarias en territorios que ya enfrentaban los efectos de la violencia, la pobreza y una limitada presencia institucional. Esta combinación de emergencias puso aún más presión sobre las capacidades de respuesta de las autoridades locales y nacionales.
  • La intensificación de las hostilidades y el control territorial de grupos armados siguen deteriorando las condiciones de vida de comunidades rurales y étnicas.
  • Los confinamientos, restricciones a la movilidad y limitaciones de acceso a bienes esenciales persisten como una de las afectaciones más críticas, incrementando riesgos de protección, inseguridad alimentaria y vulneración de derechos.
  • El terremoto de magnitud 7,4 ocurrido en agosto evidenció la fragilidad de territorios ya vulnerables y donde las capacidades de respuesta locales ya enfrentaban desafíos y limitaciones. Más allá de la emergencia inmediata, el sismo incrementó las necesidades, mientras confirmó la urgencia de fortalecer la preparación, resiliencia comunitaria y capacidad de respuesta frente a crisis complejas y concurrentes.
  • Los ataques indiscriminados con drones cargados con explosivos siguen en aumento ocasionando daños a la infraestructura civil y aumentando los riesgos a los que se exponen los civiles.

items.title: Rwanda Population Movement 2025 - DREF Final Report MDRRW024
items.blurb:
Countries: Rwanda, Democratic Republic of the Congo
Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

Please refer to the attached file.

What happened, where and when?

On 7 December 2025, renewed fighting in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, particularly in South Kivu Province, triggered a significant movement of people towards Rwanda. The initial influx was concentrated in Rusizi District, with asylum seekers arriving through border entry points and being received at the Nyarushishi Transit Centre and surrounding reception sites. The sudden increase in arrivals placed additional pressure on existing shelter, water, sanitation and hygiene, health, protection and basic assistance capacities

The IFRC-DREF operation was launched on 16 December 2025 to support the Rwanda Red Cross Society in addressing the immediate humanitarian needs of people arriving from eastern DRC. While the initial operation was designed around an estimated 2,000 people, implementation took place in a context of continued population movement and evolving needs. During the four-month implementation period, the Rwanda Red Cross Society provided assistance through shelter and non-food items, health and first aid, WASH, Protection,
Gender and Inclusion (PGI), and Community Engagement and Accountability (CEA) activities. The response also focused on strengthening the capacity of volunteers to provide timely assistance and referrals at reception and transit locations.

By the end of the operation on 30 April 2026, the Rwanda Red Cross Society had assisted 3,100 people . Assistance included 400 households receiving shelter and essential household items, health and first-aid support, WASH assistance, protection and child-focused services, as well as community engagement and feedback activities.
The response therefore evolved from an initial emergency response to a broader effort to address the needs of both newly arriving asylum seekers and people already accommodated in or around the reception areas. The operation also strengthened the preparedness and response capacity of Rwanda Red Cross volunteers through training in first aid, epidemic control, psychosocial support, WASH, shelter, PGI and CEA.

items.title: oPt: Gaza: Working alongside communities to prepare for winter rains
items.blurb:
Country: occupied Palestinian territory
Source: International Committee of the Red Cross

The first week of November brought heavy rains to Gaza. Raed Al-Ramlawi, 55, woke in the middle of the night to find rainwater pouring into his family’s tent in Al-Manasra Camp in southern Gaza.

“Most of the tents in the camp were flooded – including ours,” he said. “Our neighbours rushed to help us in the darkness.”

The rainwater, mixed with sewage, destroyed Raed’s family’s belongings, including bedding, blankets and food. The water level in the tent was so high that he and his children had to use plastic jugs to bail the water out. Afterwards, his children became sick because of the wet and the cold.

Raed’s family was not alone. The rains have flooded low-lying areas, soaking and damaging beyond repair the belongings of many families.
And these were only the first rains of winter.

People in Gaza have few options to shelter from harsh weather. Most still live in tents that offer little protection from the elements – tents that leak, collapse and cannot properly protect those inside. Some families have sought refuge in damaged buildings that could collapse around them. More durable shelter solutions are needed.

The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) is working with communities in Gaza on practical measures to help mitigate the impact of flooding. This includes the provision of sandbags to help prevent the tents of around 20,000 people, who have been displaced, from being swept away. Raed and others in his community were among those provided with sandbags, which hopefully will help prevent water from entering his tent when the rains come again.

We have also donated basic items for thousands of families who urgently need them to get through the winter. This includes blankets, tarpaulins and mattresses. Given the restrictions on construction materials entering Gaza, we are working with communities to develop improved shelters using locally available items.

We are also supporting the Coastal Municipalities Water Utility (CMWU) to clear blocked drainage systems and improve wastewater management. We have provided portable suction pumps to help with the removal of accumulated wastewater. Recently, we also delivered eight sewage vacuum trucks to the CMWU, enabling them to clear blocked drains and reduce flood-related sanitation risks in affected areas.

The scale of humanitarian need remains immense. With winter just beginning, ICRC teams on the ground will continue working with communities to help them prepare for ever-worsening conditions. But there simply aren’t enough materials currently available in Gaza to meet the scale of needs.

This is the fourth winter that people are living in tents or damaged homes since October 2023. Restrictions on the entry of materials that could be used to provide more durable housing, or to repair damaged infrastructure, make it hard to help people in Gaza live through winter in health and with dignity. People in Gaza need more than temporary fixes; they need sustainable solutions.

items.title: Indonesia: ASEAN Weekly Disaster Update Week 47 | 16 – 22 November 2026
items.blurb:
Countries: Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand
Source: ASEAN Coordinating Centre for Humanitarian Assistance

Please refer to the attached Infographic.

EGIONAL SUMMARY:

During the forty-seventh week of 2026, a total of 30 disasters were reported across ASEAN, including floods, landslides, and wind-related disasters. In Indonesia, Badan Nasional Penanggulangan Bencana (BNPB) reported floods, landslides, and wind-related disasters in Aceh, Bengkulu, Jakarta, Central Java, East Java, West Kalimantan, Lampung, West Nusa Tenggara, Riau, South Sulawesi, North Sulawesi, West Sumatra, and North Sumatra. In Malaysia, Agensi Pengurusan Bencana Negara (NADMA) reported floods and landslides in Selangor, Perak, Pahang, Negeri Sembilan, and Melaka. Meanwhile, in Thailand, Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation (DDPM) reported flooding in Phatthalung. In addition to these reported disasters, a M7.2 earthquake occurred in Banda Sea on 21 Nov 2026 at 1642H UTC+7, with a depth of 125 km, as reported by Badan Meteorologi, Klimatologi, dan Geofisika (BMKG). According to BNPB Indonesia and Civil Protection Authority (CPA) of Timor-Leste, the earthquake was felt in several areas of Maluku Barat Daya and Tanimbar Islands in Indonesia, as well as in Timor-Leste, including Dili. As of the time of reporting, no significant damage or impacts had been reported.

HIGHLIGHT:

As the Northeast Monsoon and wet season set in across the southern part of the ASEAN region, heavy rainfall has triggered a series of floods in Indonesia, southern Thailand, and Peninsular Malaysia this week. In Indonesia, flooding in Kapuas Hulu, West Kalimantan, which began on 19 November following prolonged heavy rainfall and increased water discharge from upstream areas, caused rivers to overflow across seven districts. According to BNPB, as of 23 Nov at 0030HRS UTC+7, the flooding had affected approximately 11.1K families (28.9K people) and 11.1K houses. Several areas across Sumatra were also affected by flooding, including Aceh, North Sumatra, West Sumatra, Riau, and Bengkulu. Meanwhile, several provinces, including Aceh, West Sumatra, and West Kalimantan, are currently under alert status for hydrometeorological disasters. Relevant authorities continue to undertake response measures to address the situation.

HYDRO-METEO-CLIMATOLOGICAL:

During the past week, data from the ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre (ASMC) indicated the highest seven-day average rainfall was recorded over the Indian Ocean west of Sumatra, extending along the island’s western coast. Moderate to heavy rainfall also fell over northern Sumatra, southern Thailand, Peninsular Malaysia, Kalimantan, southern Sulawesi, Mindanao and Papua. As of this report, no active tropical cyclone is being monitored within the ASEAN region. INVEST 96S, which was monitored last week west of West Sumatra, is no longer listed in the advisories. Two other tropical disturbances, INVEST 97S and 98S, are being monitored over the southern Indian Ocean but are not expected to directly affect weather conditions in the region (JTWC).

GEOPHYSICAL:

Nine (9) significant earthquakes (M>5.0) were recorded by Indonesia’s Badan Meteorologi, Klimatologi, dan Geofisika (BMKG) and the Philippines Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS). Mount Semeru (alert level III), Ibu (alert level II), and Dukono (alert level II) in Indonesia, and Bulusan (alert level 1), Mayon (alert level 3), Kanlaon (alert level 2), and Taal (alert level 1) volcanoes in the Philippines reported recent volcanic activity according to Pusat Vulkanologi dan Mitigasi Bencana Geologi (PVMBG) and PHIVOLCS.

OUTLOOK:

According to the ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre (ASMC), for the coming week, wetter than usual conditions are predicted over most of the western and central Maritime Continent, while drier than usual conditions are predicted over much of southern and eastern Mainland Southeast Asia. Additionally, warmer than usual conditions are predicted over most of the Maritime Continent and the southern part of Mainland Southeast Asia. For regional assessment of extreme, there is a small increase in chance of very heavy rainfall conditions to occurs over parts of northeastern Myanmar and northwestern Lao PDR, parts of northern Sumatra and northeastern Borneo. Meanwhile, extreme hot conditions are predicted with moderate increase in chance over central Philippines, southern Mainland Southeast Asia. The ENSO monitoring system state is “El Niño Conditions”. El Niño conditions are predicted to persist until at least Marcy-April 2027, with strong conditions continuing until early 2027. El Niño at this time of the year, typically brings drier conditions for much of the Maritime Continent, and to a lesser extent, some parts of Mainland Southeast Asia. Positive IOD conditions were present in October 2026. Models predict the positive IOD conditions to persist through November 2026, followed by a weakening and a return to neutral in January 2027.
