items.title: World: Zero-dose children cannot become the next global health crisis – Save the Children
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: Save the Children

Despite decades of progress, millions of children continue to miss out on life-saving immunisations, putting them at greater risk of preventable disease, disability and death and leaving the world off track to meet its commitment to halving number of zero-dose children and ending the preventable deaths of children under the age of five.

ADDIS ABABA, 23 November 2026 - Children who have never received a single vaccine must remain a priority for all stakeholders, Save the Children said today as leaders gather for the 5th International Conference on Public Health in Africa (CPHIA 2026).

Despite decades of progress, millions of children continue to miss out on life-saving immunisations, putting them at greater risk of preventable disease, disability and death and leaving the world off track to meet its commitment to halving number of zero-dose children and ending the preventable deaths of children under the age of five.

Samy Ahmar, Head of Global Health at Save the Children UK who is attending CPHIA this week said:

"Vaccines are one of the greatest public health achievements in history, yet millions of children are still missing out on this life-saving protection. Across Africa and around the world, the children most likely to be missed are often those facing the greatest barriers to healthcare: children living in conflict, displacement, multidimensional poverty, urban poor and remote communities.

“Unvaccinated children are often affected by multiple, overlapping deprivations, including malnutrition and a lack of access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene services. These factors weaken immune systems and increase susceptibility to infection. Together, they create a perfect storm in which the same children face a heightened risk of disease, severe illness, and death.

"The world has set ambitious goals to reach more children with immunisation and cut the number of zero-dose children in half and end the preventable deaths of children under the age of five, but we remain off track. At a time of growing financial pressure on countries and increasing strain on health systems, we cannot allow children to die from causes that we can easily prevent due to a lack of political will. Reaching every child with vaccines is not only a health imperative, but also a test of our collective commitment to equity.

"As leaders gather at CPHIA, we have an opportunity to reset our focus on what matters most: ensuring health systems are sustainably financed, and communities are empowered to help shape solutions that work for them. Progress will depend on moving beyond fragmented approaches and international donors and partners aligning behind country-led priorities that can deliver for children over the long term, in line with the recommendations of the Accra Reset. The Gavi Leap is an example of how global health institutions can make concrete steps towards this goal for greater health sovereignty."

"Through Save the Children’s work with partners, including governments and communities around the world, we have seen that zero-dose children can be reached with vaccines and other essential health services when barriers are understood and addressed. The challenge is not knowing what works. The challenge is finding stronger political will, financing and accountability to bring those solutions to the scale children need.

"No child should die from a disease that we know how to prevent. As governments, donors, health institutions and partners meet in Addis Ababa, we must all seize this moment to turn ambition into action, because for every under vaccinated child, the cost of inaction is far too high."

Anab and her colleagues, Maryam and Kaltun, deliver life-saving vaccinations against diseases including diphtheria, pneumonia and measles to some of Somalia’s hardest-to-reach communities. Hundreds of thousands of children remain unvaccinated across the country. If children miss these vital vaccines before the age of five, they may never receive protection against these life-threatening diseases. Last year, Save the Children’s integrated health outreach programme reached more than 135,000 children, with over 43,000 receiving their first vaccination and 26,000 treated for other life-threatening illnesses. Working alongside community mobilisers Mohamud and Bisharo, the team travels up to 300 kilometres by ambulance, donkey and on foot to reach families beyond the reach of health facilities. Maintaining the cold chain every step of the way, they bring vaccinations, malnutrition screening and essential healthcare directly to children who might otherwise go without. Brian Otieno/ Save the Children

Health worker Anab and her colleagues Maryam and Kaltun travel by ambulance, on foot and by donkey to bring routine vaccines to remote and nomadic families in Puntland, Somalia. The hardest part of the job is not the distance. It is trust, and they are winning it.

The polio vaccination campaign in Gaza has begun on 1 September following the arrival of 1.26 million doses of OPV2 vaccines and 500 insulated vaccine carriers. Save the Children's Primary Health Care Centre (PHCC) in Deir Al-Balah has been designated as one of the key vaccination sites (there are 51 in total ). We are overseeing site operations, coordinating community outreach, and ensuring an efficient vaccination process to maximise coverage quickly. Additionally, Save the Children is disseminating health promotion messages to educate communities about preventing polio and other infectious diseases. On Sunday 1 September, 1,825 children were vaccinated in our clinic. The campaign will run for two more days (today and tomorrow), followed by a "follow-up" day for anyone missed.

Tens of thousands of children have missed routine immunizations, and many newborns received none at all after 16 months of bombardment by Israeli forces and restrictions on entry of medical supplies brought Gaza’s healthcare system to the brink and saw polio re-emerge for the first time in 25 years.

The measles outbreak is affecting all eight divisions in Bangladesh, prompting an emergency vaccination campaign across the country. In the last month, nearly 18 million children have been reached with at least one dose of the vaccine, according to government data.

items.title: COP 31: World leaders fail climate action
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: CARE

Billed as an “implementation COP”, the conference ended with little concrete action, with no credible pathway providing adaptation finance and no mention of phasing out of fossil fuels, the root cause of the climate crisis, in its final decisions. Once again, self-interest and unilateralism have prevailed over the urgent need to protect lives and livelihoods.

From Latin America to the Horn of Africa to South Asia, communities across the globe are fighting to protect their crops, secure water and rebuild after devastating droughts and floods, with women and girls often bearing the heaviest burden. Their resilience cannot substitute for political responsibility.

Multilateral cooperation remains essential, but its credibility depends on world leaders honouring their commitments. The true measure of COP31 is not the agreement reached on paper, but whether governments deliver the resources and action needed to protect those least responsible for the crisis.

Marlene Achoki, Global Policy Lead Climate and Resilience, said:

“A profound lack of political ambition for climate action from world leaders has defined the outcomes of COP31, exposing the failure of the dual COP Presidencies to deliver on the promise of an ‘Implementation COP.’ Developed countries came to the negotiations empty-handed, unwilling to put forward the finance needed to support adaptation and loss and damage in climate-vulnerable countries. At a time when the world is overshooting temperature limits, climate impacts are intensifying and communities are already paying the price, leaders with the greatest responsibility and capacity to act have failed to rise to the moment.”

Obed Koringo, Climate Policy Adviser - CARE Denmark, said:

“COP31 promised delivery. All it delivered was more delays. With pledges to the Adaptation Fund falling far short of what is needed and no credible pathway to triple adaptation finance by 2035, vulnerable communities are once again being left to face escalating climate disasters without adequate support. Promises will not protect crops from drought or homes from floods. As COP32 heads to Africa, governments must stop talking about adaptation and start paying for it, with predictable, accessible and grant-based finance that reaches those who need it most.”

John Nordbo, Senior Climate Adviser - CARE Denmark, said:

“Developed countries are leaving COP31 with no credible plan to deliver the climate finance they have already promised. Meanwhile, more than 90% of the most climate-vulnerable countries are in or at significant risk of debt distress, spending far more on debt repayments than on climate action. Within a decade, developing countries could be paying back more on climate loans than they receive in new lending. This is climate finance in reverse: the countries least responsible for the crisis are being handed the bill. They need grants, not more debt.”

Rosa van Driel, Policy Adviser Climate Justice, said:

“The devastating floods in Nepal and the destruction they cause are a stark reminder of why loss and damage finance cannot wait. Yet the international support available remains a tiny fraction of what is needed. When disasters strike, communities cannot be left to rebuild alone or forced deeper into debt. Loss and damage finance is not charity: it is a matter of climate justice and responsibility. The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage needs to be filled at once.”

Kerime van Opijnen, Policy Advisor Gender Equality and Climate Justice - CARE Netherlands , said: “Governments at COP31 spent more time defending their red lines than protecting the lives on the line. With no meaningful progress on a just transition and no concrete figure for tripling adaptation finance, communities are once again being left to confront the climate crisis without the resources they desperately need. By sidelining gender equality and inclusion, world leaders have also turned their backs on those already bearing the heaviest burden. This is not climate justice.”

Mrityunjoy Das, Deputy Director – Humanitarian and Resilient Futures - CARE Bangladesh, said:

“COP31 falls short of confronting the near-term overshoot of 1.5°C, offering no plan to limit the peak and no commitment to a ‘decline trajectory’ that brings temperatures back to or below 1.5°C by the end of the century. The only encouraging sign is the target of 35% electricity in final energy demand by 2035, alongside tripling renewables and doubling energy efficiency by 2030. Yet how will such a shift benefit the most vulnerable people without just transition pathways that deliver decent work, finance and technology?”

Media enquiries

Spokespeople are available. For all press enquiries, please email press.uk@careinternational.org

items.title: World: COP31 ends without agreement, leaving girls facing worsening climate impacts
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: Plan International

COP31 ends without agreement, leaving girls facing worsening climate impacts

23 November 2026

COP31 ended in Antalya, Türkiye, without an overarching climate agreement after 2 days of overtime, leaving girls facing worsening climate disasters with no clear plan to protect them.

Governments remained deeply divided over cutting greenhouse gas emissions, as global warming heads past 1.5°C and every fraction of a degree raises the risk of extreme weather and irreversible damage for current and future generations.

“COP31 was meant to change the trajectory of climate action, but for too many girls, it has failed to change their forecast. Girls are already paying the price of the climate crisis, through lost schooling, health care they can’t reach, and greater risks of child marriage and violence. Governments cannot claim success while leaving girls to bear the consequences of inadequate climate action,” said Stu Solomon, Global Lead at Plan International’s Climate Hub, who attended the summit.

Girls are already paying the price of climate change

Plan International’s Change Her Forecast research, with 5,000 girls and young women in Bangladesh, Kenya, Peru, Senegal and Zimbabwe, found that among girls whose most severe climate event was drought, 60% had seen more girls marrying before 18 in their communities, with girls linking this to families struggling for money and food, and to schools closing.

Key commitments left unresolved at COP31

The final draft agreement, which was rejected, had dropped explicit references to moving away from fossil fuels. It also dropped proposed language recognising the disproportionate impact of the climate crisis on children, protecting essential services and advancing gender equality.

Countries also failed to agree on how to deliver the existing commitment to at least triple adaptation finance for lower-income countries by 2035, leaving unresolved the starting point for measuring progress and how additional funding would be provided.

Governments did not agree a 5-year plan to strengthen climate education, access to information and young people’s participation in climate decisions, with talks set to continue in Bonn, Germany, in June 2027.

Young people remain excluded from climate decisions

“How can we have inclusive, safe and meaningful participation in climate action when children and young people, especially girls, are the last to be heard or not heard at all? How can countries say they are committed to creating a healthy and liveable future for all when listening to climate science has become contentious?

“The recognition of children and youth, especially girls, and their rights in climate action should have been the basis of consensus for countries at COP31. It is unacceptable for countries to negotiate the future of children and youth without including them from the very beginning,” said Tegan, Youth Advocate, Plan International Australia.

COP31 also failed to acknowledge a landmark 2025 advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice, the United Nations’ highest court. The Court affirmed that governments have legal obligations to protect the climate and uphold human rights, including children’s rights, obligations that matter especially for children and future generations.

The conference has exposed a deeper crisis of international cooperation, as powerful political and economic interests continue to stand in the way of action, while girls and the communities least responsible for the climate crisis bear its greatest consequences.

Climate inaction puts girls’ rights at greater risk

The breakdown comes as the World Meteorological Organization warns that this year’s very strong El Niño will act as a “risk multiplier”, raising the risk of extreme heat, drought and heavy rainfall well into 2027, with growing risks for agriculture in areas already facing high food insecurity.

The climate crisis deepens the pressures that put girls at risk of child marriage. As the world prepares to mark the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage on 27 November, Plan International is calling on governments to live up to their responsibilities, take strong and urgent climate action, and put children’s rights, especially girls’ rights, at the heart of climate decisions.

See how climate change is impacting girls’ lives

Girls are already experiencing the consequences of the climate crisis. Based on research with 5,000 girls and young women across 5 countries, Change Her Forecast reveals how droughts, floods and other climate shocks are affecting education, health, safety and child marriage, and what must change to protect girls’ rights.

items.title: Namibian and Brazilian Officials Visit WFP-Supported Food Production Project Benefiting School Meals
items.blurb:
Countries: Namibia, Brazil
Source: World Food Programme

STAMPRIET, Namibia – Hellen Likando, Namibia’s Director of Disaster Risk Management in the Office of the Prime Minister and Brazil’s Ambassador to Namibia, H.E. Pedro de Castro da Cunha e Menezes, today visited a Brazil and United Nations World Food Programme (WFP)-supported project producing locally grown vegetables and eggs for school meals in one of the country’s most drought-prone regions.

Since December 2021, the Stampriet Integrated Community-Based Food Systems project has produced 3.3 mt of vegetables and eggs, helping to make school meals more nutritious for 300 learners at Stampriet Combined School. Combining horticulture and poultry production with the participation of local farmers, the project contributes to the Government of Namibia’s Home-Grown School Feeding Programme and also supplies community soup kitchens serving older persons, orphaned children and other vulnerable groups.

During the visit, Likando saw how shade-net greenhouses, drip irrigation and a poultry unit with 300 egg-laying hens are strengthening local food production in the Hardap Region.

“The Government has committed to cutting Namibia’s food imports by 80 percent by 2030. That ambition will be realised not in policy documents alone, but in places like Stampriet, where food production potential is being realised,” she said on behalf of Prime Minister Dr Elijah Ngurare.

Stampriet is one of five integrated food systems sites supported through the Namibia-Brazil partnership, with technical support from WFP. Since 2021, the partnership has supported sites across the Hardap, Kunene, Omaheke, Ohangwena and Otjozondjupa regions, connecting local food production with access to nutritious food.

Brazil has contributed financial resources and technical expertise to food security initiatives in Namibia since 2019, focusing on local food production and school feeding. In 2026, Brazil contributed $120,000 to WFP to support resilient food systems and food security initiatives in Namibia.

“Linking school meals to local food production helps reduce hunger, improve nutrition and create opportunities for farmers. We are proud to share this experience through South-South cooperation and to stand with Namibia as it strengthens its Home-Grown School Feeding Programme,” said Pedro de Castro da Cunha e Menezes, Brazil’s Ambassador to Namibia.

“Stampriet shows what is possible when local food production is connected directly to school meals,” said James King'ori, WFP Representative in Namibia. “With communities at the centre and strong government leadership, initiatives like this can strengthen local food systems while improving the food available to children. We thank the Government of Brazil for its support.”

# # #

The United Nations World Food Programme is the world’s largest humanitarian organization saving lives in emergencies and using food assistance to build a pathway to peace, stability and prosperity for people recovering from conflict, disasters and the impact of weather extremes.

items.title: Somalia: Radio Ergo Weekly Feedback Report, Issued: 20 Nov 2026
items.blurb:
Country: Somalia
Source: Radio Ergo

Please refer to the attached file.

Brief Summary

Calls to Radio Ergo’s nationwide audience feedback platform in the week 12-18 November 2026 indicated beneficial rainfall across many central and southern parts of the country, notably regions in Jubbaland, Hirshabelle, and Galgadud. Several callers in Bari region noted rain, but some said it was scant. Two callers in Jowhar, Middle Shabelle, said their farms had been flooded by the river. With much farming activity ongoing, many called for advice about crop pest control especially from southern regions. The calls also indicated a few persistent pockets of drought and livelihood losses in locations in Togdher, Bari, Hirshabelle, and Gedo, accompanied by high temperatures in Gedo and Middle Shabelle. The following summarises the calls by theme.

Floods – two callers in Jowhar said they had experienced flooding, with one saying their farms were everything for them so they faced difficulties. A caller in Beletweyne, Hiran, wanted updated weather forecasts to keep them abreast of flood risks. A female caller in Abudwak noted people’s concern over the risk of flooding and how to cope if it occurred.

IDPs – a caller in Mubarak camp in Dollow, Gedo, appealed for aid saying they faced food and water shortages and lived in poor shelter.

Health – a caller in Bardera, Gedo, said the rain had caused an influx of mosquitoes. Another in an unspecified location said as they lived on their farmland, they were plagued by mosquitoes and needed bed nets. A caller in Baidoa asked about recognising the first symptoms of someone infected with Ebola. (Radio Ergo is broadcasting information about Ebola as part of a public awareness campaign in collaboration with Africa CDC).

Nutrition – two female callers in Abudwak and Beletweyne asked for advice about nutrition and shortage of breast milk. One of the women said her children were all malnourished.

Mental health – several callers were interested in the causes and treatments for stress and anxiety and memory loss. A female caller in Beletweyne was keen to know how to help her elderly mother who was talking without making sense.

Food security – a caller in Abudwak complained that despite the rain, people were destitute and lacked jobs. A caller in Barawe, Lower Shabelle, was pleased that the price of fish had fallen considerably from $3 to $0.5 per kilo.

Conflict – a caller in Baidoa said people were living in fear due to the conflict and insecurity and that all those who could afford to leave the city had gone.

Governance – a caller in Bardera, Gedo, raised the long-standing complaint that the damaged bridge over the river needed reconstructing.

Locusts – one caller in Mudug region said they were concerned by locust swarms destroying their crops. He said the locusts had wreaked havoc and people needed to know how to control them.

Agriculture – farmers calling the weekly farming programme for expert advice had problems with pests and disease damaging a range of crops, including tomatoes and onions, mangoes, lemons, grain and sorghum. A caller in Bay region said as well as advice they needed access to pesticides.

Livestock – a caller in Burhakaba, Bay, complained that ineffective veterinary medicines that could be fake were in circulation. They wanted to know which good products to use to treat their livestock. Other callers noted various diseases including CCPP, foot and mouth, and botulism.

Rainfall – callers in several parts of Togdher region cited rainfall, noting that some areas remained dry. Three female callers in Bari region said their livestock were giving birth as rain had improved conditions, although one of the callers said the rain was scant. In Galgadud, callers in Abudwak, Adado, Balanbale, Godinlabe and Guriel said beneficial rain had filled the water catchments and helped livestock to recover. Callers in the Shabelles also welcomed rain. Among those from Baidoa, one female caller said the farmers’ beans and maize crops were thriving. Callers in Buale and Sakow in Middle Juba said they were doing well with the rain. Among several in Kismayo, one caller was thankful that the heavy rain had not caused any adversity. A caller in Lower Juba said their bananas and lemons were almost ready for harvest. In Gedo region, several callers in Bardera said the rain was enough to fill the catchments and for storage, and that their farms were doing well. items.title: World Children's Day: Almost 1 in 4 children are living in conflict zones
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: War Child UK

150 million more children are living in conflict zones than just six years ago, putting millions more childhoods, rights and futures at risk.

Almost 1 in 4 children worldwide – 589 million – are now living in conflict zones. That's 150 million more children than just six years ago. And the number is still rising.

Behind this growing number are millions of childhoods being shaped by violence, fear and uncertainty. As more children are caught up in conflict, more are growing up without the safety and stability every child deserves.

Every child has rights, even during war.

Every child is born with fundamental rights, regardless of where they live, their background or the circumstances they face. The right to safety, education, healthcare, protection from violence and to have a say in the decisions affecting their lives. These rights belong to every child without exception, and must be respected and protected in all circumstances, including during war.

In 1989, the United Nations adopted the Convention on the Rights of the Child, marking a turning point in how the world recognises and protects children's rights. Today, 196 countries have formally committed to the Convention, making it the most widely accepted human rights treaty in history.

Since then, important progress has been made in strengthening children's rights, including the adoption of an additional agreement in 2000 to protect children from recruitment and use in armed conflict. But recognising these rights is only the beginning. Ensuring that every child can enjoy them remains an ongoing responsibility.

The lasting impact of conflict on children

For millions of children living through war, the rights promised under the Convention are still far from being realised. Conflict puts children's lives at risk, disrupts their education, separates families and exposes children to violence and exploitation. Repeated exposure to violence can cause ongoing trauma, severely affecting children's ability to learn and develop. The impact on children's mental health lasts long after the immediate violence ends, making access to appropriate support essential during conflict and throughout recovery.

Protecting children's rights must be a priority.

More than three decades after its adoption, the Convention remains as important as ever. It is not simply an agreement made in the past but a tool for holding governments accountable and pushing for the changes children need today.

With almost a quarter of the world's children now living in conflict zones, the need to turn these commitments into meaningful action has never been more urgent. For children living through war, these rights are not just promises on paper. They mean having the chance to feel safe, continue learning and receive the support they need to recover and shape their own futures.

This World Children's Day, War Child is calling on governments to uphold their commitments to children's rights and take action to protect children living through conflict. This means protecting children from violence and exploitation, safeguarding access to education and healthcare, and ensuring child protection and mental health support are recognised as life-saving priorities and central to humanitarian responses to conflict.

items.title: Colombia: Ten years after peace deal, civilians see rising violence | NRC
items.blurb:
Country: Colombia
Source: Norwegian Refugee Council

“A decade after the signing of the peace agreement, conflict in Colombia has again intensified and continues to tear lives apart – and for millions of Colombians the violence never stopped,” said Jan Egeland, Secretary General of the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC).

Press release

Colombia Published 23. Nov 2026

24th November marks ten years since the signing of the peace agreement between the Colombian state and FARC, the country's largest organised armed group. Yet, needs continue to increase. Whilst 5.8 million people needed humanitarian assistance when the accord was signed in 2016, today that figure has surged to more than 8.1 million – an increase of nearly 40 per cent.

“Decades of visiting Colombia's remote regions have shown me the resilience of its people, but also the heavy price the rural populations pay when promises are broken,” said Egeland. “On the 10th anniversary of the peace agreement, the government and international donors must step up to make sure that the peace holds, and humanitarian needs are met”.

Despite the undeniable achievements of the peace process in Colombia, the conflict parties have fractured and there are now more organised armed groups operating in the country than when the peace agreement was signed.

“Almost half of the people we have recently assisted report living with constant anxiety, as the rules imposed by organised armed groups dictate the specific hours when they can enter and leave their homes, what they must plant in their fields, and the colour of the clothes they wear,” said Egeland.

In a new NRC survey conducted among communities receiving humanitarian assistance across several conflict prone areas, 75 per cent report they see the same or more violence than when the peace agreement was signed ten years ago.

A father who had to flee with his family told NRC “we could not leave our territory without permission from the armed group controlling the area. There was no food; we only had water when it rained, and those who fell ill had to endure the pain in silence”. The family fled under cover of darkness, trekking across treacherous mountains.

“For millions of rural communities, indigenous people, and afro-Colombians in remote regions, the violence never stopped, as state institutions failed to establish a lasting presence,” said Egeland. “Real peace is not only measured by the number of pledges signed on paper. It is measured on the ground, by whether a mother can send her children to school without fear of forced recruitment, and whether displaced families can return home with dignity and safety.”

“With only five years left of the agreed schedule to realize the peace deal by 2031, time is running out. We cannot turn our backs on the communities bearing the brunt of this ongoing violence, and we must guarantee that innocent people caught in a conflict receive the life-saving aid they urgently need,” said Egeland.

Notes to editors:

  • Photos are available for use here.
  • Signed on 24 November 2016 between the Colombian Government and the FARC, the Peace Agreement brought an official end to fifty years of armed confrontation between the two parties. With a 15-year implementation horizon extending through 2031, the accord is structured around six core pillars: comprehensive rural reform, political participation, disarmament and reincorporation of combatants, a solution to illicit drugs, a comprehensive transitional justice system for victims, and verification mechanisms for implementation.
  • The 40 per cent surge in the number of people in need of humanitarian assistance reflects the percentage difference between 2016 (5.8 million people) and 2026 (8.1 million people).
  • Following the 2016 peace agreement, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) identified five active armed conflicts in Colombia by 2018. By 2025, that number had escalated to eight. NGOs in Colombia report a more than 20 per cent increase in the ranks of organised armed groups.
  • Between September and November 2026, NRC conducted a multiple-choice survey among 150 people who received humanitarian aid in the departments of Arauca, Cauca, Chocó, Nariño, and Norte de Santander. Survey results reveal a concerning trend in Colombia's conflict-affected regions: nearly half of respondents (46 per cent) perceive current conditions as harder than a decade ago, and 29 per cent said the conditions remain just as difficult as when the peace agreement was signed ten years ago. Participants placed personal and community security as their primary concern (51.9 per cent). To address these challenges, communities stress the need for direct international field presence (54.2 per cent) and emergency response (42.7 per cent). The findings also underscore the vital role of aid organizations, with over 93 per cent of participants confirming that humanitarian operations directly contribute to community stability.
  • Colombia remains one of the world’s most neglected displacement crises, according to NRC.
  • Colombia hosts one of the world's largest populations of refugees and migrants, the vast majority of whom have arrived from Venezuela, and remains among the top 3 countries with the highest number of Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) in the world, surpassed only by Sudan.
  • According to UN OCHA, between January and April 2026 alone, over 630,000 people were affected by Colombia's armed conflict.

For more information or to arrange an interview, please contact:

  • NRC global media hotline: media@nrc.no, +47 905 62 329.
  • Ana Milena Ayala Sanchez, advocacy and communication officer in Colombia: ana.ayala@nrc.no, +57 3232746021.

items.title: Historic failure at COP31 is a devasting blow to children around the world – Save the Children
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: Save the Children

Children are extremely vulnerable to the impacts of the climate crisis, with an average of 330 million children per year experiencing severe climate disasters between January 2022 and September 2026—up nearly 50% in the previous five-year period.

ANTALYA, 22 NOVEMBER – Children have been dealt a devastating blow at COP31 today after countries failed to agree on a final deal that would deliver a meaningful response to the climate crisis, Save the Children said.

The inability of countries to reach agreement on issues such as transitioning away from fossil fuels and on providing the scale and quality of climate finance needed has left COP31 without a meaningful outcome. While backsliding was avoided, failure cannot be mistaken for progress, said Save the Children. At a time when children are already facing escalating climate impacts, this outcome signals that protecting their lives and futures remains secondary to preserving the systems and industries driving the crisis.

Children are extremely vulnerable to the impacts of the climate crisis, with an average of 330 million children per year experiencing severe climate disasters between January 2022 and September 2026—up nearly 50% in the previous five-year period.

Shruti Agarwal, Senior Climate Adviser, Save the Children UK, said:

"COP31 will be remembered as the conference where the world turned its back on climate ambition. Children are the ones most impacted by this failure; their lives and futures continue to be the ones to suffer.

"While decision makers spent days negotiating behind closed doors, they ultimately failed to reach an agreement, leaving children to bear the consequences of a climate crisis they did not create. Across the world, children are missing school, losing safe places to play, being forced from their homes and seeing their futures threatened by floods, wildfires, drought and extreme heat. The impacts may look different from one child to the next, but the reality is the same: no child should pay the price for a crisis they did not cause.

“Crucially this summit has failed to deliver the progress needed to transition away from fossil fuels or provide the scale and quality of climate finance that children and families urgently need.

"Every decision on addressing climate change shapes the world children will inherit, and today's failure to act will be felt for years to come. The progress made in recognising and advancing children's rights must not be allowed to unravel in future negotiations. Instead, it must serve as the foundation for greater ambition and urgent action.

"What happens next matters. Governments must return to the table next year ready to collaborate and determined to put children, especially those living on the front lines of the climate crisis, at the heart of the decisions that will define their future.”

ENDS

Peter is 14 years old and lives in Western Province in Zambia with his mother, Masiye (28), his brothers Munkobwe (2) and Mudla (12) and his sister Namasisku (7). Masiye farms maize, ground nuts and beans to provide for her children. The rainy season in Zambia normally stretches from October to March, but during the 2023/24 rainy season there have been intense dry spells and Masiye says they have gone days, weeks and months without rain. Her ground nut and bean crops have failed, and her maize crops – which were due to be harvested in May – have already shrivelled up and died. Masiye says they have cut back to two meals a day and that her children tell her constantly that they’re hungry. Masiye and her children have resorted to foraging for wild fruits and nuts – which are also in short supply due to the failed rains – but they have to be careful what parts of the fruits and nuts they eat as they can be toxic. There are also days when their borehole dries up and they have to dig a hole in the ground to get water. Peter says when he’s hungry he feels dizzy and can’t see properly, and this is impacting on his studies. He says sometimes he doesn’t go to school because he’s too hungry or because he must help his mother find food and water. Seven out of 10 provinces in Zambia have been impacted by the country’s worst drought in 20 years and the government has declared a national emergency. More than 1 million children are facing severe food shortages and hunger as the El Niño induced dry spell kills crops and dries up water sources. Sacha Myers / Save the Children

Since 2022, one in three children worldwide, or 911 million children, have been exposed to climate disasters.

12-year-old Jamer, lives in a small community called a “rancheria” in La Guajira on the northern tip of Colombia. He is part of the largest indigenous group in the country, the Wayuu tribe, and lives with his mother, stepfather and five siblings, the youngest is just a baby. The continuing drought and unpredictable seasons have hit his community hard. The once reliable rain patterns, guiding their crop cultivation, have shifted, leading to food shortages. The lack of water is taking its toll, especially on children. Jamer speaks of sickness and, sadly, cases where children have lost their lives due to water-related diseases. One of the main water sources they have available is the “Jaguey”, an open pool that relies on rainwater, several miles from his home that is also used by livestock. They often have to drink it despite the risks to their health. If the rain doesn’t arrive, there is a deep well close to their home, but that is saline, and dangerous for children. He’s exhausted by their daily hunt for fresh water in the blistering heat and worries for his younger brothers and sisters that they may go without. Other families in the community now pay for water to be trucked to their communities, but Jamers home is too remote and difficult for lorries to reach, so they must survive with what they have. Due to the years of drought when it does rain the rivers become impassable due to flooding, and the damage they have caused has created ravines in the landscape. He is concerned about what the impending impact of El Nino will be on his community, given the struggles they already face. But he still dreams of a better future for his community – one with access to clean water, quality education, and the ability to grow crops. Jamer is part of a Save the Childre program to promote resilience amongst the Wayuu community to the changing climate and promote traditional cultural practices. Strong quotes: "We are exhausted searching for water. The worst is that the easy one to find is the salty one, that's all." "The El Niño phenomenon is not convenient for us; it is better the La Niña phenomenon because it brings rain, if we want pure water because it is pure and comes from the sky." "The environment is also polluted when the garbage is burned, and the air is polluted, and the children are the ones who suffer from that." "We are very affected by the El Niño phenomenon because it has not rained, so the well is always contaminated." "Water is indispensable for our planting because it has not been raining lately." "Our crops die quickly; last time we planted beans, and they died as well as the corn because we poured the brackish (salty) water on them and left them." Angela Ponce / Save the Children

With climate disasters increasingly disrupting children's lives, education and futures, young people across the world are finding creative ways to influence decisions that will affect the planet they inherit.

items.title: Disease Outbreak News: Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus- Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kenya and Nigeria (20 November 2026)
items.blurb:
Countries: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kenya, Nigeria
Source: World Health Organization

Please refer to the attached file.

Situation at a glance

Since the publication of the previous Disease Outbreak News on 6 November 2026, additional confirmed cases and deaths have been reported in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. While some areas have seen a slight decline in cases, sustained, high-level transmission continues overall in the country. As of 17 November 2026, a total of 11 613 confirmed cases, including 5678 deaths (crude case fatality ratio: 48.9%), have been reported across 68 health zones in eight provinces, with active transmission ongoing in 48 health zones. Ituri and Nord Kivu remain the most affected provinces, while Sud-Kivu and Sud Ubangi have not reported cases for more than 42 days. The high proportion of deaths occurring in communities, meaning outside of dedicated treatment centres, especially among young children, continues to highlight challenges in early case detection and timely access to appropriate care. Of the 720 deaths reported since 28 October (last three weeks), 452 occurred in communities and 268 in treatment centres. Since the last Disease Outbreak News, no new cases have been reported from Kenya or Nigeria; and no new country has reported confirmed cases. Both countries have started a 42-day countdown to declare the end of their outbreaks. However, the high-level transmission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo calls for continued need for readiness in the region, including cross-border surveillance, points of entry monitoring, timely case detection and coordinated preparedness and response measures. Six months into the outbreak of Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the response has expanded significantly, but further scale up is needed, with rising insecurity remaining the greatest obstacle to the expansion of operations. The next phase must prioritize quality, reach and community trust, alongside sustained funding, coordination and security to save lives and end the outbreak. On 18 November 2026, the Director-General of WHO, concurring with the advice of the IHR Emergency Committee formulated at its third meeting, on 17 November 2026, determined that the event continues to constitute a public health emergency of international concern (PHEIC). Updated recommendations to the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and all other States Parties will be issued in the coming days.

Description of the situation

Cases have been reported in five countries since the declaration of the outbreak on 15 May 2026: the Democratic Republic of the Congo, France, Kenya, Nigeria, and Uganda. The outbreaks in France and Uganda have been controlled since August, while Kenya and Nigeria continue with heightened surveillance as they count down to 42 days, completing two maximum incubation periods since the last confirmed cases were either discharged or medically evacuated from the country.

On 26 October 2026, Switzerland reported the medical evacuation of the case, who received medical care in Geneva, Switzerland. The patient recovered and was discharged on 11 November testing PCR-negative for Bundibugyo virus for a second time.

On 18 November 2026, the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland reported that a medically evacuated health and care worker from the Democratic Republic of the Congo had recovered and been discharged from hospital.

Democratic Republic of the Congo

An additional 945 confirmed cases, including 480 confirmed deaths, have been reported in the Democratic Republic of the Congo since the previous Disease Outbreak News was published.

In the last 21-day period, as of 17 November, 1417 new confirmed cases were reported, with Ituri accounting for 668 (13% decrease) cases, Nord Kivu for 635 (8% increase) cases, Haut-Uélé for 90 (13% increase) cases, Tshopo for 20 (47% decrease) cases and Nord-Ubangi for four cases. No new cases were reported in Bas-Uélé, Sud Kivu or Sud-Ubangi during that period.

As of 17 November, cumulative confirmed cases have reached 11 613, including 5678 deaths and 3148 recoveries. The overall crude CFR is 48.9%.

Confirmed cases have now been identified in 68 health zones across eight provinces. Forty-eight of the 68 affected health zones reported at least one new case during the preceding 21 days, while 20 reported no recent cases. Beni, Bunia, and Mandima have reported the highest number of cases and deaths in the preceding 21 days. Ituri remains the most extensively affected province, with 28 of 36 health zones reporting cases during this outbreak, followed by Nord Kivu (17/34), Haut-Uélé (8/13), Tshopo (7/23), Bas-Uélé (4/11), Nord-Ubangi (2/11), Sud Kivu (1/34) and Sud-Ubangi (1/16). Watsa in Haut-Uélé province is the most recently affected health zone, reporting 11 confirmed cases.

Six months into the BVD outbreak, the response has expanded significantly, but transmission remains persistent and geographically widespread. WHO, the national Government and partners have strengthened surveillance, treatment, laboratory capacity and community engagement, yet high community mortality, insecurity, displacement and a fragile health system continue to undermine progress.

The next phase will need to focus on scaling up, but also on improving the reach, quality and impact of the response. Early detection, quality care, contact tracing, infection prevention and community trust remain critical. Sustained funding, strong coordination and safe access to communities will be essential.

The third International Health Regulations (IHR) Emergency Committee meeting regarding the epidemic of BVD in the Democratic Republic of the Congo took place on 17 November. Following the advice of the Committee, the Director-General agreed that the ongoing outbreak remains a PHEIC. Updated recommendations to the government of the DRC and all other States Parties will be issued in the coming days and reported in the next Disease Outbreak News publication.

While Nord Kivu reported the highest number of cases in the last seven days (235 cases (40% increase compared to the previous seven days) as of 17 November), Ituri remains the most affected province since the outbreak was declared, with 7946 cumulative confirmed cases and 3751 deaths, with CFR of 47%. Nord Kivu follows with 2996 confirmed cases and 1654 deaths, and continues to record the highest provincial CFR, at 55%. Haut-Uélé has reported 534 cases and 231 deaths, while Tshopo has recorded 109 cases and 35 deaths. The less-affected provinces continue to report substantially fewer cases, but transmission persists in several of them. The continued occurrence of cases across multiple provinces shows that the outbreak remains geographically active even as intensity varies between health zones. Sud-Kivu and Sud Ubangi have not reported cases for more than 42 days.

As of 17 November 2026, the average proportion of contacts seen daily over the previous 14-day period is 81%, remaining below the required threshold of 95% for a daily average of the proportion of contacts seen over the previous 14-day period. Two provinces were at or above the 95% threshold: Bas-Uele (100%, 56/56) and Nord-Ubangi (99%, 140/138) Five provinces were below the threshold: Haut-Uélé (86%; 1741/1495), Ituri (86% (9564/11 104), Nord-Kivu (77%; 16 015/12 313), Tshopo (68%; 720/526), and Sud-Ubangi (63%; 127/80). Strengthened contact follow-up is required, particularly in provinces below the target, to achieve the minimum threshold of 95%.

Kenya

As of 17 November 2026, the cumulative confirmed cases reported in Kenya are nine, including two deaths, with a crude CFR of 22.2%. All eight secondary cases were epidemiologically linked to the imported index case and associated with one cluster (four family members of the index case and four health and care workers). All seven hospitalized cases have recovered and been discharged (the last case was discharged on 11 November). A 42-day countdown is underway and includes heightened surveillance.

There is currently no evidence of transmission outside this cluster, and there have been no new confirmed cases since 19 October 2026. Additionally, all eight secondary cases were already under quarantine as known contacts when they developed symptoms.

As of 17 November, of the 135 cumulative contacts identified since the first confirmed case, eight subsequently became confirmed cases and nine contacts left Kenya (relevant National IHR Focal Points were notified). All have completed the 21-day follow-up on 11 November 2026.

Nigeria

On 20 October 2026, Nigeria reported one laboratory-confirmed imported case of BVD in the Federal Capital Territory Abuja. On 26 October 2026, Switzerland reported the medical evacuation of the case, who received medical care in Geneva, Switzerland. The patient recovered and was discharged on 11 November, following two PCR-negative test results for Bundibugyo virus.

As of 13 November, a cumulative of 62 contacts had been identified in Nigeria for follow-up and all the contacts have completed the 21-day follow-up period. National authorities, with support from WHO and partners, have intensified contact tracing, case investigation and infection prevention and control measures, including the provision of essential supplies and personal protective equipment for health workers. Investigations are ongoing to establish the likely source of infection and reconstruct the travel and exposure history of the imported case. WHO has urged countries across the region to strengthen surveillance, laboratory diagnostic capacity, rapid response readiness and cross-border preparedness to mitigate the risk of further transmission.

Epidemiology

Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) is a severe Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus, one of the Orthoebolavirus species. It is a zoonotic disease, with fruit bats suspected to be the natural reservoir.

Human infection is thought to initially occur through close contact with the blood or secretions of infected wildlife, such as bats or non-human primates, and it subsequently spreads from person-to-person through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs, or other bodily fluids of infected individuals or contaminated surfaces and materials. Transmission is particularly amplified in health-care settings when infection prevention and control (IPC) measures are inadequate, and during unsafe burial practices involving direct contact with deceased individuals.

The incubation period for BVD ranges from two to 21 days, and infected individuals are not infectious until symptom onset. Early symptoms such as fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache, and sore throat are non-specific, which complicates clinical diagnosis and can delay detection. These symptoms then progress to gastrointestinal symptoms, organ dysfunction, and, in some cases, haemorrhagic manifestations.

The CFR from the previous two BVD outbreaks, reported in Uganda and in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2007 and 2012, were 30% and 50%, respectively.

Differentiating BVD from other endemic febrile illnesses such as malaria is challenging without laboratory confirmation. Outbreak control relies on rapid case identification and investigation, isolation and care, contact tracing, safe burials and strong community engagement, as no approved vaccines or specific treatments currently exist for BVD.

Since first detected in May 2026, this BVD outbreak has rapidly evolved into a large and geographically expanding epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with sustained transmission, high mortality and an increasing risk of further international spread. The current outbreak is the second documented Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the country, after the 2012 outbreak, and the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo irrespective of virus species. The population at greatest risk of exposure is concentrated in communities living in and moving through the health areas with active transmission.

Public health response

For detailed information about the ongoing public health response actions by the Ministry of Health, WHO and partners please refer to the latest situation reports published by the WHO Regional Office for Africa: Ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo | WHO | Regional Office for Africa.

Democratic Republic of the Congo

Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in collaboration with WHO and partners, are continuing to implement and coordinate extensive public health measures. These include disease surveillance; laboratory testing; IPC; clinical care; community engagement; research; logistics; and support for response interventions and essential health services, including for the ongoing concurrent humanitarian crisis; engaging donors and mobilizing additional resources to address critical funding gaps and sustain response operations across affected and at-risk areas. A substantial scale-up is ongoing across all response pillars to get ahead of the outbreak.

Kenya

On 11 November 2026, Kenya discharged its last confirmed BVD case after two negative tests, released the remaining contacts from quarantine, and began the 42-day countdown to declaring the end of the outbreak. Following the start of the 42-day countdown, Kenya has maintained cross-border surveillance and screening at all designated points of entry.

Nigeria

Nigeria has maintained a high level of alert for BVD since the outbreak began in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in May 2026. As of 13 November, all identified contacts had completed the 21-day follow-up period.

Following the medical evacuation of the case on 26 October, the country is continuing with the 42-days countdown to declare the end of the outbreak and is maintaining heightened surveillance.

On 17 November 2026, WHO reassessed the risk of the BVD outbreak. The risk assessment categorizes States Parties into five groups based on population mobility from areas with community BVD transmission and response capacity.

The risk in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the only State Party with currently documented community transmission, remains very high, reflecting the intensity and geographic expansion of the outbreak, ongoing undetected transmission, community deaths, health-care transmission, insecurity, laboratory constraints, gaps in community engagement and funding, and the continued potential for national spread.

The risk for States Parties with confirmed cases but without community transmission, including Kenya and Nigeria, is assessed as high, given the potential for onward and secondary transmission following importation, challenges in early detection, uncertainty around transmission chains, and the continued possibility of additional introductions.

The risk is also assessed as high for States Parties with substantial population connectivity to areas with community transmission, or with moderate connectivity but low response capacity. High population mobility, formal and informal cross-border movement, the possibility of undetected importation, variable surveillance and response capacities, and humanitarian and access constraints increase the likelihood of delayed detection and onward transmission.

The risk for States Parties with substantial connectivity but high response capacity is assessed as low. Although importation remains possible because of travel and other connections with affected areas, strong health systems and demonstrated outbreak-response capacities reduce the likelihood of sustained community transmission.

Finally, the risk for all other States Parties remains low. Transmission remains concentrated in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with no evidence of sustained transmission beyond the country. However, further international exportation remains possible, requiring continued surveillance, preparedness, rapid detection and containment of any imported cases.

Based on the currently available information, WHO advises against any restriction of travel to, or trade with, States Parties experiencing and/or responding to the public health event. The Temporary Recommendations issued to States Parties on 24 August 2026 underscore the importance of coordinated outbreak control, strengthened cross‑border collaboration, and sustained surveillance and preparedness to prevent further regional spread and ensure an effective public health response. Rapid recognition of cases, testing and optimized supportive care can reduce mortality, and improve community perceptions and acceptance of health care within the response.

Following the advice formulated by the IHR Emergency Committee regarding the epidemic of BVD in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Director-General of WHO determined that the event continues to constitute a PHEIC. An updated set of Temporary Recommendations will be issued to States Parties, and this will be reported in the next Disease Outbreak News publication.

items.title: Indonesia: Pangandaran marks 20 years since the 2006 tsunami
items.blurb:
Country: Indonesia
Source: UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction

“Are you ready to stay alert?” calls a young woman to a group of high school students.

“Ready!” they reply, standing in neat rows in their light-blue batik uniforms.

“Ready to save yourself? Ready to follow instructions? Ready to help others?”

“Ready!”

The students break into song, repeating the words they have just learned: “Tsunami – run quickly! Go to higher ground! Stay away from the shoreline! Help others!”

There is laughter, energy and plenty of enthusiasm. But the message is serious. The students are practicing the new Tsunami Song, created especially for this year's World Tsunami Awareness Day activities in Pangandaran, Indonesia. Its simple lyrics turn essential safety messages into something children can sing, remember and share.

For Pangandaran, this is more than a school activity. It is part of an effort to keep the memory of a devastating event alive – and to make sure a new generation knows how to respond if it happens again.

Remembering what happened

On 17 July 2006, a magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck beneath the Indian Ocean, off the southern coast of Java. The earthquake generated a tsunami that swept along around 300 kilometers of coastline, including the popular coastal town of Pangandaran.

The earthquake was unusual: its shaking was relatively weak, even in places that were later hit by powerful waves. With no local tsunami warning system capable of alerting coastal communities in time, people had little opportunity to prepare. More than 600 people lost their lives along the southern coast of Java, including hundreds in and around Pangandaran.

Today, Pangandaran is once again a lively seaside destination. Visitors from Jakarta, Bandung and beyond come to enjoy its beaches, restaurants and coastal atmosphere. Tourism brings opportunities to the community, but it also means that many people – including visitors unfamiliar with the area – need to know what to do when a tsunami threatens.

Twenty years is a long time. Survivors and older residents remember the 2006 tsunami, but an entire generation has grown up since then. Many of today's schoolchildren were not yet born or were too young to remember what happened.

Keeping the memory alive, and passing on the lessons, is therefore essential.

Learning through action – and a little music

This year's World Tsunami Awareness Day activities put children and young people at the heart of preparedness. Students from high school and primary schools took part in classroom sessions, discussions and practical exercises.

At the National High School No. 1, students explored what would happen if a tsunami warning were issued during the school day. Taking on the roles of teachers, principals and school administrators, they considered how to organize an evacuation, communicate instructions and help everyone reach safety.

The learning continued outside the classroom, with earthquake drills and tsunami evacuation exercises involving the wider school communities. And, of course, there was the Tsunami Song.

Building on the experience of a similar initiative in Timor-Leste in 2025, the song brings together key messages on recognizing danger, evacuating to higher ground or inland, and helping others. The idea is simple: when important information is set to music, learning can become more engaging – and the messages easier to remember.

The song also made its way beyond the school gates. At a Zumba dance session by the beach, women and children danced and sang along, turning tsunami awareness into a lively community activity. It was a reminder that preparedness can be something people learn and practice together, in ways that are accessible, creative and enjoyable.

From recognition to continued readiness

Pangandaran has made important progress since 2006. Working with national, provincial and local authorities and technical partners, the community strengthened its preparedness and, in 2022, became one of Indonesia's communities recognized under UNESCO's Tsunami Ready Recognition Programme.

The programme supports communities in putting practical measures in place – from understanding tsunami risks and ensuring people know the warning signs, to establishing evacuation routes, conducting drills and making sure warnings can reach those at risk.

The work matters all the more as Pangandaran continues to attract growing numbers of visitors. A warning can only save lives if people understand it and know how to act. That means preparedness needs to reach not only residents, but also schoolchildren, businesses and tourists.

A community effort, looking ahead

World Tsunami Awareness Day 2026 brought together local communities, schools, authorities and technical partners for several days of learning, exercises and commemoration. The public programme on 6 November attended by around 500 people, offered a moment for the wider Pangandaran community to come together, remember those who lost their lives and recognize the progress made over the past two decades.

Twenty years after the tsunami, the message from Pangandaran is both a tribute to those affected and a commitment to future generations: remembering matters but knowing what to do can save lives.

And sometimes, the best way to make sure a message stays with us is to sing it together.

World Tsunami Awareness Day activities in Pangandaran were made possible thanks to financial support from the Government of Japan and organized by UNDRR, UNESCO, Pacifico and U-Inspire Indonesia, in partnership with national, provincial and local authorities, including BMKG, BNPB, BPBD and FKDM.

items.title: Landmark ICJ Judgment on Rohingya Genocide Must Mark a Turning Point for Atrocity Prevention in Myanmar
items.blurb:
Country: Myanmar
Source: Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect

The Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect welcomes the landmark judgment by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Gambia v. Myanmar. By finding Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, the Court has delivered a historic affirmation of the rights of Rohingya survivors and a powerful reminder that all states parties to the Genocide Convention share an obligation to prevent and punish genocide.

In a nine-to-six decision, the Court found that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in northern Rakhine State during the military’s 2017 “clearance operations,” including through killings, the infliction of serious bodily and mental harm and the imposition of measures intended to prevent births within the group. Taken together, the Court is convinced that the most logical conclusion is that Myanmar intended to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population.

The Court also found that Myanmar failed to prevent acts of genocide by individuals acting alongside its security forces, failed to punish genocide and other prohibited acts and failed to enact the domestic legislation necessary to give effect to its preventive obligations under the Genocide Convention. It further found that Myanmar had violated the Court’s third provisional measure in its January 2020 order to prevent the destruction and ensure the preservation of evidence of alleged genocidal acts.

The judgment is historic for international justice. The ruling marks the first time that a state has been found responsible for genocide. The judgment also marks an important development in international law. Building on its 2007 ruling in Bosnia v. Serbia, the ICJ has now explicitly clarified that states can be held responsible for failing to prevent genocide even if genocide does not ultimately occur. The obligation to prevent arises as soon as a state knows, or should normally know, of a serious risk of genocide. This reinforces the preventive nature of the Genocide Convention: states cannot wait for genocide to happen before they are required to act.

For Rohingya survivors, this ruling is an important step towards recognition, justice and redress. The Global Centre recognizes the courage of Rohingya and Myanmar civil society advocates, particularly women human rights defenders, who documented atrocities and demanded accountability at the national, regional and international level at great personal risk. Nearly a decade after the military’s 2017 “clearance operations” forced more than 900,000 Rohingya to flee Rakhine State, this judgment represents a historic milestone for a population that has endured decades of persecution, culminating in a genocide. Although no judgment can undo their suffering or restore the lives lost, it affirms a truth that Rohingya survivors have courageously fought for the international community to recognize.

Prior to the ruling, the perpetrators of atrocities against the Rohingya have enjoyed near-total impunity. The ICJ proceedings have provided a critical avenue for holding Myanmar accountable under international law, while reaffirming that sovereignty cannot shield states from their international legal obligations or excuse atrocity crimes committed against populations under their protection. We commend The Gambia, the Organisation for Islamic Cooperation and the 11 states who intervened in the case for their efforts to ensure justice for the Rohingya.

Savita Pawnday, Executive Director of the Global Centre, said, “The ICJ judgment is a historic recognition of the genocide committed against the Rohingya, but it must also serve as a call to action for every state party to the Genocide Convention. The obligation to prevent genocide does not end with a court ruling. States that welcome this judgment must now demonstrate their commitment by using every available political, economic and diplomatic lever to end support for those responsible for atrocities and protect the Rohingya and all populations at risk in Myanmar.”

Accountability for past atrocities must be accompanied by urgent action to prevent further crimes. Failure to translate this historic ruling into concrete preventive action risks perpetuating the conditions that enabled the Rohingya genocide. The Rohingya, both inside Myanmar and displaced beyond its borders, continue to face grave risks, including ongoing widespread abuses by the military and the Arakan Army. The same military responsible for the 2017 atrocities continues to commit war crimes and crimes against humanity across Myanmar following its 2021 coup. These ongoing abuses, compounded by discriminatory laws, the denial of citizenship, restrictions on movement and protracted displacement, perpetuate the conditions that enabled the 2017 genocide and place the Rohingya at heightened risk of further genocidal acts.

The judgment must be a catalyst for action. The Global Centre calls on all states, but particularly the states parties to the Genocide Convention, as well as relevant regional and international institutions, to take the following urgent actions:

  • Enforce the Court’s judgment and ensure survivor-centered reparations. Press Myanmar to comply fully with all binding orders, including investigations, punishment of perpetrators, legislative reform and guarantees of non-repetition. Support implementation and monitoring of restitution and compensation measures, ensuring the meaningful participation of Rohingya survivors and civil society, including women-led organizations, in shaping and overseeing reparations.
  • End relationships that enable atrocities. Review and suspend military, financial and technical cooperation that enables the Myanmar military to commit atrocities. Halt transfers of arms, dual-use technology, aviation fuel and other materiel that could facilitate further violations. Review commercial ties, including with entities that finance or supply the military and close channels through which the military obtains revenue or equipment used in attacks on civilians.
  • Impose coordinated sanctions and an arms embargo. Call on the UN Security Council (UNSC) to adopt a comprehensive arms embargo and targeted sanctions against those responsible for atrocities. Where the Council remains blocked, states should act collectively and unilaterally to impose sanctions.
  • Ensure the protection of civilians and humanitarian access. Demand that all parties to the conflict cease attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, as well as allow safe, rapid and unhindered humanitarian access. - Pursue justice through every available accountability mechanism. Reiterate the call for a UNSC referral of the situation in Myanmar to the International Criminal Court, support investigations and prosecutions under universal jurisdiction and strengthen support for the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar and other accountability efforts.
  • Protect refugees and ensure any return is voluntary, safe, dignified and sustainable. Any return must be grounded in guarantees of full citizenship, equal rights and fundamental freedoms and must be accompanied by the restitution of property and the restoration of conditions necessary for a safe and sustainable life. No repatriation process should proceed while conditions in Rakhine State remain unsafe or the necessary protections are absent.
  • Address the root causes of persecution and ensure affected communities shape their future. Demand that the Myanmar authorities repeal discriminatory laws – including the 1982 Citizenship Law – restore Rohingya citizenship and fundamental rights and end policies and practices that sustain persecution. Ensure the meaningful participation of Rohingya communities, particularly women, in all decisions affecting their future, and provide sustained support for Rohingya-led and women-led civil society organizations.

The Global Centre urges Myanmar to comply fully and without delay with the Court’s binding judgment, including by enacting legislation, conducting credible investigations and prosecutions, providing assurances and guarantees of non-repetition and implementing the Court-ordered restitution measures. Myanmar must report to the Court within two years on the restitution measures it has adopted and, where full reparation through restitution is materially impossible, specify the amount and modalities of compensation.

Genocide does not end when a judgment is read. For Rohingya survivors, justice cannot be measured by legal recognition alone, but by whether they can finally live free from persecution, reclaim their rights and determine their own futures in safety and dignity. Every state that welcomes this ruling now faces a choice: continue business as usual with those responsible for atrocities, or use every available tool to uphold its obligations, protect the Rohingya and prevent further atrocities across Myanmar.

items.title: World: La Directora General de la OIM pide fortalecer la cooperación migratoria para ampliar las oportunidades e impulsar el desarrollo en África Occidental
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: International Organization for Migration

Dakar/Ginebra, 20 de noviembre de 2026 – Los países de África Occidental deben fortalecer la cooperación para facilitar el acceso de las personas al empleo y al desarrollo de competencias, y aprovechar el potencial de la migración para impulsar el desarrollo, garantizando al mismo tiempo la protección de las personas en tránsito, señaló la Directora General de la Organización Internacional para las Migraciones (OIM), Amy Pope, en la Conferencia inaugural sobre el Proceso de Cooperación Regional en materia de Migración en África Occidental, celebrada del 18 al 20 de noviembre en Dakar, Senegal, bajo el liderazgo del Gobierno de Senegal.

La conferencia marcó el lanzamiento del Proceso de Dakar, una plataforma liderada por los Estados para fortalecer la cooperación regional en materia de migración. Reunió a ministros y altos representantes de 16 países de África Occidental con el fin de identificar prioridades comunes y acordar medidas concretas para articular la gobernanza de la migración, la protección y el desarrollo a través de las fronteras. Su agenda va más allá de la migración irregular y abarca las oportunidades que una movilidad bien gestionada puede generar para las personas y las comunidades.

"La mayoría de las personas que se desplazan en África Occidental permanecen en la región, y muchas de ellas buscan trabajo. Demasiados jóvenes siguen arriesgando sus vidas en viajes peligrosos, y ya no podemos esperar más para actuar", afirmó la Directora General Pope. "Los países deben trabajar conjuntamente a lo largo de estas rutas e invertir en empleo, competencias y desarrollo. Y esto no puede limitarse únicamente a frenar los viajes peligrosos. Tiene que ver con la creación de oportunidades en los lugares de origen, la apertura de vías de migración regular para cruzar las fronteras y la garantía de seguridad de las personas en cada etapa del camino".

La conferencia concluyó con la adopción de la Declaración de Dakar y una Hoja de Ruta Regional para 2027-2028, que establece prioridades de acción compartidas. Entre ellas figuran la ampliación de las vías de migración regular, la inversión en empleo, competencias y comunidades resilientes, y el fortalecimiento de la gobernanza de la migración y la protección de los migrantes. Salvar vidas, abordar los factores que impulsan a las personas a emprender viajes peligrosos en situación de migración irregular y apoyar el retorno voluntario asistido y la reintegración sostenible forman parte de esta agenda más amplia.

La adopción de la Declaración de Dakar y de la Hoja de Ruta Regional marca el comienzo, y no la culminación, del Proceso de Dakar. El objetivo ahora es transformar el acuerdo político en una cooperación sostenida: llevar adelante las prioridades acordadas, movilizar las alianzas y las inversiones necesarias para materializarlas y mantener el impulso mucho más allá de la conferencia.

Las regiones de África Occidental y Central albergan a más de 11,3 millones de migrantes internacionales. Aproximadamente el 77 % proviene de la propia región, lo que subraya la importancia de una cooperación que apoye la movilidad entre países vecinos. La población joven de la región ofrece un considerable potencial de crecimiento y desarrollo, lo que sitúa el acceso a la educación, las competencias y el trabajo decente en el centro de esta agenda. Sin embargo, las oportunidades limitadas, los conflictos, la inseguridad y las presiones climáticas llevan a algunas personas a emprender viajes peligrosos.

El Proceso de Dakar ofrece a los países de África Occidental un espacio común para establecer prioridades compartidas, coordinar sus esfuerzos y transformar los compromisos políticos en resultados concretos a nivel nacional y regional.

La conferencia también presentó fotografías y testimonios personales que documentan experiencias a lo largo de la Ruta Atlántica de África Occidental, aportando una perspectiva humana a los debates sobre protección, vías seguras y oportunidades económicas.

La OIM brindará apoyo técnico y de secretaría al Proceso. Aprovechando los datos empíricos disponibles, su experiencia técnica, sus alianzas y su presencia operacional en toda la región, la Organización apoyará a los gobiernos en la articulación de prioridades a través de las fronteras, el seguimiento continuo y la movilización de las alianzas y los recursos necesarios para traducir la Declaración de Dakar y la Hoja de Ruta Regional en acciones concretas. El apoyo de la OIM abarca la gobernanza de la migración, las vías de migración regular, la protección de los migrantes, las competencias y los medios de vida, la reintegración sostenible y el desarrollo comunitario.

"Apoyaremos a los Estados Miembros en la transformación de los compromisos asumidos en Dakar en resultados concretos", afirmó Pope. "El éxito se traducirá en más oportunidades en los lugares de origen y a través de las fronteras, comunidades más sólidas y una migración segura y bien gestionada. Se trata de permitir que las personas alcancen su pleno potencial y de garantizar que la migración contribuya al desarrollo".

Para más información, visite el Centro de Medios de la OIM.
