items.title: Shot During Kasab’s Arrest on 26/11, This Retd Cop Now Helps Families With Last Rites & Legal Issues
items.blurb: On the night of 26 November 2008, Mumbai Police officer Sanjay Govilkar was shot while helping capture terrorist Ajmal Kasab at Girgaum Chowpatty. Across Mumbai, terrorists were attacking several locations. People across India followed the news from their homes, fearful of what might happen next. Police officers responded across the city, and many lost their lives in the process. Sanjay survived the bullet injury. Years later, he continues to speak about that night, the colleagues he lost, and the work that has filled his life beyond the police force. From writing books to helping families through an NGO he founded with friends, he has found different ways to serve people. The Better India spoke to the former officer about the arrest of Kasab and the experiences that shaped his life afterwards. ‘Unfortunately, he never returned’ “I consider myself very lucky, as the bullet Kasab fired at me hit the left-hand side of my abdomen and not the right,” he smiles. Around the time of the attacks, Sanjay had been excited about the release of his book, Stopwatch . He was going around his colleagues' desks to distribute copies to everyone. Shortly before the attacks began in Mumbai, he visited his boss Hemant Karkare's cabin to give him a copy. “Hemant sir was not there for some reason, so I left a copy for him on his desk. Unfortunately, he never returned,” Sanjay recalls. The night he helped capture Kasab alive “As the attack unfolded, we were tense, but we had only one goal: to serve our nation. The moment I heard that my boss, Hemant sir, had been attacked and lost his life, I was upset,” he shares. Later that night, Sanjay and his fellow police officers confronted Kasab at Girgaum Chowpatty. During the encounter, Sanjay was shot. “My colleague wanted to immediately shoot him down, but I convinced him to arrest him, as he was a key witness,” Sanjay shares. Capturing Kasab alive became an important part of the investigation and trial that followed. Sanjay and his fellow police officers confronted Kasab at Girgaum Chowpatty. During the encounter, Sanjay was shot. “After the arrest, I was immediately rushed to the hospital, where I received treatment for five to six days. I was asked to stay away from the news and was given counselling by a group of doctors. Finally, when I was discharged, I saw that all the noise was settling. My doctors and my family took great care of me,” he smiles. The experience left Sanjay with a sense of pride in his service, though he is careful to share the credit with his colleagues. When asked how it feels to have achieved something so significant, he says, “I am extremely proud of serving my country, and I would never want to take advantage of this.” He goes on to credit his entire team for the recognition. Why a police officer began writing about health While Sanjay says that being a cop and serving the country was his duty, he was always driven by another passion away from work: writing. Sanjay has so far written and published five books, all of them on health, mental health and relationships. One of those was Stopwatch , the book he had just published when the 26/11 attacks took place. “At one point in my career, I was posted as an immigration officer at the airport and had erratic shifts. This took a toll on my health and prompted me to write the book Stopwatch . It is a must-read for all people who work night shifts,” he shares. “I never let my professional experiences shape my writing. I incorporate the lessons I have learnt, but never let them influence my writing,” he says. Sanjay maintains clear boundaries between his profession and passion. “I never let my professional experiences shape my writing. I incorporate the lessons I have learnt, but never let them influence my writing,” he says. ‘My biggest asset is my close friends’ His friendships have also shaped another important part of his life. Together with his close friends, Sanjay runs Jeevarang, an NGO inspired by a deeply personal experience. “Twenty-five years ago, I lost my grandmother. She was very dear to me. We cremated her in my village, and the next day, when we visited the site to collect her ashes, we saw dogs feeding on the remains. I was heartbroken by what I saw,” he shares. The memory stayed with him and became one of the reasons he wanted to help families give their loved ones a dignified farewell. Through Jeevarang, Sanjay and his friends assist families who have lost their loved ones across 21 villages in Maharashtra. They provide support in cash or kind, depending on what the families need. The NGO began operations in 2007 and also encourages writers by sponsoring the publication of their books. A fraud case that inspired his next chapter Sanjay retired from the police in July 2026. But his interest in helping people facing difficult situations has continued into his retirement. He now runs his own legal and risk advisory firm. The idea goes back to a case he encountered during his police career, involving a mother and daughter who lost their livelihood to online fraud. “I came across a peculiar case in my career in 2009. Online fraudsters tricked a mother and daughter. They were told they had won a lottery and were asked to pay a huge sum of money. The women were innocent and, assuming they would receive a large amount, they sold their small pull-cart shop in Mumbai and lost all their money. The department, however, intervened and cracked the case. This incident stayed with me, and I decided that I wanted to help people who feel stuck in legal issues. That’s when I came up with this idea,” he shares. The mother and daughter's experience stayed with Sanjay, much like what he had witnessed after his grandmother's cremation years earlier. Both experiences influenced the work he eventually chose to pursue outside policing. When Sanjay speaks about 26/11, he credits his colleagues for what they achieved together. In the years since, he has continued to act on the concerns that have stayed with him, from helping families arrange a dignified farewell to supporting people facing legal difficulties. Individuals seeking guidance or assistance with legal matters and risk-related concerns can find information about the services offered by Govilkar Legal & Risk Advisory on its official website . The firm aims to help people understand complex legal situations and consider their next steps.

items.title: How Can the Process That Purifies Water Leave Behind a Possible Carcinogen?
items.blurb: You twist open a sealed bottle of water and drink without a second thought. It's clear, it's sealed, and it's been purified. Behind that bottle is more checking than most of us realise. Since November 2024, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has treated packaged drinking water as a "high-risk" food. The label doesn't mean the water is dangerous. It means the product gets stricter scrutiny: inspections before a licence is granted, annual inspections, and regular testing of both the water and its packaging. Those checks exist because some things in water can't be seen, smelt or tasted. A recent case shows why they matter. FSSAI has sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd after a water sample from its Goa plant was declared unsafe. The sample reportedly contained bromate at 12 micrograms per litre, above the limit of 10. A referral laboratory later also found polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, or PAHs. Bisleri disputes the findings. It says independent testing found bromate within the limit, that its water is safe, and that it will cooperate with the regulator. Whatever the outcome, the case raises a question most of us have never thought to ask: if water has been purified, how can chemicals linked to cancer end up in it? Here's what bromate and PAHs are, how they get into water, what levels are considered acceptable, and what the rules say about keeping them out. What happened at Bisleri's Goa plant? On 30 September 2025, FSSAI officials collected six samples from Bisleri's Goa facility. According to the company, five met the standards. The sixth showed bromate at 12 micrograms per litre, two above the limit. FSSAI has sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd after a water sample from its Goa plant was declared unsafe. Photograph: (Plastic Pollution Coalition) Bisleri says it appealed on 22 November 2025, and the sample went to a referral laboratory. That lab found bromate within the limit, but detected PAHs. Bisleri also had the same sample tested at an FSSAI-approved lab, which it says found bromate within the permitted limit. It sent those results to FSSAI's Western Regional Office on 2 February 2026 . After that, the company says, it heard nothing more and assumed the matter was closed. FSSAI, however, declared the sample unsafe and sanctioned prosecution under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. It has also said it plans to test more samples from Bisleri and other packaged water companies. A prosecution sanction is not a conviction. And because the labs reported different results, it matters to separate what each test actually found from what is still disputed. How does bromate get into water? Surprisingly, bromate often comes from the very step meant to make water safe. Many bottlers disinfect water with ozone, a powerful gas that kills bacteria and viruses. But some water sources naturally contain bromide. When ozone meets bromide during treatment, the reaction can produce bromate. The World Health Organization (WHO) says this treatment process, called ozonation , is the main reason bromate shows up in drinking water. Normally, it isn't found in water in any significant amount. How much forms depends on four things: how much bromide was in the water to begin with how much ozone is used the water's pH (how acidic or alkaline it is) how long treatment runs Get the balance wrong and levels can climb. The WHO has recorded bromate anywhere from under 2 to 293 micrograms per litre in ozone-treated water. Many bottlers disinfect water with ozone, a powerful gas that kills bacteria and viruses. Photograph: (The Hospital of Central Connecticut) Bromate can also form when chlorine-based disinfectants are produced using salt that contains bromide impurities. So bromate in water doesn't necessarily mean the source was polluted. It can be a by-product of cleaning the water, which is why the treatment process itself needs close watching. How much is too much? Bromate worries scientists because it caused cancer in laboratory animals. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classifies potassium bromate as Group 2B, or "possibly carcinogenic to humans". Its 1999 review found strong evidence of cancer in animals, but not enough evidence in humans. That difference matters. A chemical being a possible cancer hazard doesn't mean every exposure carries the same risk. How much is present, and for how long someone is exposed, both count. The WHO's provisional limit for bromate in drinking water is 10 micrograms per litre (0.01 milligrams per litre). India's standard for packaged drinking water, BIS IS 14543:2024, also lists bromate as a chemical that must be tested. In the Bisleri case, 12 micrograms is two above the limit. That's a regulatory concern, but it doesn't mean anyone who drank the water will develop cancer or fall ill. Judging the real risk would need three things: how concentrated it was, how much someone drank, and for how long. Two things are true at once. Detecting a chemical doesn't automatically make water unsafe, because it's the amount that counts. And staying within the limit doesn't mean manufacturers can stop checking. What are PAHs, and how do they get into water? PAHs are a large family of chemicals, built from two or more linked rings of carbon atoms. They form mainly when things don't burn completely, such as coal, wood, petrol and other organic material. Vehicle exhaust, factory emissions and other burning release them into the air and the environment. PAHs don't dissolve easily in water. Instead, they tend to cling to tiny particles. According to the WHO , one known route into drinking water is the coal-tar coating used inside older water pipes to stop them corroding. Pollution from burning can also settle on soil and water, and wash into water sources as runoff. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classifies potassium bromate as Group 2B, or "possibly carcinogenic to humans". Photograph: (Image generated by AI) One PAH, benzo[a]pyrene, is a particular concern because it can cause cancer. The WHO's limit for it is 0.7 micrograms per litre. But PAHs are not all alike. One compound causing cancer doesn't mean they all carry the same risk. Finding PAHs in a sample also doesn't tell us how they got there. In the Bisleri case, we would need to know which compounds were found, and in what amounts, to judge how serious the finding is or where it came from. What about the plastic bottle? Bromate comes mainly from treatment, not the bottle. But scientists have looked at whether chemicals can leach from packaging into water. A 2022 study in the Bulletin of Environmental Contamination and Toxicology tested PET bottles and low-density polyethylene water packets in India. It found that the amount of plasticisers seeping into water depended on the packaging material, how long the water was stored and how hot it got. Leaching was higher at high temperatures, especially in recycled PET bottles and plastic packets. That's a good reason to pay attention to packaging and storage. But the study looked at phthalates, not bromate or PAHs, so it doesn't show that bottles caused either contaminant discussed here. What checks are already in place? Under FSSAI's 29 November 2024 order , packaged drinking water is a high-risk food category. This means: manufacturers must be inspected before they get a licence or registration inspections happen once a year centrally licensed manufacturers need an annual third-party food safety audit by an FSSAI-recognised agency From 1 January 2026, a new FSSAI testing scheme also requires manufacturers to: test their source water at FSSAI-notified, NABL-accredited labs before using it, and test any new source before it's used test for microbes every month, and for several chemicals every quarter test every parameter in the standard at least once every six months test monthly if a parameter fails, until three batches in a row pass The packaging is covered too. Bottles, jars and caps must be tested every six months for "overall and colour migration", meaning whether material or colour seeps from the packaging into the water. Manufacturers must keep these records for inspection. How does a failed sample end up in court? The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 , sets out the steps (Sections 42, 46 and 47): A Food Safety Officer collects a sample and sends it to a Food Analyst, who usually has 14 days to report. If the manufacturer disputes the result, it can appeal to the Designated Officer, who can send the sample to a referral laboratory. If the findings show a violation serious enough to prosecute, the case goes to the relevant authority for sanction. A 2022 study in the Bulletin of Environmental Contamination and Toxicology tested PET bottles and low-density polyethylene water packets in India. Photograph: (Food & Wine) In the Bisleri case, the company challenged the first result, the sample went to a referral lab, and FSSAI then sanctioned prosecution. Bisleri's independent results and its response are part of a dispute that will now be settled through the regulatory and legal process. Should consumers be worried? Chemical contaminants can't always be detected by taste, smell or look. Clear water isn't necessarily free of chemicals . But the Bisleri findings concern one regulatory sample. They don't prove that all packaged water, or every batch from the company, is unsafe. Safe drinking water depends on consistent testing and monitoring. Purification is non-negotiable, but the chemicals that can form during treatment, and contamination from storage and pipes, deserve just as much attention.

items.title: 71% of 27,000 Orchids Survived: How Kerala Researchers Rescued Plants That Were Marked for Felling
items.blurb: When trees along a road are marked for felling, the loss extends beyond their shade and canopy. For thousands of orchids growing on their trunks and branches, the removal of a single tree can mean losing their entire habitat. In Kozhikode, Kerala, researchers faced this challenge as road-widening projects threatened mature trees supporting native orchids. Instead of allowing the plants to be lost along with the trees, they began rescuing and relocating them to other landscapes. A study published on 15 October 2026 in the scientific journal Plants has now documented the outcomes of this effort. Researchers assessed 27,324 native orchids belonging to 21 species that were relocated to three sites in Kozhikode. After monitoring them for 12 to 24 months, they found that 19,511, or 71.4%, had survived. Why roadside trees matter to orchids Unlike terrestrial orchids that grow in soil, epiphytic orchids grow on the trunks and branches of other plants. They use trees as support, relying on their bark, moisture, shade and surrounding canopy conditions to survive. When a mature host tree is felled, the orchids growing on it can lose their habitat at once. The scale of this dependence is evident from an earlier survey in Kerala. A 2025 study, Distribution and Abundance of Native Orchids on Roadside Trees in a Global Biodiversity Hotspot , recorded nearly 10,000 orchids belonging to 13 species on approximately 600 trees across Wayanad. The trees represented 72 different taxa, and the orchid population included six regional endemics. The October 2026 study notes that road construction and widening have increasingly threatened these mature host trees and the orchid communities they support. The researchers involved in the latest study included Mithun Venugopal and Pradeep N Sukumaran of the KSCSTE-Malabar Botanical Garden and Institute for Plant Sciences in Kozhikode, and Viswambharan Sarasan of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, in the UK. More than 17,000 native orchids representing 22 species had initially been transferred to Sarovaram Biopark as part of the earlier rescue programme. The subsequent effort also involved relocating orchids to two other sites: the Malabar Botanical Garden and Kappad Beach. Three sites, different survival outcomes The researchers examined how the rescued plants adapted to three distinct environments, all located in Kozhikode's coastal region. Sarovaram Biopark, an urban wetland with mangrove cover, provided a humid and relatively sheltered environment. The Malabar Botanical Garden offered a mix of shaded, marshy and moderately elevated areas. Unlike terrestrial orchids that grow in soil, epiphytic orchids grow on the trunks and branches of other plants. Photograph: (tspkumar via iNaturalist) Kappad Beach, meanwhile, exposed the orchids to stronger winds, direct sunlight and salt spray. The differences were reflected in their survival. According to the study, Sarovaram recorded the strongest overall establishment , while the exposed coastal location presented greater challenges for the plants to take root and survive. However, Kappad recorded the highest flowering rate among surviving orchids, at 35.6%. It also had the highest proportion of flowering plants producing capsules, at 62.3%. At Sarovaram, the corresponding figures were 26.3% and 34.8%, while the Malabar Botanical Garden recorded 27% and 40.1%, respectively. What the findings mean for conservation The study also examined 6,126 rescued orchids belonging to 12 regionally endemic species. Of these, 3,368 survived, translating to a survival rate of 55%. The group included eight species endemic to India and four shared between southern India and Sri Lanka. This was lower than the overall survival rate of 71.4%, highlighting the additional challenges involved in relocating species with more restricted natural distributions. The researchers found that some high-altitude and mist-forest-associated orchids also managed to survive and reproduce after being moved to lower elevations, although their establishment depended more on the receiving site. Orchids of India Calanthe biloba Lindl. #Orchids #India #Conservation #Biodiversity @ForestDeptt @Sdg13Un https://t.co/mZDyHDj2Mc — Dr. Sanjeet Kumar (Ecologist) (@BiotechSanjeet) October 19, 2026 Beyond survival, the researchers also looked at whether the rescued orchids could reproduce in their new surroundings. They found capsules containing embryos among the relocated plants , indicating that some had progressed beyond simply adapting to their new locations. However, the team stresses that relocation is not a substitute for protecting natural habitats. It is an additional conservation measure for situations where the removal of orchid-bearing trees cannot be avoided. Before a tree is marked for felling to make way for a wider road, there may be dozens of plants growing quietly on its trunk and branches. For orchids, the loss of that tree can mean the loss of an entire habitat. Identifying these plants before construction begins can make room for infrastructure without overlooking the smaller ecosystems that depend on the trees being removed. items.title: Two Surgeons, Five Robotic Arms & A Surgical Robot Built In India
items.blurb: #thebetterindia What if surgeons could perform a heart bypass without stopping the heart? Two Indian doctors just made it possible! At Medanta Hospital in Gurugram, Dr Nitin Kumar Rajput and Dr Lalit Malik performed a complex heart bypass using five robotic arms controlled through two separate surgeon consoles. The procedure, called Totally Endoscopic Coronary Artery Bypass (TECAB), was performed through tiny incisions without the conventional large chest incision or stopping the heart. A specialised stabiliser held the area being operated on steady while the heart continued beating. No heart-lung machine was needed. This was the world’s first reported dual-console, five-arm robotic beating-heart TECAB procedure. And here’s another reason to celebrate: the robot used was SSi Mantra, developed in India by SS Innovations, founded by cardiac surgeon Dr Sudhir Srivastava. The patient’s recovery has been encouraging. items.title: Once Hunted for Fur, Kashmir’s Eurasian Otters Are Reappearing. Here’s What a New Study Reveals About Them
items.blurb: This story is part of The Better India’s new wildlife series, Species in Focus: 52 species. 52 stories. 52 reasons to protect India’s wildlife. One species at a time, the series explores India’s rare, endangered and lesser-known wildlife, their habitats, behaviour, ecological roles and conservation status. For years, the sight of an otter swimming through Kashmir's rivers had become rare. Once found across the Jhelum River basin, the Eurasian otter (Lutra lutra) had nearly disappeared from the valley, its numbers declining amid fur-driven poaching, habitat destruction and water pollution. Now, after decades of little evidence of its presence, the elusive mammal is being spotted again in Kashmir's waterways. A study published in the journal Biological Diversity on 23 October 2026, titled Re-Emergence of Eurasian Otter (Lutra lutra) in the Valley of Kashmir, India: A Conservation Triumph and a Challenge , documents recent sightings and field evidence of the species in the valley. Authored by Irfan Khursheed Shah and Sohail Ahmad Wagay, the study brings together reports that suggest the otter is reappearing after decades of near-local extinction. The researchers identify historical hunting for fur, habitat destruction, and water pollution as major reasons behind the species' decline. Srinagar had once served as a commercial centre for the valley's pelt and fur trade. Although wildlife protection measures introduced from the late 1970s onwards helped curb hunting and the trade, the otter population had already fallen sharply. The return was first noticed in 2025 According to the October 2026 paper, the first widely reported public evidence of the otter's return emerged in June 2025, when a video of an animal in a tributary of the Lidder River went viral. Viewers initially mistook it for a crocodile. The researchers say that professional enhancement of the footage helped establish that the animal was a Eurasian otter, a species that had become unfamiliar to many residents. For now, the recent records establish the Eurasian otter's presence in Kashmir's river systems, rather than a confirmed recovery of its population. Photograph: (IUCN Otter Specialist Group Bulletin) Following the video, camera traps were installed along the Rambiara and Lidder tributaries in July 2025. Although these did not capture the animals, researchers photographed spraints (otter droppings), which can help establish an animal's presence in an area. Another video subsequently surfaced from Ganderbal district, showing an otter feeding on a fish in the Sindh stream, another tributary of the Jhelum. Together, these records provided evidence of the animal's presence across different parts of the valley . The findings also build on earlier field research. A separate study published in the IUCN/SSC Otter Specialist Group Bulletin in January 2026 documented Eurasian otters in the Hirpora Wildlife Sanctuary, along the Rambiara River catchment in Shopian district. The Wildlife Trust of India researchers Tanushree Srivastava, Manvi Singh, Muneeb Nazir and Ishwar Narayanan, along with Sohail Ahmad Wagay of the J&K Department of Wildlife Protection, recorded an initial direct sighting during fieldwork in March 2024. They subsequently conducted a systematic survey between April and June 2025, covering a 12-km stretch of the river. The team recorded 21 signs of otter presence, including one direct sighting, spraints, pugmarks, tracks, fish-feeding remains, and camera-trap photographs. The study reported an average encounter rate of 0.34 signs per kilometre and a camera-trap capture rate of 4.31 captures per 100 trap nights. However, neither study establishes the total number of otters now living in Kashmir Valley. Why the return matters for freshwater ecosystems The Eurasian otter is classified as Near Threatened on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List. It is a semi-aquatic mammal that inhabits rivers, streams, and other freshwater environments. As a top predator, it helps regulate prey populations and is considered an indicator of freshwater ecosystem health. A separate finding from the Hirpora study also points to the importance of involving local communities in conservation. Only 15% of respondents recognised the Eurasian otter, although 92% supported its conservation. More than half reported declining fish populations in the area, indicating potential ecological pressures that also affect otter habitats. What could threaten their return? The October study cautions that the conditions in Kashmir's waterways have changed considerably since the period when otters were commonly reported. Urban expansion over paddy fields, conversion of agricultural land into apple orchards and construction along riverbanks have reduced and fragmented potential habitats. The decline in traditional irrigation canals has further affected the network of waterways available to the animals. The researchers also identify river pollution from heavy metals, pesticides, microplastics, and plastic waste as potential threats. Destructive fishing practices involving chemicals and electric currents, human disturbance and the increasing presence of stray dogs could further affect their survival. We are into the middle stage of our ’13 Weeks of Otters’ series, and next up we have one that the IOSF are very familiar with, the Eurasian Otter! Photo by Terry Evans! #Conservation #Eurasian #Otter #Wild https://t.co/NBY5RQ0ZNR https://t.co/CklFyxizXv — International Otter Survival Fund (IOSF) (@IOSF) August 8, 2022 Climate change presents another challenge. Changes in water levels, floods, landslides and prolonged dry spells can damage or expose the sheltered riverbank spaces, known as holts, where otters rest and raise their young. The researchers also flag the possibility of conflict with expanding trout farms , which are an increasingly important source of livelihood in the valley. What conservation efforts need to focus on The October 2026 paper recommends a coordinated conservation plan involving researchers, wildlife authorities and conservation organisations. This includes protecting and improving river habitats, addressing pollution, preventing hunting and monitoring the species across its newly documented locations. It also calls for public awareness campaigns to address misconceptions about otters. The researchers recommend educational initiatives in schools, awareness material in local languages and outreach at tourist destinations to help residents recognise the species and understand its behaviour. The authors note that otter encounters rarely result in harm to humans globally, and that most interactions are neutral. Better public understanding, therefore, is an important part of ensuring the animals can persist in waterways shared with people. For now, the recent records establish the Eurasian otter's presence in Kashmir's river systems, rather than a confirmed recovery of its population. Sustained monitoring and protection of these freshwater habitats will be necessary to determine whether the species can establish a lasting presence in the valley. items.title: 2 Delhi Teens Fit Rs 140 Filters Onto School Fans, Turning Them Into Air Purifiers for 20000 Kids
items.blurb: A classroom fan spins above a group of children bent over their notebooks. As the teacher moves between desks and lessons continue, the fan keeps the air circulating. But in a city like Delhi, where pollution often makes its way indoors, circulating air does not necessarily mean breathing clean air. Project Vayu's balloon-shaped filter fits over ordinary table and wall fans, helping capture fine particulate matter from classroom air. For thousands of children studying in schools that cannot afford expensive air purifiers, this is an everyday reality. They spend several hours a day inside classrooms, often with little protection from fine particulate matter suspended in the air. Two Delhi teenagers, Krish Aggarwal and Samarth Meattle, decided to look at this problem differently. Instead of asking schools to invest in expensive purification systems, they wondered if the fans already fitted in classrooms could be made to do more. Their idea took shape as Project Vayu, an initiative that has developed an affordable filter that fits over ordinary table and wall fans, helping turn them into air purifiers. At approximately Rs 140 per filter, the innovation offers schools a way to tackle indoor air pollution without having to invest in entirely new equipment. "Growing up in Delhi, we've personally experienced the effects of air pollution," the duo say. "What bothered us was that while some schools could afford expensive air purifiers, thousands of students in under-resourced schools had no protection." What if a classroom fan could also clean the air? Rather than building a new appliance from scratch, Krish and Samarth decided to work with the infrastructure schools already had. The biggest technical challenge was developing a filter that could trap fine particulate matter, particularly PM2.5, without restricting the airflow of an ordinary fan. "We experimented with different designs before arriving at our balloon-shaped filter, made from electret media with electrostatically charged fibres," they explain. The filter uses electrostatically charged fibres that attract and capture tiny airborne particles. It fits over an existing table or wall fan with the help of an elastic lining. Once the fan is switched on, the airflow inflates the filter into a balloon-like shape, increasing its surface area for filtration. There is no need for additional motors, electrical modifications or specialised installation. The filter can be fitted in under a minute, without tools. To develop and test the technology , the teenagers approached Hollingsworth & Vose, a filtration media manufacturer. They initially emailed the company's India team with their idea and were surprised by its willingness to support them. The company provided filtration media free of cost and collaborated with the team on research and development. Priced at approximately Rs 140, the filter offers under-resourced schools an affordable alternative to expensive air purification systems. "The technology to clean air already exists. Schools just can't afford it. By using fans that classrooms already have, we eliminated the need for expensive motors and additional infrastructure," they say. This support has helped keep the manufacturing cost at approximately Rs 140 per filter. What difference can a Rs 140 filter make? For the young innovators , developing an affordable product was only half the task. They also needed to establish whether it could make a measurable difference to indoor air quality. According to the founders, independent and external testing, along with joint research and development with Hollingsworth & Vose, has produced encouraging results. In a closed room measuring approximately 200 square feet, PM2.5 concentrations reportedly dropped from 158 to 11 micrograms per cubic metre within an hour of using the filter, a reduction of over 90%. The results, however, depend on the room's size and conditions. In a larger classroom, the team recorded a 60% reduction in PM2.5 levels over an hour, with further reductions over several hours of use. There is also a visible reminder of the particles being trapped. "One of the most striking things is seeing the filters turn from white to grey or even black after a few weeks of use. It's a visible reminder of just how much particulate pollution is present in classrooms," they say. From 295 classrooms to thousands of students Getting schools to trust an unfamiliar technology developed by high school students was not easy. Project Vayu began with a pilot covering 295 classrooms and around 8,000 students. It has since reached approximately 20,000 students across more than 10 schools. Initially, many institutions were understandably hesitant. Demonstrations and explanations of the testing behind the filters, however, helped the team build confidence. Project Vayu began with a pilot covering 295 classrooms and approximately 8,000 students. The initiative has since expanded to more than 10 schools and has reached around 20,000 students. The team has also installed filters in several under-resourced medical clinics. Their work has not been without challenges. Identifying schools, securing permissions and navigating institutional processes have often slowed installations. "Balancing Project Vayu with academics has definitely been challenging. A lot of our time goes into approaching schools, coordinating installations, and following up on approvals," they say. The effort has also brought recognition. Krish was named to the 2026 Diana Award Roll of Honour for his work with Project Vayu. For him, the recognition belongs to everyone who helped build the initiative, including Samarth and their collaborators. "Project Vayu has taught me that innovation doesn't always require inventing something entirely new. Sometimes it's about making existing technology more accessible," Samarth adds. What's next for Project Vayu? The duo now hopes to expand Project Vayu to more schools across Delhi and eventually other parts of India. They are keen to work with government bodies, school principals, teachers and organisations that can help take the filters to children who need them. Their ambition is rooted in a simple belief: access to cleaner air should not depend on how much a school can spend. For Krish and Samarth, the idea was never just about making a fan work differently. It was about looking at something already available in classrooms and asking how it could serve children better. And sometimes, making a difference does not require an entirely new machine. It begins with finding a new purpose for something that is already there. items.title: Women in a Karnataka Village Just Won Rs 10 Lakh for Protecting What Their Grandmothers Grew
items.blurb: A handful of seeds can carry generations of farming knowledge. In Karnataka's Dharwad district, a group of women has been collecting, preserving, and sharing these seeds, helping farmers continue cultivating indigenous crops suited to the region's rainfed conditions. On November 12, 2026, the Bibi Fatima Women's Self-Help Group (SHG) from Teertha village in Kundgol taluk received the Plant Genome Saviour Community Award, along with a cash prize of Rs 10 lakh, a citation, and a memento. The recognition acknowledges the collective's efforts to conserve more than 250 indigenous seed varieties and revive traditional millet-based mixed cropping systems across 30 villages in Dharwad's rainfed farming areas. The initiative began in 2018, when farmer Bibijaan Maulasaab Halemani brought together 14 other women to establish the collective. Its work includes promoting multi-cropping, maintaining community seed banks, and encouraging sustainable agricultural practices. Photograph: (The Hindu) According to Bibijaan, her interest in seed conservation came from her father, who also preserved seeds. Speaking to The New Indian Express in a report published on November 5, 2026, she said, “My father used to conserve seeds, and I too developed an interest and took to seed conservation.” She established the SHG and its seed bank in 2018, with the aim of making good-quality indigenous seeds accessible to farmers and encouraging traditional crop cultivation. A seed bank with more than 250 varieties The group's community seed bank preserves a wide range of indigenous crops, including: - Jawari (sorghum) - 70 varieties of finger millet - 25 varieties of little millet - Two varieties of browntop millet - 10 varieties of foxtail millet - 25 varieties of horse gram - 10 varieties of chickpea - 25 varieties of paddy - Three varieties of green gram - Around a dozen oilseed varieties - Several varieties of vegetables These varieties form part of the region's traditional agricultural diversity. The indigenous millet varieties, in particular, are adapted to local agro-climatic conditions and can withstand variations in weather. The collective has also worked to revive millet-based mixed cropping, in which farmers cultivate multiple crops together rather than depending on a single crop. According to the United Nations Development Programme's Equator Initiative, the group now supports more than 5,000 farmers across 30 villages. Its work includes promoting multi-cropping, maintaining community seed banks, and encouraging sustainable agricultural practices. Beyond seed conservation, the collective has expanded into agricultural processing and livelihood activities. It operates a solar-powered millet processing unit, which helps women produce value-added millet products. The initiative also works on livestock rearing, horticulture, and improving household food and nutritional security. Recognition for community-led seed conservation The national award is not the group's first recognition for its work. In August 2025, the United Nations Development Programme announced Bibifathima Swa Sahaya Sangha as one of the 10 winners of the Equator Prize 2025. The award recognised community-led initiatives working on nature-based solutions under the theme 'Nature for Climate Action', with a focus on women's and young people's leadership. According to the UNDP's August 20, 2025 announcement, the collective received recognition for its work combining traditional agricultural knowledge, seed conservation, renewable energy and climate-resilient farming. Each winning initiative was awarded $10,000. The initiative also works on livestock rearing, horticulture, and improving household food and nutritional security. Photograph: (National Commission for Women/Facebook) For the women of Dharwad, their work continues to centre on collecting indigenous seeds, keeping traditional crop varieties in cultivation and helping farming communities access planting material suited to their local conditions. Sources: ‘Karnataka: Bibi Fatima group bags award for saving desi seeds’ : By Subhash Chandra N S, Published on 5 November 2026 ‘UNDP Equator Initiative Award’ for Bibi Fatima SHG of Teertha village' : By The Hindu Bureau, Published on 9 August 2025

items.title: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s EU intentions: undogmatic consensus building is a sensible strategy | Editorial
items.blurb:
On treacherous political terrain, the government is right to want to proceed with caution and at a pace of its own choosing

During the 1980s and 90s, the French president of the European Commission, Jacques Delors, consciously pursued deeper EU integration via a gradualist approach that sought to minimise confrontation. Rather than focusing on ambitious end-goals, risking a showdown with some member states, Delors calculated that taking steps such as the creation of the internal market, in 1993, would eventually generate the momentum to go further. One thing would lead to another, in a logic of deeper union.

Mindful of the unique capacity of the Brexit debate to divide and polarise, Andy Burnham appears, for the time being, to be adopting a version of this strategy. On Friday, the prime minister rightly hailed the signing of a reset deal with the EU on food exports, emissions trading and youth mobility as a “good day” for the UK. He then reiterated that further discussion was needed on finding the right long-term relationship with Brussels.

items.title: Kemi is beside herself that Burnham is trying to salvage a Brexit deal. Can’t we all stop talking about it? | John Crace

Badenoch ends her anti-EU speech by calling herself ‘the leader of common sense’. Really?

When you’ve got David Cameron, Theresa May, Boris Johnson and Rishi Sunak saying you’ve got it wrong on Brexit, then the chances are Andy Burnham must be doing something right. These four are the former prime ministers that are largely responsible for the mess the UK is currently in. Lord Big Dave had never really given the possibility of leaving the EU much thought. The Maybot spent three years saying nothing more intelligent than “Brexit means Brexit”. Boris lied through his teeth to get his deal over the line. And as for Rishi? It’s hard to think of anything he achieved.

All of which makes life tricky for Kemi Badenoch. Because in an ideal world, Kemi would rather we all forgot about Brexit entirely. Not because it is going so well, but because it it isn’t. She would like you to believe that Brexit was nothing to do with her – even though she was a hardline Brexiter – or the Tories. Rather it was some kind of paranormal event that just happened to the country while the Conservatives were in power. Correlation does not imply causality and all that. In KemiWorld we would pretend that everything is more or less OK and that the noblest course of action is to live with the self-inflicted injury.

items.title: Haigh tells CBI that even US which is ‘hardly a hotbed of socialism’ has more public control of utilities than UK – UK politics live
items.blurb:
First secretary of state gives further detail on Burnham’s plans and says the government is not against the markets

The full text of Louise Haigh’s speech to the CBI is now on the Cabinet Office’s website.

In her speech to the CBI, Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, delivered one of the most detailed explanations we have had from a minister as to what Andy Burnham means when he calls for more public control of utilities.

Now I know the word privatisation can start an argument. So let me be precise. This is not about whether markets work. They do. Where there is genuine competition, as in telecoms, markets have given consumers choice and kept prices low while delivering infrastructure.

The social licence to operate must be won every day by building trust and having the best value, product or service. Where competition exists, it should be left to thrive, supported by our strong, independent Competition and Markets Authority.

To make the experiment work, successive governments leant on regulation, first to try to recreate competition from monopolies through a spreadsheet; then to manage what private markets would never price on their own, like the spare capacity that keeps the lights on; then to deliver social policy, treated as a free good because it went on the bill, not the budget.

Ofgem now has six times the staff it had in the early 2000s, almost three times the administrative budget in real terms, and a rule book more than six times longer. We’ve got a hulking, complex behemoth of a regulatory state. It satisfies no one. Not consumers, not investors. When you prioritise everything, you prioritise nothing.

items.title: Undoing Brexit is the right thing to attempt – but sadly, I can't see Andy Burnham pulling it off | Paul Taylor
items.blurb:
Brussels rolled out a warm welcome for the PM but toxic UK politics around rejoining have not gone away

Despite the beaming smiles and the symbolic triple handshake, the summit intended to reset the UK’s tortured relationship with the EU showed just how difficult undoing Brexit will be a decade after Britons voted to leave.

To be sure, Brussels laid on a warm welcome. Andy Burnham’s first summit with the heads of the EU institutions felt like the homecoming of an old friend who had been away too long, rather than a meeting to settle some awkward leftovers of a bitter divorce.
